items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: Following discussions at the
Business Committee, I seek leave for the House to adjourn on Thursday, 24 July and
suspend on Wednesday, 30 July at the conclusion of the last valedi ctory statement for
each day.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Leave is sought for that particular purpose. Is there any objection?
There is none. Leave is granted.
Regional Economies—Employment, Development, and Economic and Social
Inequality
1. Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE (Leader of the Opposition)  to the Prime Minister:
Does he stand by all his statements on regional development; if so, is the real median
weekly income for all people in the Gisborne/Hawke’s Bay region, according to the
New Zealand Income Survey, higher or lower now than when he took office?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes, and to the second part of the question,
I am advised that there is no official series that matches what the member is asking for,
but I can tell him from the New Zealand Income Survey that median weekly income
from all sources in the Gisborne and Hawke’s Bay region went from $500 in 2009 to
$506 in 2013. For people in paid employment, median weekly earnings in that region
went from $720 in 2009 to $756 in 2013.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Can the Prime Minister confirm the New Zeal and Income
Survey statistics that the Gisborne and Hawke’s Bay pre -tax real median weekly
incomes have fallen $61 a week —$61 a week —that over 2,000 more people are
unemployed, and that 843 people have left Gisborne since he took office?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: No, we do not accept that.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: After the Prime Minister has checked the Statistics New
Zealand website and found that those figures are correct, will he be prepared to consider
restoring the Gisborne to Napier rail line to encourage regional growth?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: No, I do not think that is likely. I think it is worth
remembering with the Gisborne to Napier rail line that it accounted for 2 to 3 percent of
freight in the East Coast. Ev en if revenue picked up, the service was expected to run at
an annual loss of between $5 million and $8 million a year —but we all know that the
Labour Party runs at a loss in so many areas.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: What does the Prime Mini ster say to the Waikato region and,
in particular, the 114 workers who have lost their jobs at Canpac in Te Rapa today, or is
he now a little bit sorry that he has got a so -called rock star economy where the bottom
has fallen out of the dairy market by one-third in just 6 months?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Once again, the member is wrong. The second thing I would
say is that 14,000 people have not lost their jobs; 14,000 more people have jobs in the
Waikato region. Fewer people are unemployed and th e unemployment rate has dropped
by 1.6 percent. Fonterra employs around 2,000 people in the Waikato region. Although
not every job can be guaranteed, I know they will be working hard to find jobs for other
19378 Questions for Oral Answer 23 Jul 2014
people as best they can. Thirdly, what I would say to the people of the Waikato is that if
you want to keep your job, vote National; if you want to lose it, vote Labour.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: If the Prime Minister will not give a straight answer today to
those 114 workers whose jobs are  on the line in Te Rapa, will he confirm today, as he
refused to do yesterday, whether he is happy with the current situation where half the
families in Kawerau live on less than $40,000 a year and a third of the town depends on
a benefit, but in other are as over half the families earn over $100,000 and less than 10
percent are on a benefit? Is that fair, Prime Minister?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I suspect that the position in Kawerau has been one that has
been in that kind of condition for quite a  long period of time. Secondly, one of the ways
to assist the people of Kawerau is to do what the Government is doing, actually—that is,
both in terms of the infrastructure we are developing around the country, making sure
we do not overtax our businesses with a capital gains tax as that member would, and
making sure we actually have a welfare system that readies people for work and expects
them actually to move into work, along with the other welfare reforms. If the member
really thinks that a $200 million  slush fund spent over 4 years is going to do anything,
then he needs to go and review all of his other policies. When he is finished with all
that, he needs to look—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! That answer is quite sufficient.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Why is he so negative about the regional development fund —
[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Why is he so negative about the regional development fund
when people actually involved in local government such as Lawrence Yule, president of
Local Government New Zealand, say that Labour’s regional development fund is a step
in the right direction?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I call the right honourable Prime Minister, insofar as there is prime
ministerial responsibility.

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I am not negative. If the member wants to see negative, he
should see the comments that his caucus colleagues make behind his back about the
member.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Will the Prime Minister say to the people of the Bay of Plenty
that he is prepared to support Labour’s forestry package, which has led Red Stag
Timber to commit to a 70 percent expansion of production, taking it to 1.2 million cubic
metres a year, or is he happy to export raw logs and close down timber mills across the
North Island and import our own timber back from China to rebuild Christchurch?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: A number of things: firstly, Red Stag Timber is a company
that has actuall y been expanding quite successfully over the course of the last 6 or 7
years without some random policy. The second point I would make is if the member
cares so much about forestry—does he? Does the member care about forestry and about
logs?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Just answer the question.

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: OK, here is an idea: let us go and pick up the thousands of
them lying on the West Coast and mill them. Oh, that is right —they do not want to do
that with wind -blown timber, but they wa nt some dodgy policy for Red Stag Timber.
[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Question No. 2, Dr Russel Norman. [ Interruption] Order!
The member Dr Russel Norman has every right to ask a question.
23 Jul 2014 Questions for Oral Answer 19379
Economy—Science and Research Funding, Export Sector, and Investment Focus
2. Dr RUSSEL NORMAN (Co -Leader—Green) to the Prime Minister: Does he
stand by all his Government’s policies?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Does he stand by his Government’s economic strategy to focus
on expanding simple commodity exports such as milk powder, raw logs, and minerals—
a pollution -based ec onomy—rather than investing in research, science, and
development to create a smarter, greener economy?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: The member is really away with the fairies if that is what he
believes, because in every single Budget since 2009 thi s Government has increased its
expenditure on science. This year alone we are spending $1.5 billion in that area. In
fact, the science and high -tech area is growing rapidly under a National -led
Government. So if the member thinks we are solely a commodity -based economy, he
needs to get his head out of the clouds and look at what is actually happening around
New Zealand. What I do know is when he goes around New Zealand and implements
the sorts of policies he would like to do, he will be sending most New Zea land workers
to the dole queue. I will be pointing that out to them over the course of the next 60 days.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Why is his Government planning to cut Government spending
in science and research by over 10 percent in real terms over the next 3 years?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: The member is making it up.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Has the Prime Minister actually read the Draft National
Statement of Science Investment —which the Government just issued, for the Prime
Minister’s benefit—which says that Government investment will be dropping from $1.4
billion in 2014-15 to $1.35 billion in 2017-18 in nominal terms, which in real terms is a
cut of 10 percent in 3 years?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: The member is misinterpreting the data. The correct data
represents what I have been saying, which is that the Government has been increasing
expenditure in science and technology every year. Even in the worst of the financial
conditions we have been doing that. That  is why you are seeing some of the stellar
results that are being delivered around the country.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: I seek leave to table a document from the Parliamentary Library
showing Government investment in science to drop by 10 perc ent in real terms over 3
years, and 21 percent—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The document has now been satisfactorily described. I will
put the leave. Leave is sought to table that—

items.speaker: Hon Steven Joyce
items.text: Mr Speaker—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Does the member want to speak to the point of order?

items.speaker: Hon Steven Joyce
items.text: I am just interested to know what that data is from. He said data
from the library, but—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member has described it. It is now over t o the House. It
was information prepared by the Parliamentary Library. Leave is sought to table that
document. Is there any objection? There is objection.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Does New Zealand’s prosperity lie in selling more milk powder
and polluting more rivers, or does prosperity lie in investing in people and smart, green
innovation—something that the Government is cutting, according to its own
documents?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: In relation to the last point, the member is wro ng, and he
knows he is wrong. In relation to the earlier points, in fact, New Zealand’s prosperity
lies in doing a combination of lots of things. There will be an increasing demand, I
suspect, around the world, particularly from Asian nations, for continue d commodities
19380 Questions for Oral Answer 23 Jul 2014
from New Zealand, but there is equally, as we can see, a rapid move up the value curve.
We are seeing that with UHT milks and the like. We are seeing it with nutraceuticals. In
the information and communications technology sector, generally w e are seeing quite a
significant expansion. We have had the manufacturing sector expanding month after
month after month. The member lives in a world where he wants to believe a few
things. Unfortunately, the reality does not actually fit with the narrativ e that he, in his
own little mind, wants to believe is true. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I will be reluctant to ask a member to leave the House, but if
the member continues to interject with that barrage, then I will be doing so.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: With regard to manufactured exports, is he proud of his
Government’s record of simplifying our export economy, given the 19 percent fall in
real terms of the value of manufactured exports since the National Government took
office? Real statistics, real facts—just try dealing with them, Mr Prime Minister.

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: OK, well, we will deal with the facts. Fifty billion dollars’
worth of goods was exported over the last 12 months out of New Zealand. I will tell you
the way to kill those exports markets. That is, one, to stop signing free -trade
agreements—oh, yes, that is the Green Party policy. Two—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! It is not necessary for the member to be commenting on
another party’s policy.

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. In relation to the answer,
it is actually germane if the member is going to ask a question about a specific point
about our strategy for growing the economy. It is quite fair and right, actually, to
contrast—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I have heard enough from the Prime Minister. On many of
the questions we have had so far, members themselves have asked for comment on
policies of the Labour Party and the Green Party, and in that case I will be perfectly
accepting of an answer that makes comment on those particular policies. But on this
particular occasion, the question did not raise any other political party’s policy. On that
basis, I am not accepting the answer.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Is t he best way to add value to our exports to simply produce
more and to pollute more, or is investing in manufacturing, information and
communications technology, and innovation a smarter, greener alternative; if so, why is
the Government cutting spending on  research and development and science, according
to the Government’s own predictions as confirmed by the Parliamentary Library
document that his members stopped me tabling?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The right honourable Prime Minister—either of those questions.

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: The member’s question was quite instructive, actually,
because his argument was that to produce more, you have to pollute more. On this side
of the House, we actually totally and utterly disagree with that, but it doe s show what
the member is thinking, and that is, of course, if you want to pollute less —which is
something we accept the Green Party wants to do —you have to produce less, and, boy,
will the Greens be producing less if they ever assume the Treasury benches.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: How does the Prime Minister expect New Zealand to move
towards a smarter economy when New Zealand’s investment in research and
development has barely lifted as a proportion of GDP during National’s Government,
and languishes at only 54 percent of the OECD average, and, according to Government
predictions, is going to drop even further?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: The member is wrong. I am not surprised that the member is
using dodgy numbers, because most of his policies are backed up by dodgy numbers—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Answer the question.
23 Jul 2014 Questions for Oral Answer 19381

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: But this is the way to grow the New Zealand economy, and
that is to follow the prescription that the National Government has been following in the
last 6 years we have been here. Have a tax system that actually encourages
investment—something that this Government has been doing. Sign free -trade
agreements so that we have better access to international markets —something that this
Government has been doing. Invest in science and innovation —something that this
Government has been doing. Invest in skills —something that this Government has been
doing. Invest in infrastructure —something that this Government has been doing. Make
sure our bu sinesses face less regulation and less red tape —something that this
Government has been doing. Make sure that our businesses face a fair carbon tax, not
something that is disproportionate to what is happening around the world—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! That answer now is quite long enough.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: If any of what he has just said in his answers this afternoon
is correct, how does he explain two things —[Interruption]—and, “Big Ears”, you can
help out as well—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Just ask the question.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Well, how does he explain two things, if any of that is true:
one, the growing nervousness of the National Party backbench, and, two, the internal
polls of the National Party showing him that it is well behind where it was this far out
from the 2011 election? [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I have a particular interest in listening to the answer.

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: If the member genuinely believes that the National backbench
is demonstrating nervousness, then what I think the member should do is look left,
because out there they are terrified, buddy.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Members will resume their seats. I am on my feet. Now, I
gather there is a point of order from the Rt Hon Winston Peters. It will be heard in
silence.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Look, I can not let a misnomer like that start running, and
the Prime Minister must not call someone “buddy” in the House.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member now will resume his seat because that is not a
point of order.
Economy—Credit Rating and Forecasts
3. JOHN HAYES (National —Wairarapa) to the Minister of Finance : What
recent reports has he received supporting the Government’s economic programme?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Earlier this month the credit rating
agency Fitch Ratings confirmed that it had revised New Zealand’s AA credit rating
outlook from stable to positive. This indicates the credit rating’s likely direc tion over
the next year or two. Fitch Ratings said that the Government’s fiscal consolidation and
track to surplus in 2014 -15 are increasing the resilience of New Zealand’s sovereign
credit profile, and it noted that the Government has a credible plan to l ift fiscal
surpluses in the years ahead and to reduce net core Crown debt to 20 percent of GDP by
2020. Fitch Ratings also said that New Zealand’s economic policy framework, business
environment, and standards of governance ranked among the world’s stronge st from a
credit perspective and warranted high-grade sovereign ratings.

items.speaker: John Hayes
items.text: In confirming the positive outlook for New Zealand’s credit rating,
what did Fitch Ratings say about New Zealand’s current and future economic growth
prospects?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: It noted that New Zealand’s macroeconomic record and
prospects are supporting its credit rating. It said that real GDP grew by 2.7 percent in
19382 Questions for Oral Answer 23 Jul 2014
2013 and is expected to increase to 3.8 percent in 2014. This will be supported by,
among other factors, reconstruction in Canterbury; dairy prices, which have moderated
but are still at elevated levels; and a house -building catch-up. Fitch Ratings noted that
although New Zealand’s average GDP growth over the past 5 years, a t 1.6 percent, is
lower than the median among AA rated countries, it was less volatile and was higher
than the 1.2 percent median growth rate among AAA rated countries.

items.speaker: John Hayes
items.text: What other factors did Fitch Ratings note in respect of its po sitive
ratings outlook for New Zealand?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: One of the factors Fitch Ratings noted was New Zealand’s
historical vulnerability around high net external debt and persistent current account
deficits. I am pleased to report that  both of these indicators have improved significantly
in recent years. For example, the unadjusted current account balance in the March
quarter was a surplus of $1.4 billion —the largest dollar surplus ever recorded —and the
annual 2.8 percent deficit is wel l under half the deficits of around 7 percent of GDP in
the 3 years to 2008. So our net international liability position has improved. It was 65
percent of GDP in March this year, well down from a recent peak of 85 percent of GDP
in early 2009.

items.speaker: John Hayes
items.text: And for my last question, what other reports has he received about the
state of the New Zealand economy?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I have seen one report claiming that Government debt is
larger as a percentage of GDP than New Zealan d had during World War II. This is
completely false. Gross Government debt is currently around 35 percent of GDP. At the
end of World War II it was around 150 percent of GDP. David Cunliffe has again
completely misled New Zealanders.
Regional Economies—Employment, Development, and Economic and Social
Inequality
4. Hon DAVID PARKER (Deputy Leader —Labour) to the Minister of Finance:
Does he agree that there are growing gaps among the regions  of New Zealand, making
the economy and society increasingly unbalanced; if not, why not?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: No, I do not agree with that. A
variety of data sugg ests the regions have led New Zealand’s recovery. Statistics New
Zealand regional GDP data shows that Bay of Plenty, Gisborne, Hawkes’s Bay, Nelson-
Tasman, Canterbury, Otago, and Southland, of course, all grew faster than the national
average in the 5 year s to 2013. The most recent ANZ Regional Trends survey shows
rural regions growing faster than urban areas, and just last week I received reports from
Queenstown, in my own electorate, of a significant boost from a long holiday by the
Leader of the Opposition. But if the member wants to talk down the regions, then I hope
he declares a crisis, because on recent established history every time Labour declares a
crisis, things come right pretty quickly.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Does he agree that whe n the top few percent own most of the
wealth the squeezed do not have enough to spend and invest and the economy will not
perform to its fullest potential until the imbalance is fixed?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: No. In fact, in respect of the dist ribution of benefits of
growth I can tell the member that the number of people on working -age benefits in
Greymouth dropped 5 percent in the last year. In Blenheim it dropped 9 percent. In
Napier it dropped 8 percent in the last year, and in Wanganui the n umber of people on
working-age benefits also dropped 5 percent. Those people are now enjoying the
benefits of more jobs and a stronger economy.
23 Jul 2014 Questions for Oral Answer 19383

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Then why is it that after 6 years, aside from Canterbury, the
unemployment rate is higher in every region of New Zealand than it was when he took
office?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Well, on “Planet Labour” there was no global financial
crisis—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Just answer the question.

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: —and the member should take that into account when he
uses those measures. Of course, in the real world, which is not where the Labour Party
is, there was a major recession and unemployment did rise rapidly. Fortunately, it is
now dropping consistently.

items.speaker: Tim Macindoe
items.text: Which regions have seen the strongest increases in economic
activity?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The most recent regional trend survey shows that the
strongest growth in economic activity in the March quarter was, in order, Northland, the
highest, at 3.4 percent, followed by Bay of Plenty, then Waikato, then Nelson -
Marlborough, then Otago, then the West Coast, and then Canterbury. ANZ reports that
Northland was also the fastest -growing region in the year t o March at 7.4 percent.
Business confidence is at a 9 -year high in the survey and the top two areas for business
confidence are Otago, despite the complaints of its civic leadership, and the Waikato.
As I said, the evidence tends to suggest that the regions have led the recovery not lagged
it.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Is his selective use of statistics because the latest Statistics New
Zealand figures on per capita GDP show that per capita GDP in the last year has gone
backwards, not just in Gis borne, Hawke’s Bay, Taranaki, Manawatū, Wanganui,
Marlborough, and on the West Coast but also in his own province of Southland?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: No, I do not agree with that. But what I do agree with is the
proposition that a significant  carbon tax, a capital gains tax, and water rules that mean
that every river has to be absolutely pure, will have dramatic economic effects on the
regions and they will all be negative. That is why the regions are turning up to meetings
all over the countr y, to tell us how determined they are to stop the Greens and Labour
taking over Government.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: How can he say that regional growth is not in balance when
according to the 2013 census the gap between median household income s in Northland
and Wellington has grown to around $30,000 a year?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I have not seen those figures, but that is a bit rich coming
from the party that complains because the Government put constraint on Public Service
salaries.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: I seek leave to table the per capita GDP figures from Statistics
New Zealand for the regions for the year ended 2013.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: If they are published by Statistics New Zealand, they are available
to be referenced.
Local Government—Rules Reduction Taskforce
5. MAGGIE BARRY (National —North Shore)  to the Minister of Local

items.speaker: Government
items.text: What recent announcements has she made about reducing red tape for
property owners?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: Our new Rules
Reduction Taskforce will weed out pedantic and loopy rules that frustrate ho meowners.
I constantly hear complaints from homeowners about rules brought in over years by
both central and local government that are confusing, onerous, and costly, even if they
are well intentioned. This task force will give New Zealanders an opportunit y to submit
19384 Questions for Oral Answer 23 Jul 2014
their ideas about which rules need axing. The group will then look at what should stay
and what should go, so that people can get on with the job of building and renovating,
without having to wade through unnecessary bureaucracy.

items.speaker: Maggie Barry
items.text: What suggestions has she already seen about pedantic red tape?

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: Is that the red scarf?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: No, she did not say red scarf. She said red tape. The
country has got more important things to worry about. In just a few hours yesterday
more than 400 comments had been made on the Stuff website by people frustrated by
loopy rules. I have heard everything, from people being told where they can put their
shower curtain, to someone being told thei r pool fence was not compliant because a
jasmine plant was growing up the side of it. I have even heard of a person being told
that they had to put windows in to let the light in, even though they had just installed a
ranchslider, but, of course, it was co nsidered a door. There is no doubt that every time
someone has to comply with one of these rules, it holds back what should be common
sense for a property owner to be able to do.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker . In the normal way, if the
Minister has been reading from official advice, I would like her to table that, please, and
in particular confirm—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Was the Minister quoting from an official document?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: No, I was quoting from a website.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I hope it is a point of order.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Further to the last point of order, an d I thank you for allowing
us to proceed, to get to the bottom of the Minister’s assertion—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Can the member come to his point of order.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Could the Minister please table the source regulation that she
was referring to, perhaps about the shower curtain?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! That is not a point of order.

items.speaker: Maggie Barry
items.text: What is the skill set that you are looking for for the people in the task
force?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: I have been thinking about people who might be of value
on this task force —people who know that they should not stand up and apologise for
being a man, for example—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: They are people who no longer think about red scarfs
actually being what is holding them back from getting their message across. Those
kinds of loopy—

Canterbury, Recovery—Lincoln University Rebuild and Lincoln Hub
7. Hon KATE WILKINSON (National —Waimakariri) to the Minister for
Tertiary Education, Skills and Employment : What investment is the Government
making in the recovery of Lincoln University?
Hon STEVEN JOYCE (Minister for Tertiary Education, Skills and
Employment): Last week I announced that the Government has approved in principle
to provide up to $107.5 million in additional capital funding towards the rebuilding of
Lincoln University’s science facilities destroyed in the Canterbury earthquakes. Lincoln
suffered very significant damage in the earthquakes, losing 40 percent of its academic
23 Jul 2014 Questions for Oral Answer 19387
floor space, including much of its facilities for science, teaching, and research. The
Government funding of up to $107.5 million is almost one -third of the projected cost of
the total campus rebuild, and will involve demolishing the badly damaged Hilgendorf
and Burns buildings, and replacing them with modern new facilities.

items.speaker: Hon Kate Wilkinson
items.text: Why is the Government investing in new science facilities for
Lincoln University?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: The Canterbury earthquakes did cause, as I said, very
significant damage to the university. It has been using tem porary facilities since the
earthquakes. And, of course, since the earthquakes, it has had a drop in student
numbers, as has Canterbury University. This funding will help the university with its
rebuild programme and get it back fully on its feet. Of cours e, the agricultural sector,
which is Lincoln’s area of speciality, earns New Zealand $36 billion in exports each
year, and the university is a leading player in the sector’s teaching and research, helping
to ensure increasing amounts of innovation in that sector. The new facilities will be a
huge asset to Lincoln, significantly assisting its recovery and student numbers, and, of
course, also providing opportunities for those export earnings to continue to increase as
productivity increases.

items.speaker: Hon Kate Wilkinson
items.text: How does the Government’s investment in Lincoln
University assist the development of the Lincoln Hub?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: The Lincoln Hub is a partnership between the university,
Dairy New Zealand, and a num ber of Crown research institutes. It will be an incubator
for research, innovation, and wealth creation in the agricultural sector, with one of the
highest concentrations of agricultural and environmental scientists in the southern
hemisphere working toget her to bring new ideas to market and develop new export
opportunities. Part of the Government’s agreement with Lincoln for this new funding is
the integration of its new facilities with the other major partners in the hub. The rebuild
of the university, to gether with the existing campus development plans of the research
institutes located at Lincoln, mean we have a unique, once -in-a-generation opportunity
to combine the physical operations of all these entities in one integrated campus serving
900 scientists, students, and industry.

year of reporting, which has  been remarkably consistent given the very early stages of

anything we have had in the past. It is helpful to schools, which can now identify early

succeed.

items.text: Obviously the Taranaki Daily News is something that we
all should be reading. Having said that, of course, the recorded crime rate is not on the
number of prosecutions; it is actually on the reported crime. I am sure t hat that member,
if he has a look at his notes, would find that I am correct and he is wrong.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: Does she accept that, as Minister of Justice, when she first
discovered there had been a misreporting of crime statistics in Counties Manukau, she
should have passed the information on and done something with the information to see
how it would affect her justice sector targets, rather than ignoring it because she was no
longer police Minister?

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: Well, absolutely not. This Government does not deal in
rumour and gossip. If, of course, we did, then I might start talking about that member
talking to the Sunday Star-Times—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I do not think the answer is going to assist the order.
23 Jul 2014 Questions for Oral Answer 19393

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: Will she accept that the combination of arbitrary targets and bonus
payments to senior  police officers is leading to manipulation and utter deceptive
conduct in relation to the recording of crime figures, and that New Zealanders can have
no confidence that crime is reducing, as the Government claims?

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: No, that is an outrageous suggestion to make —that the
New Zealand police would ever, as a body, engage in that sort of behaviour. The New
Zealand police are the finest police in the world, and I am proud to be part of a
Government that supports the police  and gives them the tools to do what they need to
do. They are fantastic. I am ashamed that that member would say it. He should be
saying sorry just like his leader always does.
Freshwater Management—Water Quality of Rivers
11. EUGENIE SAGE (Green)  to the Minister for the Environment : Does the
Government’s National Policy Statement for Freshwater Management require the 61
percent of monitored recreational river sites that are graded “poor” or “very poor” to be
safe for swimming?

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: The national policy
statement requires all fresh water to be at a level that experts tell us will protect aqua tic
species and human health. Beyond that, it does not set requirements on a river -by-river
basis. They are national standards, and above the bottom lines, it is for each community
to decide what goal will be set in each case.

items.speaker: Eugenie Sage
items.text: Does she think it acceptable that these sites, chosen because they are
popular for swimming, are actually too polluted to safely swim at and that her weak
bottom lines will not make a difference?

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: Well, the member is quite wro ng in her assertion. First of all,
what we are talking about here is 94 sites out of a total of 425,000 kilometres of
waterways, and even fewer than that actually measuring as potentially at risk, and even
those are generally safe for swimming most of the time.

items.speaker: Eugenie Sage
items.text: When the Minister said that we need to manage popular lake and
river swimming spots for swimming, did that include the Waikirikiri Selwyn River on
her doorstep, which has multiple sites that are unsafe for swimming, and w hich her
national bottom line—that rivers have to be fit only for wading and not for swimming—
will not clean up?

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: What we have said consistently is that we trust local
communities to know which sites they want to protect for s wimming and to take the
necessary steps to do that. I back my community to make decisions about what it wants
to protect for swimming, and I am not going to impose costs on every community, every
business, and every household in New Zealand because the Gre ens want every drainage
ditch to be managed as if it was a swimming pool. It is ludicrous.

items.speaker: Eugenie Sage
items.text: What advice has the Minister had on the cost to local authorities of
multiple regional plan processes and court litigation that result f rom her decision to
leave it to councils to determine whether rivers should be clean and safe for swimming,
rather than having a national bottom line?

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: What I can tell that member is that, of course, at the moment—
and the situ ation that that member’s party was quite happy with when it was in a
position to do something about it —these decisions are entirely for councils, the
difference being that at the moment the Government provides no assistance, no national
consistency, and no  standardised science. That is what we have done and that will
significantly reduce the time and the cost on each community in making those
decisions. I am just surprised that member does not back local communities.
19394 Questions for Oral Answer 23 Jul 2014

items.speaker: Eugenie Sage
items.text: Can the Min ister confirm that she is abandoning annual reporting on
recreational river quality in the suitability for swimming indicator report because the
National Government is trying to hide the bad news?

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: That member well knows that we are moving to the most
comprehensive system of environmental reporting that this country has ever had, under
which water quality will be reported twice in every 3 years —a system, by the way, that
did not exist in 2007 when the Greens were propping up a Labour Government that
picked and chose what information it wanted to give to the public.
Aotea Conservation Park, Auckland—Establishment
12. SIMON O’CONNOR (National —Tāmaki) to the Minister of Conservation:
When will the new Aotea Conservation Park in Auckland announced on Sunday be
formally gazetted and opened?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: I have made the decision to
proceed with the Aotea Conservation Park proposed by local MP Nikki Kaye last
October, but the formal gazettal and opening has been delayed by the recent storm
damage to tracks and facilities on the island. The decision to proceed with the new park
enables the tracks and facilities to be rebuilt to the higher standard and to recognise the
new Aotea Conservation Park. This is expected to cost $2.5 million and will be
completed over summer. The Department of Conservation’s intention is to open the new
park early next year.
Simon O’Connor: How does this new park compare with others in Auckland, and
were any changes made during the process of consultation?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: The new park is 12 ,109 hectares, and it will be the largest
Department of Conservation park in Auckland. It will be similar in size to the two
regional parks in the Hunua and Waitakere ranges. The significance of this park is that it
is the largest forest that is possum and  stoat - free anywhere in New Zealand. It is
particularly rich in trees like pōhutukawa, kauri, and tree daisy and birds like kākā and
brown teal, and it has the largest population of black petrel anywhere in New Zealand.
There were 2,800 submissions on th e proposal. On the basis of representations from the
Auckland Council, I decided to exclude a small area that it required for a small
cemetery.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I move, That the
House take note of miscellaneous business . In the general debate this afternoon I think
we should, on this occasion, start with apologies. I think we should start with apologies.
I would like to l ead off with a few apologies. No. 1: I am sorry for being a man. Has
that been done before? [Interruption] Oh, OK, I will try this one—I will try another one.
I am sorry for having a holiday.

items.speaker: Hon Bill English
items.text: That’s been done before, too.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Oh, OK. I am sorry for wearing a red scarf. [ Interruption]
No. Oh, I know —I am sorry for having a moa resuscitation plan. That has got to be
new—that has got to be new. [ Interruption] No? Another one —for you, Mr Spea ker: I
am sorry for having a secret trust. That would be—

items.speaker: Hon Bill English
items.text: No, that’s been done.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: That has been done? I am sorry for not telling you about
my secret trust, Mr Speaker. Has that been don e? And, most of all, Mr Speaker, I am
sorry you found out about my secret trust. I have another one: I am sorry for being
tricky. That has been done before? Well, we have seen a lot of apologies, but from now
23 Jul 2014 General Debate 19395
on I am going to be straight up. I am going to stick to the Labour knitting. That is what I
am going to do, with the exception of the scarf.
This train is leaving the station. It has left a few times before, but this time it is
definitely leaving the station. This is my team. This is my team, except, to be fair, Shane
Jones. He is not on the team any more, no. Dover Samuels —he is not on the team any
more. Andrew Little —he is not really on the team any more. Damien O’Connor and
Rino Tirikatene—they are not really on the team, because they crossed the fl oor. But
aside from Shane Jones, Dover Samuels, Andrew Little, Damien O’Connor, and Rino
Tirikatene, this is my team.

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: What about Annette?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Well, actually, not Annette. She is not really on the team ,
either, or Phil, because they work hard. They get out in the country, working hard.
Clayton is not really on the team. To be fair, I do not think he has ever been on the
team. Trevor is not so much on the team—not really on the team. But aside from Shane,
Dover, Andrew, Damien, Rino, Annette, Phil, Clayton, and Trevor, this is my team.
This is my team. Well, actually, you have got to exclude Grant, to be fair, because Grant
is not really on my team, or David Parker—he is not on the team—or Chris Hipkins. He
is not on it.
I am not sure about Stuart Nash. I think he is on the team. He must be on the team
because he said: “It wasn’t me.” He said in the Hawke’s Bay Today  that he denies the
claim that he criticised Cunliffe, although, on the other hand, he als o said this: “I must
admit when I read it [the newspaper quoting the party source], apart from the swearing,
it sounds a little bit like me.” “It sounded like me.”, Mr Nash said. And he said that he
was not the source and that the comments could have come from “any of the 15,000
members who were out putting up hoardings in the rain or delivering pamphlets in the
cold or this sort of carry-on”.
So this is my team, except for Shane Jones, Dover Samuels, Andrew Little, Damien
O’Connor, Rino Tirikatene, Annett e King, Phil Goff, Clayton Cosgrove, Trevor
Mallard, Grant Robertson, David Parker, Chris Hipkins, Kelvin Davis, Stuart Nash, and
the 15,000 members of the Labour Party who would have said what I did not say in the
newspaper. That is my team. It is game on —it is game on. The Labour Party is
marching to the election, united as a single team. That is what is going on. And, of
course, we now have the regional growth policy, which we share with the Greens.
The regional growth policy—here it is. It is out today : one, put a capital gains tax on
every productive business; two, have a carbon tax at five times the current price; three,
introduce big levies for the use of fresh water; four, restore a national awards system,
which would force regional employers to pay what they pay in Auckland; five, stop any
more trade deals; six, clamp down on the dairy industry; seven, clamp down on the oil
and gas industry. And then, the coup de grâce, when that has all been done and the
regions have all fallen over, is to give them a $200 million slush fund to make them feel
better. The Labour Party should apologise for that, as well.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: For a time during that speech
from Mr Joyce, I thought that his underpants were on too tight. New Zealand First
wishes to raise an important matter going directly to competent, accountable
Government. We are aware of serious complaints against a Mr Bryan Staples and his
companies operating in Christchurch on a range of matters. Reliable information has
come to us of a long list of fraudulent practices carried out by Bryan Staples and his
various companies. Mr Bryan Staples has used his companies to defraud , mislead, and
cheat people —[Interruption]—and it is not a laughing matter, I say for Jami -Lee
Whyte’s benefit. We want to set out the nature of the serious concerns that we are
19396 General Debate 23 Jul 2014
raising today, which have been raised with authorities, which have clearly fai led to act
to apprehend and stop this man’s so-called business activities.
The main activity of complaint was his companies’ purporting to carry out technical
inspections of properties for earthquake compensation purposes, which neither he nor
his companies and the people they employed were qualified to do.

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: That’s right.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: It is not a laughing matter, Mr Brownlee. They were
paid, but did not actually provide genuine techni cal reports. The reports supplied were
useless. His companies and Mr Staples also employed a number of subcontractors who
carried out work on damaged properties. Mr Staples and his companies got paid but the
subcontractors did not, I say to Mr Jami-Lee Whyte—

items.speaker: Hon Members
items.text: Ha, ha!

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: —Ross, rather. We understand that he and his
companies had no intention of paying numerous subcontractors.
Mr Staples carried out work and registered for GST as a business, and he accepted
payment for work, which he then issued GST invoices for, but he did not file returns nor
pay the GST. It would also appear that Mr Staples directly instructed his company and
his employees not to pay GST. It appears he employed the old tact ic that whenever
people demanded payment, he began to pretend that there was a dispute. Then Mr
Staples would use every delaying tactic possible, never intending to actually defend any
claim nor pay any part of it.
He also brought in Filipino workers under contract. There are two issues. How did he
get these people by Immigration New Zealand and the Ministry for Business,
Innovation and Employment, and how did he influence those two departments to allow
these people in? It is clear from the evidence that h e had no intention of treating these
immigrant workers lawfully, which raises the issue of why, before they obtained
immigration status, these two departments did not do due diligence to avoid such
breaches of our employment law. The second issue is that h e simply did not pay these
Filipino workers. He left them in dire straits. He and his companies failed to make
Inland Revenue Department returns or make payments of PAYE tax for the Filipino
workers. He instructed his company employees not to file PAYE ret urns and not to pay
their PAYE taxes. The list goes on, but in the time available those are the main matters
that we have got to say today.
My concern is that if New Zealand First is aware of them, what on earth is going on
with the Minister and the releva nt Government departments? The Inland Revenue
Department, the Ministry for Business, Innovation and Employment, the Serious Fraud
Office—what have they been doing? There has been no firm action from these agencies.

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: You were backing Mr Staples 12 months ago.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: I ask Mr Brownlee to stop bleating and explain what
you have not done. Why do you not get off your broad half -back and do something for
these people down there who are  not being paid and being robbed blind as immigrants?
The so-called pro-immigrant party could not give a tinker’s damn about them.
Mr Staples is the man, of course, who has been painting himself on TV as the
modern Robin Hood. Well, he is halfway there. H e is taking from ordinary people, but
he is not giving to the poor. He is Robin Hood in reverse. Mr Brownlee and Mr Dunne
and Mr Joyce—what have you not done and why have you not done it?
I want to close with this statement about an MP who is now escaping  scrutiny by
Parliament and by the media because she has gone to ground. You see, she misused her
credit card.
23 Jul 2014 General Debate 19397

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: Oh, no, no. Mr Key made the call on Sunday nigh t
because there were blatant financial irregularities that neither she nor the National Party
could reconcile. That is a fact. The second thing is that Mr Key said that her breaches
were unintentional and that he was “not aware of further misspending”. The n he
claimed that he did not have any advice on that. That is false. He does. I want to know
why someone can just say “I’m not standing at the next election.” and there is no
punishment, no chastisement. She just says “I’m not going to stand.” and goes to
September being paid full pay as an MP and then for 3 months after that.

items.speaker: Andrew Williams
items.text: Five more months.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: For 5 more months —someone who has badly
breached the parliamentary rules, far beyond  $200, the lousy amount that those
Ministers over there are shouting about. You have got the Minister of Police and all
sorts of Ministers, all the way to the Prime Minister, giving assurances. Let me tell you
about Mr Key’s statement. He said: “I pledge greater transparency”—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member’s time has expired.

items.speaker: TE URUROA FLAVELL
items.text: Speaking of individuals,
not that  I do want to, I note that Colin Craig wants to be an MP, and Colin Craig
introduced his latest attempt at a headline by calling it a wild and crazy idea. He is not
wrong there. But more than that, the Conservative Party’s policies to get rid of the
Māori seats, shut down the Waitangi Tribunal, and implement one law for all are
ignorant, are dangerous, and are not welcome in the political system of our country. It is
election time and once again political parties that are in trouble choose to pull the race
card out of the hat to scratch the redneck part of our society. I can tell you that Māori
are sick of it, as is this nation.
Politicians have a responsibility to educate and inform, not act in such a way as to
provoke racial division and tension. New Zeal and needs leaders who understand that
indigenous rights are human rights, that cultural diversity and representation are good
for democracy, and that the constitutional basis of our nationhood lies in Te Tiriti o
Waitangi. I for one am proud to say that th is has been the consistent call of the Māori
Party since we first entered this Parliament.
We want all aspiring members of Parliament to understand that dedicated Māori
electorate seats distinguish our democratic process here in Aotearoa. Actually, we mus t
not forget that the first race -based law was introduced in 1858 and was called the
English Laws Act. It was one single statute that imposed the culture, customs, and
conventions of Britain on all New Zealanders. The Māori electorate seats are a
conversation between Māori and the Crown —not for the majority of New Zealand
making a decision for a minority.
As the Chief Judge of our court Taihākūrei Durie said: “Like the Treaty of Waitangi,
the Māori parliamentary seats stand as an enduring symbol of their c onstitutional
status—and historic statements of principle, like symbols, are essential tools in re -
building our national identity.” Ever since the English Laws Act we have been in catch -
up mode, trying to build a more representative Parliament that encompa sses all New
Zealanders, not just those with a British passport. The Māori seats have been an
important mechanism to try to protect and develop Māori interests.
Colin Craig needs to know that his party has no right —no right—to step in and try to
take the rights away from tangata whenua. Only tangata whenua have the right to
determine what is in our best interests. As parties to the Treaty, Māori should at least be
guaranteed representation in the organs of kāwanatanga. In the past Labour tried
measures lik e the Foreshore and Seabed Act, and it opposed the United Nations
Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples —and look how that went down. We
have been down that track before and we do not want a repeat run. The reality is that the
19398 General Debate 23 Jul 2014
New Zealand Governme nt, after advocacy from the Māori Party, signed up to the
Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples in 2010 and it is here to stay.
In fact, the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples states
that indigenous peoples have the right to participate fully, if they so choose, at all levels
of decision making in matters that affect their rights, lives, and destinies through
representatives chosen by themselves in accordance with their own procedures. So we
are where we should be, and  we should not have to put up with the divisive rants of
some.
We have had over 170 years of attempts at assimilation, from various politicians and
parties, and we continue to suffer from the consequences of those sorts of policies
today. The old assimila tion policy is hidden behind a few new terms and slogans, such
as “one law for all”, or “we are all one people, we are all Kiwis”, and even “some of my
best friends are Māori”. But the intention is the same, and we know all about that. In
this day and age there is no place for political leaders who know nothing about our
history and know nothing about us. There is no excuse for being ignorant and we, the
people, will never ever tolerant policies that aim to take away from us, without our
informed consent. T hat will not happen. Māori must make decisions about Māori
representation.

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: It is always a pleasure to follow Mr
Te Ururoa Flavell. He i s always a thoughtful speaker, and I think he has put a lot of
effort into what he has had to say today. I would like to say, however, that I am actually
feeling a little bit sorry for David Cunliffe.

items.speaker: Dr Cam Calder
items.text: No!

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: Yes, I am, because I know he is sorry for everything. But
what I am really sorry about is that poor old David Cunliffe —we saw it today; the lack
of discipline in his party. Where was the shadow Leader of the House? Was he popping
up and down? No, it was David Parker trying to take on that role. Then we had Trevor
Mallard trying to take on the role. Then we had Grant Robertson finally getting himself
out of his seat to raise a point of order and to try to take over the role. What we saw
today, in question time, were leadership bids going on for post this election.
Poor old David Cunliffe. You would have to wonder. He has had so much advice
given to him today. I think the press was pretty good today. Members of the press told
him to stop saying sorry. Actually, he cannot. He has started now. He is sorry for being
a man. Well, I can tell the House that 49 percent of New Zealanders are men. They
should not be sorry for being men, just as someone like me, who is a mother, is not
sorry for being a mother, even though there are some mothers who kill their children, or
beat them, or whatever. I am not sorry for being a mother. What I am sorry for is that
they are mothers. That is what David Cunliffe should be saying. Instead, what he said to
all men in New Zealand was that they too should feel ashamed.
He was also sorry to be on holiday. Well, he should just stay away, really. He is sorry
for not knowing what was happening in the polls. He would be the only one in New
Zealand who was not aware. H e is sorry that he has got Trevor Mallard on the moa
farm. I think it is fair enough that Trevor Mallard wants a moa farm. It would be a bit
funny if he had a duck farm, would it not? He is sorry he has got a do -up in the elite
suburb of Herne Bay. He is s orry that Grant Robertson spent 3 years of parliamentary
time talking about the Government Communications Security Bureau (GCSB). It is not
an issue, I have to say, that anyone in the Papakura electorate has raised with me. That
is probably because we have  got an army camp in the town, and they actually like
having some help from the GCSB.
I would also say to that member —what is his name? Williams from New Zealand
First—Mr Williams. I cannot remember his first name, sorry. He has got a policy about
23 Jul 2014 General Debate 19399
drunkenness in a public place. I bet he is sorry too. I bet he is sorry. I just wonder
whether his leader thinks that Parliament is a public place, or else he will be sorry as
well.
Labour has got a man ban. Its members are sorry about that. But I thought, apart
from the man ban, what was really good, what I really loved, was the cosmetics ban.
Who did they have to run it? Trevor Mallard. What would Trevor know about
cosmetics? What would Trevor know? I see Su’a William Sio laughing away, because
he would have th ought that there are lots of other people in the Labour Party who are
much better qualified than Trevor to run an anti-cosmetics campaign.
Then we would have to say that David Cunliffe could also be sorry for undermining
Phil Goff when he was leader. He c ould be sorry for undermining David Shearer. But I
think most of all he should be sorry for being so jealous of Shane Jones that he drove
him out of Parliament. That is what he really should be sorry about, because Shane
actually has charisma and a personality, and he has got followers, which poor old David
Cunliffe does not have.
But over on this side we are not sorry at all. We are really proud of the hard work
that we are doing. In the justice sector we are so proud of the police and of corrections
staff. I am proud of my colleagues, I am proud of the courts, and I am proud of my
Ministry of Justice. I am proud of the team that we have —the Attorney -General, the
Minister for Courts, the Minister of Police, and the Minister of Corrections. I am proud
of the fact that we have a team that is united and working for New Zealand, not working
for the Labour Party flunkeys over on the other side of the House.

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: For the National Government members, of course, it is
politics as usual this afternoon, along with their lame jokes and their nasty little gibes
that they are coming out with. Meanwhile, the regions lie bleeding —meanwhile the
regions lie bleeding —and they laugh. Anne Tolley finds that fu nny. Well, Mrs Tolley,
go and face those 114 workers in Hamilton who have had news today that their jobs are
going. Laugh in their faces, and see how that one goes. On this side of the House we are
talking about the issues that matter to people—the issues that matter to people—because
those people, under that Government, are losing their jobs. It is not only those people
but their families who will be affected. There are 114 more jobs going from the
Hamilton economy, as if we can afford that. This comes on the back of 130 jobs going
from New Zealand Post—yes, a Government-owned entity. One hundred and thirty jobs
had already gone from New Zealand Post in Hamilton —yes, a Government -owned
entity—from their distribution centre. About 200 jobs have gone from the  Huntly mines
over the course of the last few years —yes, a Government -owned entity. The
Government is pulling out of town in Hamilton and it is hurting. It is hurting our
economy. But there are other jobs that are going as well —120 jobs went a few months
ago from the Goodman Fielder factory in Frankton, the Hutton’s plant, and 180 jobs are
set to go next year from AgResearch in Ruakura, Hamilton —yes, a Government-owned
entity. The Government is pulling out big time in our city. Unemployment is going up,
and the economy is suffering as a result.
The members over there have gone a little quiet. Well, so they should because in the
Waikato region unemployment is going up —it is going up. In March 2013, when you
could have argued that the global financial crisis was still at its height, there was 5.6
percent unemployment in the Waikato region. In March 2014, when we were supposed
to be climbing out of the global financial crisis, there was 7 percent unemployment in
the Waikato region. It is going backwards, and th at is under the National Government.
Unemployment is rising and GDP per capita is going backwards in that same region.
Yet the Waikato region should be humming. It should be humming. It is coming off the
back of the highest dairy prices that we have ever h ad in this country. In the Waikato
19400 General Debate 23 Jul 2014
region that should mean plenty of jobs and better economic activity. But under this
sorry Government, with its lack of a regional economic development plan, guess what?
Unemployment is going up in the Waikato. It is the d airy giant region of the world, and
this Government cannot get it right.
What is the Government doing in the Waikato region, in an area that should be
humming, with the high dairy prices that there have been? Well, it is pulling out the
agricultural scien tists from the Waikato region. How dumb is that? This is from a
Government that has no strategy for delivering to regions’ strengths. When those 180
jobs come out of Ruakura, there will be more money out of our local economy and there
will be more jobs dow n the track after that. As it is, there are 114 jobs under threat
today at Canpac in Te Rapa, in the electorate of Tim Macindoe. He asked a question at
question time today about regional economies, and not once did he mention the 114 jobs
going in his own electorate, because he does not care. He does not care about those jobs
going, and I think that is a disgrace. But with those jobs going, $6 million in spent
wages will come out of the local Hamilton economy every year, from losing those jobs.
Do you know what is going to happen next under this Government? There will be more
jobs from our local economy after those wages stop being spent there.
A Labour-led Government has a plan for regions like the Waikato. We just yesterday
announced a plan to put $200 mi llion into the regions to ensure that we can actually
create jobs, improve economies, and take care of the regions. Well, they may joke while
the regions lie bleeding, but in the Labour Party we are making a plan for regional
economic development so that w e can actually improve those economies, get jobs in
there, help families, and make a difference.

items.speaker: Hon CRAIG FOSS
items.text: I would, first of all, like to
acknowledge my co lleague, my good mate the Hon Chris Tremain, CJ, who has
obviously just run a quick triathlon or something in the last 40 minutes. It seems like
just yesterday that the two of us turned the bay “blue”. CJ turned the good seat of
Napier to National, after 5 2-odd years of Labour representation —a feat that will go
down in history. He has done such an awesome job, with his passion for and love of our
province and Napier. He is just a top man. Also, his achieving the status of Cabinet
Minister, the first Napier MP to be a Cabinet Minister —CJ, you’ve done really well,
mate.
The joint sheer drive between myself and Chris for an even better Hawke’s Bay,
being relentlessly positive for our beautiful bay, has been recognised by the good people
and the voters in the Hawke’s Bay, as the party vote for National across the Hawke’s
Bay has increased in each and every single election since. In fact, it has increased to the
point where my opponent and the Opposition candidates up there this time are not even
campaigning for the party vote. They are not even on the list this time. I have got plenty
of stories I would love to tell. I have got only a few minutes, but I also know that Chris’
valedictory is pretty soon and he will have the last word, so I had better not wind him up
too much.
Of course, there has been interesting attention on the regions in the last few days —
fair enough—but I would just like to note that like the rest of New Zealand, the region
of the Hawke’s Bay is actually performing very, very well. It has awes ome
opportunities in front of it and good leadership, and there is commitment, faith, and
confidence in our region. We will continue to absolutely fly.
Interestingly, with Labour’s announcement yesterday, I would just like to note that
the last time Labou r paid any attention to the province of Hawke’s Bay or the region
was actually when one David Cunliffe as health Minister sacked our district health
board. Incidentally, the health board has since been essentially re-elected and essentially
unchanged, twic e. I do note that his last commentary on the Hawke’s Bay was his
23 Jul 2014 General Debate 19401
famous quote where he described our health board of the time —remember, this is the
man who wants to be New Zealand’s Prime Minister —and he overreached. Yes, there
was a situation in the Hawke ’s Bay. He overegged it. He overreached, and basically he
stuffed it up. He described the good members of the Hawke’s Bay District Health Board
at that time as a nasty mess of self-perpetuating provincial elites. That is from the mouth
of the person who wants to be the Prime Minister for New Zealand and the regions. We
should note that that was the last time he paid any attention.
Incidentally, he is now busy saying sorry for being a man. He is saying sorry for
wearing a scarf. He is saying sorry for being  sorry. He is saying sorry for all sorts of
things. But you know what? It would not take much, but he is yet to apologise and say
sorry for what he did to the Hawke’s Bay District Health Board. Yes, it was a few years
ago, but, quite frankly, that shows th e nature of the man who wants to be the Prime
Minister of New Zealand. If anyone wants to know what he is like under pressure, have
a look at how he reacted, have a look at the paperwork, and have a look at the affidavits
of what he did to the Hawke’s Bay District Health Board.
National is continuing to promote initiatives across the country and in the regions.
Hawke’s Bay is one. Across the Hawke’s Bay, due to our policies, we have seen 27
more full-time equivalent doctors. We have seen 116 more full -time equivalent nurses
across the Hawke’s Bay just in the last few years. There is about a 100 percent increase
in foot patrols of police on the beat in eastern districts in 2013, and crime is low. There
has been an investment of $2 million in the clean -up of rivers in the Hawke’s Bay, and
13,322 Hawke’s Bay homes have been insulated because of the good policies of this
National Government.
I acknowledge again my good mate CJ Tremain. Hawke’s Bay is in a much better
state because of the work you have done and because of your passion for our province.
Cheers.

items.speaker: Dr RUSSEL NORMAN
items.text: Together it is possible to build a
cleaner, fairer, smarter New Zealand —a New Zealand in which our rivers are clean
enough to swim in again and our beaches are safe from oil spills, a New Zealand in
which every child has enough to thrive, and a New Zealand that is built on a smarter,
greener economy that benefits every one of us.
However, this vision of a richer country is not the New Zealand that National has left
after 6 years in Government. Under National, two -thirds of our monitored river
swimming sites are now so polluted that they are considered unsafe for swimming.
Swimmable rivers are a birthrig ht of our children, but the opportunity to swim in our
sea and our rivers is not the only birthright that National is denying our children. There
are 35,000 more children in severe poverty in New Zealand now than when the National
Party was elected to Government. Fifty percent of all New Zealanders have seen no real
increase in their net income at all, once housing costs are taken into account.
It is really no surprise that only a small number of New Zealanders are getting ahead
under this Government. Nati onal’s pollution economy is jobs poor. It favours low -
value, simple commodities over high-value innovation. Evidence of National turning its
back on an innovation economy is its plan to cut Government research and development
spending by 10 percent in real  terms over the next 3 years, according to its own
statistics. Three more years of National is not a safe option for New Zealand. Three
more years will put our environment, our children, and our economy at risk.
The Green Party has a comprehensive plan fo r a cleaner, fairer, smarter New
Zealand. We will make our rivers clean enough to swim in once again. In Government,
the Greens will establish a protective rivers network to permanently safeguard our most
precious rivers. We protect the best of our habitats and our landscapes in national parks;
we can do the same for our rivers. We will also keep our wild rivers wild by not
19402 General Debate 23 Jul 2014
building any new dams on our wild rivers. We will put in place proper water rules that
ensure that no New Zealand river is allowed to d egrade further and that our rivers and
lakes are clean enough for swimming once more.

items.speaker: New Zealanders have a choice
items.text: the Green Party’s plan for rivers that are clean
enough to swim in, or National’s plan for polluted rivers that are so polluted that even i f
you touch them, if you dip your toe in them, you have a serious risk of a serious
infection. I know which option I prefer.
Persistent and damaging poverty and inequality, another legacy of this Government,
grate with the sense of who we are as a nation.  But child poverty can be eliminated. We
need to have a plan, and the Green Party has a credible and costed plan to ensure that all
New Zealand children have enough to thrive. For a start, in Government, the Green
Party will extend the 20 hours early child care subsidy to every 2 -year-old. For parents
of the 40,000 children aged between 2 and 3 years who currently miss out on the 20
hours of funding support, this will mean they will be up to $95 a week better off.
At the same time as reducing the cost of ea rly childhood education to parents, we
will embark on an ambitious plan to improve the quality of early childhood education
for all our children, starting with restoring full funding to those centres that employ 100
percent trained teachers. Good quality early childhood education has a profound lifelong
impact on a child, one the Government simply does not understand. It can mean starting
school ready to learn and being in a position to get the most out of education. Research
shows that investing in early c hildhood education is one of the most effective
investments a society can make. For every dollar spent on early childhood education,
between $3 and $16 is returned. The Greens will invest in our kids so they can thrive,
and we will get them out of National’s poverty trap.
It is time also to get serious about building a smarter economy. If we want to provide
for our social needs and aspirations, we need to be at least as innovative as other
nations. That means making high value -added manufactured goods and services, and
not simply selling commodities like raw logs and milk powder, as is the National
Party’s plan. To kick start a transformational shift in how our economy creates wealth,
the Green Party will invest $1 billion in new Government funding into res earch and
development, unlike cutting it, as the Government proposes. We will also fund an
additional 1,000 places at tertiary institutions for students of engineering, mathematics,
computer science—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member’s time has expired.

items.speaker: IAN McKELVIE
items.text: That speech by Russel Norman was
without a doubt one of the most boring obituaries I have ever heard in my life. It was, in
my view, a gross misuse  of facts to run down rural New Zealand. It will not help our
cause. Regional New Zealand has faced its share of challenges in the past 40 years as
our population and economy have adjusted and acclimatised to change. The progress we
have made in the past 6  years under this Government is now having positive effects as
the buoyant world food market and demand lifts farmer confidence, optimism, and
ability to invest further in their industry. New tourism initiatives such as the Forgotten
World Adventures, cycl e trails, and walking tracks are appearing. The growth in these
businesses is leading to new opportunities for growth and investment in our regions.
The announcement in Levin last week by Ministers Joyce and Guy of an ambitious
plan to double my region’s agribusiness production by 2025, after some early feasibility
studies by mayors Margaret Kouvelis and Jono Naylor, who of course is the very good
candidate for National in Palmerston North, is another example of a proactive
Government determined to enable our regions. The interesting point to note is that this
agribusiness strategy is not all about increasing agricultural production, as the previous
23 Jul 2014 General Debate 19403
speaker would have us believe. It includes science, tourism, and the manufacturing
sectors, which complement our traditional farming activities.
Fresh water is critical to t he future of our country and the Rangitīkei, as tourism and
farming rely heavily on our pristine environment for our futures. The Government has
invested heavily in this area, adding a further $12 million to it in the Budget just passed.
This is on top of $350 million already committed to lake and river clean -ups, and the
$101 million already spent in this Government’s term. The Rangitīkei has three of New
Zealand’s major rivers—the beautiful Whanganui River, which is a beautiful river and a
great tourism opportunity for that region and certainly for the electorate of the member
sitting next to me; the Manawatū, the subject already of a considerable amount of clean -
up funding and, of course, New Zealand’s first river accord; and, of course, the
Rangitīkei, one of the best fishing rivers in New Zealand.
National has also developed the Agricultural Greenhouse Gas Research centre in
Palmerston North in partnership with AgResearch and nine other partners. This, as it
progresses, will add significantly to our con tribution to climate change measures and
increase our productivity. The other key measure adding to the productivity in our
region announced in the past few weeks is the increase in the regional roading spend. In
my region the replacement of the Whirokino trestle bridge south of Foxton, which is
over 1.5 kilometres long, when completed will take some 30 kilometres off the trip for
the average heavy truck from the central North Island to Wellington —30 kilometres.
Add this to the Ōtaki to Wellington roading i mprovements, including the capital
expressway and Transmission Gully, and the benefit to the central North Island will be
significant. The Tongariro and Whanganui National Parks are a huge resource for the
people of Rangitīkei. Winter sports, walking, boating, and cycling are growing at a great
rate. On top of this, we have a net migration inflow of people into the region in the last
month, an increase in population, and a drop in unemployment. Despite the wailings of
Labour and the Greens, this Government has made significant investment in the future
of regional New Zealand, and we are seeing the benefits in our region.
One of the key challenges that our rural councils face is managing demand for access
to our vast network of paper roads, and careful thoug ht will need to be given to the
future management of these. The Walking Access Commission has started this work but
there is much to do and funding will be required in the future to complete this work.
I want to briefly acknowledge the huge role that Tari ana Turia has played in the
Māori communities throughout my region, and congratulate her as she leaves this place
on making such a great contribution to the welfare of so many. I want to briefly note the
work done by Ngāti Apa in the south of the Rangitīke i, particularly in the social field,
and now, with the acquisition of Flock House and the subsequent partnership they have
formed to farm this historic property. It will be the forerunner of things to come and
perhaps the trendsetter to help unlock the vast potential of Māori land in New Zealand.
In Taumarunui, the Kōkiri Trust is achieving fantastic results in areas such as health,
education, work projects, and aged care under the leadership of Christine Brears —
another initiative from, and thanks again to , the great work of Minister Turia. Finally, I
want to acknowledge the time that my north -western neighbour, Shane Ardern, has
spent working for the people of the north of the Rangitīkei. In the hill country of the
North Island, boundaries are obscure and challenges are the same wherever you live.
Thank you.

items.speaker: MEKA WHAITIRI
items.text: Tēnā koe e Te Kaiwhakahaere o
te Whare nei, ā, tēnā tātou katoa ngā mema o te Whare nei i runga i te kaupapa
whakahirahira o tēnei wiki, te wiki o tō tātou reo, o ō tātou rangatira. Nō reira, tēnā
tātou katoa.
19404 General Debate 23 Jul 2014
[Greetings to you, Mr Speaker of the House, and to you all, members of this House,
in regards to the matter of significance during thi s week, the week of our language and
of our chiefs. So acknowledgments to you all.]
The country deserves better. The regions deserve better. As a proud member of
Ikaroa-Rāwhiti, I think Ikaroa-Rāwhiti deserves better. This is a time and a place to put
our plans out so that the people of this country can see what type of leadership we
require in this country. Ikaroa-Rāwhiti, to remind our members, is about 657 kilometres
in distance, it takes about 9½ hours to drive there, and for the last 2 weeks, I cannot
escape the reality that is confronting the constituents whom I come to this House to
represent. I have visited towns like Gisborne, Wairoa, Napier, Hastings, Dannevirke,
Masterton, and Upper and Lower Hutt. In those 2 weeks I got to move around. I got to
speak with mayors of local councils, I got to speak to providers of social services, and I
got to speak to deliverers of business support throughout my electorate. I can quite
categorically tell you that there is struggle throughout Ikaroa-Rāwhiti.
On the weekend I was doorknocking in Elgin, a place that I am sure the current
member for East Coast, Anne Tolley, has visited often. The feedback from behind the
many doors that I knocked on was that people want sustainable, well -paid jobs in places
like Gisborne. So who are we to believe? Is it this Government, which is operating on a
two-speed economy, one for the rich and one for the people like those in Elgin whom I
doorknocked on? They are being ignored and they are being denied the basic rights to
look after themselves and their families. That is what we have with this Government.
