This is what it has delivered to the people of Elgin, of the Maraenuis, of the Pōmares —
the people whom I come to this House to represent. So Government members may get
up and say t hat the economy is doing well, but get into those suburbs —Ms Tolley, I
invite you to go to Elgin and doorknock and hear what they say, and in Kaiti.
I invite Mr Craig Foss and our departing member Chris Tremain to go and
doorknock in Flaxmere and Maraenui. You will hear for yourself —those people are
struggling. They are struggling, but they want jobs. So I come to this House, I listen to
what this Government is offering to grow real jobs in the regions, and I hear nothing. I
hear absolutely nothing . There is no hope for the people of the constituency that I
represent. I come here and I hold you to account, because what I see is nothing. They
are not even getting the bare basics of a well-paying job.
This is what Labour will do. We will develop regi onal growth plans in partnership
with local government, businesses, and iwi to identify opportunities and barriers for
growth and work in groups to overcome them. We will make an initial investment of
$200 million over 4 years in a regional development fun d, for projects that will create
jobs and growth. We will support manufacturing in the regions through the research and
development tax credit, accelerated depreciation, and our monetary policy upgrade. Yes,
we will. We will ensure that Government bodies b uy from Kiwi manufacturers
wherever possible. Let us put our Kiwi businesses ahead of overseas interests. We will
redirect capital from housing speculation into productive investment. We are going to
appoint a regional development Minister at Cabinet level . That is how serious Labour is
about our regions. That is right —a regional development Minister at Cabinet level. We
will integrate the regional development fund with a national ports strategy and regional
transport investment, and we will invest in upgra ding regional information and
communications technology.
We have also got plans for our young people in the regions, who are crying out for
more education, more training, and more employment. I have seen in my electorate the
closing of Government departments.

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.text: What is Labour’s policy solution for
everything? Talk it down, say how bad it really is, and then throw some money at it.
23 Jul 2014 General Debate 19405
That will do it —that will absolutel y do it. Oh, and have a Minister. Labour members
say “Let’s form another committee. Let’s have another Minister.” Who is that going to
benefit? Oh, yes, that is right—it is going to benefit themselves.
Do you think—or does one think; thank you, Mr Assista nt Speaker—that after flying
in over South Canterbury’s beautiful water storage facility, the Ōpuha Dam; the highly
productive dairy factories, one under full operation, one just about to be commissioned;
and the most beautiful farms in South Canterbury, w ith grain stores glistening down
below and new sheds everywhere, including milking sheds, and landing at the Timaru
airport, and this happened last week, David Cunliffe apologised to South Canterbury for
how badly the region is doing? And as he crossed the  brand-new $20 million Kurow
bridges, with their own cycle lanes, creating 150 jobs regionally, on the way through the
reinvigorated towns of Kurow, of Otematata, and of Ōmārama, following the $3 million
Alps 2 Ocean Cycle Trail, do you think that Mr Cunli ffe apologised to the locals for the
new business opportunities and the incredible new tourist traffic that is now running
through the region? And do you think after he recovered from his 2 days—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Many times the member has
brought me into the debate. You cannot mention “you”, being the Speaker.

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.text: Thank you so much —thank you so much for your help, Mr
Assistant Speaker. And do the Assistant Speaker an d the members of the House think
that once Mr Cunliffe did recover from his 2 days in beddy -byes with his man flu, he
enjoyed all the magnificence that Queenstown offers, from the restaurants to the
magnificent high life to the skiing? Some of my spies reported to me that some time last
week there was seen on the slopes of Cardrona ski field a man in a red scarf desperately
trying to be noticed. But do you think that—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.text: Oh, right. Thank you so much. Thank you so much. It is just that I
am so enthusiastic about the topic, I cannot help but try to include the Assistant Speaker
in the conversation, but I will not do that any more. But does one thin k that Mr Cunliffe
then apologised to the people of Queenstown for how well their local economy is doing,
with the expansion of the Queenstown airport and with the commitment of Air New
Zealand to bringing tourists both domestic and international into the region? And do
you think he apologised to the wineries?
Do you think —to the House —that David Cunliffe, when enjoying a Pinot noir or a
little Pinot gris, perhaps, for his cold, apologised to the wineries and said how awful it
was for them? And what about the cherry producers, the pip fruit producers, and the
apple producers, who are producing so much that this Government had to respond by
increasing the Recognised Seasonal Employer numbers and, in fact, creating a new
seasonal worker programme down south t o assist New Zealanders into the region and
into work?
You see, what we are having to do with Central Otago is have programmes to bring
workers into the regions. Unemployment is so low in Central Otago and the whole
region is so productive that we need pr ogrammes to bring people into the region. There
are jobs, all right. There are jobs in Central Otago, all right, and we are creating them.
David Cunliffe should apologise. David Cunliffe should apologise because the South
Canterbury and Otago regions are doing just fine.
Things do not feel so hollowed out when the Winter Games NZ or the Queenstown
winter festival are in full swing, or when the BMX world championships or the Wānaka
triathlon festival are all go —all supported by what? All supported by this G overnment.
Things do not feel hollowed out to the 11 Otago companies supported by the Venture
Investment Fund, or to the initiatives in the meat and wool industries through the
Primary Growth Partnerships, or to the towns of Queenstown —or what about Ōāmaru
19406 General Debate 23 Jul 2014
or Dunedin city, which have been supported with their ultra -fast broadband upgrade?
And what about the hundreds and hundreds of small businesses that now benefit from
the Rural Broadband Initiative and the New Zealand Trade and Enterprise capability
development programme?

items.speaker: PAUL GOLDSMITH
items.text: We have got valedictories coming this afternoon
from excellent National members of Parliament. I am staying, Mr Prime Minister. We
have got Cam Calder,  and we have got Hayes, King, Tremain, and Wilkinson, all of
whom have made great contributions. It is true that John Hayes has been the most
difficult to handle on the Finance and Expenditure Committee —much harder than any
of the Opposition members—but nevertheless he has made a great contribution. I notice
that the players from the Parliamentary Rugby Team are here to support Cam Calder,
and I put my hand out to you. Diversity of background is the strength of the National
Party, and these people who are g iving their valedictories today are capable people who
have other options to go to once they have made their contribution in Parliament, and
they do not have to hang around well past their use -by date. In their second to last week
of Parliament they will be reflecting on their contributions.
Of course, there will be many other people in this Chamber here today who are in
their second to last week of Parliament, but they do not know it yet. The people are
sovereign, and it could befall any of us, but I fear  that some of our colleagues on the
other side of the House will not get a chance to deliver their valedictories. Mr Muldoon
used to say that so -and-so was “a hard old dog to get off the porch”, and that is true of
Winston Peters, there is no doubt. Who kn ows whether he and his interesting collection
will be back after the election, including that fellow with the two letterboxes? I worry
about the members on the other side in the Labour Party. I worry about my cousin
Moana Mackey. I worry about Clayton Cosg rove, my good friend. All of them are in a
great deal of trouble when it comes to the election, even David Parker, whom I have
worked with in a collegial manner in the Finance and Expenditure Committee. Anybody
on the Labour Party list has something to worry about.
I have been very busy in the Epsom electorate, working hard to build up the party
vote. Like every other candidate in this party I am working to lift the party vote, because
that is the one that makes a difference. I would just like to say to La bour to rein in that
guy who lives in Parnell who keeps pinching my signs. I know who he is. When I am on
the doorsteps in Epsom, I hear deep concern about the potential for things to go wrong
if a Government comprising Annette Sykes, John Minto, Laila Har ré, David Cunliffe,
Metiria Turei, Russel Norman, and Winston Peters veers off in all sorts of directions
after this election. They are very concerned about the prospect of Asenati Lole -Taylor
overseeing the Reserve Bank. They are terrified of John Minto b eing the Treaty
negotiations Minister. Metiria Turei, said in this House that work is a trap, that it does
not pay enough, and therefore people should not bother —just imagine if she was in
charge of welfare. It is all too terrible to contemplate.
Why, when this country is heading in the right direction, guided by a strong, stable,
united, and sensible Government, and when there is so much work to be done, would
anybody put it all at risk by leaping into the unknown with this motley crew? How can
the country put its trust in David Cunliffe and the team when they cannot even organise
a decent picture of him for the soft profile piece in the Dominion Post this morning?
Did they not see that the photo they sent to the Dominion Post had him squatting beside
a ra bbit, in shorts that were clearly far too small and inadequate for the task? I
encourage you to have a look at that. That is what worries people. That is what worries
people.
The Labour prescription is bad enough. It is overturning the Reserve Bank
consensus, it is slapping a new tax on every productive business in this country, and it is
23 Jul 2014 General Debate 19407
effectively nationalising the electricity sector. That is bad enough, but if it scraped back
into power, it would not get to dictate what happens in this country. It woul d have to
give something to the Greens. Imagine what the Greens would demand, aside from their
massive carbon tax and aside from making farmers uncompetitive. What would Labour
give to Hone Harawira? It would have to free Mr Dotcom. It would have to give f ree
stuff to everybody, and that is why this country would be in a terrible state.
I am very proud of the record of this Government over the past 6 years.
Fundamentally, it has been about working to create an environment in which New
Zealanders can thrive and will only do well and will only be in the position to afford all
the sorts of things that we value —quality health-care, superannuation in old age, world-
class education, and support for the vulnerable —if we have an internationally
competitive economy. Of course, what is internationally competitive is a moving target
and it requires constant improvement not just by exporters but throughout the economy.
The debate having concluded, the motion lapsed.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: The Business Committee has
determined that the congratulatory messages following each member’s valedictory will
be held at the end. There are a number of valedictories today. I ask that we move from
member to member with their valedictories and we make our congratulatory messages
right at the end. There will be a bell at 2 minutes to go.

items.speaker: Dr CAM CALDER
items.text: Six years ago when I came into Parliament, some
queried why. Why has he come in? Does Parliament need yet another doctor? When I
announced my intention to step down, again some queried: “Why him? Surely some
mistake? Parliament is losing too many of its doctors.” There was no talk, as far as I
know, of McCully having any incriminating photographs.
I have had many different roles in my life. Building roads, and a scrub -cutter in “the
Naki”, Territorial Force soldier, dental surgeon, businessman and entrepreneur, medical
doctor in accident and emergency, and a clinical research director for a private
company—to name just a few. I have enjoyed them all. I have enjoyed them all, but at
this point I would like to place on record that serving and working as a member of
Parliament in New Zealand has been the best job that I have ever had. A huge amount of
work, work of extraordinary variety, and I have relished every day!
Though long viewing the prospect of life in the political milieu with the utmost
distaste, I sought the chance to stand as a National candidat e in 2008 because I was
extremely concerned about the future that my children would inherit if New Zealand
continued down the track it was then on. Back in 2002, upon returning from living
overseas with my family, I was shocked and disturbed at what I foun d in New Zealand.
I was shocked and disturbed at the consequences for my children, and, indeed, all New
Zealanders, if the myriad of challenges facing New Zealand was not addressed more
comprehensively and more intelligently.
As I saw it, I had three choices. I could return to live overseas, but I am a proud New
Zealander, so that option did not appeal. I could stay and do nothing other than groan
and grumble, but that did not appeal, because I believe that if one does not like
something, one should do one ’s best to change it. The third option was to stay in New
Zealand, to work to make it better, and to push my ideas for change on to the agenda.
The choice was obvious —I joined the National Party. It was a huge pleasure to be
selected to stand for National in the 2008 election in the vibrant and diverse community
of Manurewa.
19408 Valedictory Statements 23 Jul 2014
As a party we have never claimed to be perfect. We do not have a magic wand and
we cannot change things overnight. But, having come into Parliament, I was proud to
set up my office in Manurewa and work within the community and on behalf of that
community over the ensuing years. I was able to face that community in 2011, knowing
that everything we had said we would do as a Government, we had done —and more!
We are getting it right in Manu rewa, we are getting it right in my colleague Kanwal
Bakshi’s electorate, Manukau East, and in Māngere, we are getting it right for New
Zealand.
In my maiden speech—and it seems only a few weeks ago—I observed that a society
is judged by how it protects t he most vulnerable. It has been a huge pleasure to be part
of a Government that has protected the most vulnerable through the worst recession the
world has known in 75 years. More of our infants are getting immunised, more of our
young people are able to participate in early childhood education and are being screened
for the precursors of rheumatic fever, over 300,000 homes have been made warmer,
drier, and healthier, crime is at a 20 -year low, and tens of thousands more elective
surgical procedures have been improving New Zealanders’ quality of life every year. At
the same time, our economy has been among the strongest -growing economies in the
OECD, and the growing economy has led to tens of thousands more jobs in the last year
alone. More and more New Zealanders are being educated and are acquiring the tools to
fill those jobs and to unlock the ability and potential that lies within them all.
In this House I have noted in the past that no Government can legislate aroha. No
Government can legislate love, bu t through careful formulation of policies and
legislation, we are succeeding in wrapping services round the most vulnerable and the
less well loved. People need something to believe in and someone to believe in them.
The people of Manurewa and in communiti es all over New Zealand have seen the
results of this Government believing in them, and they are responding.
It has been a huge pleasure for me in Manurewa to see Pacific matai and Pacific
church leaders wearing that blue T -shirt and wearing the blue rose tte in our community
of Manurewa. The door has always been open, but now more and more the Pasifika
community is seeing evidence of the Government’s belief and walking through that
door.
As Nicolas Sarkozy said when he sought the Presidency of France “Ens emble tous
devient possible” —together, all becomes possible. He got elected, but he could not
bring l’Hexagone together, and he did not win another term. This Government has
worked with all New Zealanders, and the results speak for themselves. I am proud t o
have worn the blue jersey and to have been part of a team that is reshaping the mesh in
many different levels and areas and making our country a better place to live.
What of my own personal goals and dreams on coming into Parliament? The concept
of servant leadership has always resonated with me. Every morning when I look in the
mirror—which I do not do for long, given what confronts me —I ask myself: “Have I
done the best I possibly can to honour the hard work and commitment of all those folk
whose work on behalf of the National Party led to my working here and, indeed, have I
done the best for all New Zealanders?”. I am pleased to say that the answer is generally
yes, but from time to time I have found myself a bit puffed. I have unbounded
admiration fo r our Prime Minister, whose ebullience and mastery of detail remains
unmatched and whose workload is a log scale above that of anyone else in this House.
In my maiden speech I outlined areas of special interest to me. Among them were
tackling New Zealand’ s growing incidence of obesity, the need for more marine
reserves, and a prostate cancer awareness programme for New Zealand men. I soon
learnt some fundamental truths of Parliamentary life. Few things move fast. As the
French say “Petit à petit l’oiseau f ait son nid” —little by little, the bird makes the nest.
23 Jul 2014 Valedictory Statements 19409
One can plant seeds in soil, but the soil receiving the seed may or may not be fertile.
The idea might lie there quiescent for ever, or receive a burst of interest from an
unexpected quarter and suddenly flourish and be accepted. Certainly one never achieves
anything in this House alone, and success truly has a thousand fathers.
I am gratified to note that the Government has made progress in all the above special
interest areas that I mentioned in my maiden speech, but today I make a call for more
resources to be devoted to proven measures to combat the alarming incidence of obesity
in New Zealand. The cost of such interventions will amply repay themselves in
substantially reduced health care costs and  in thousands of New Zealanders living
longer, healthier, more productive lives.
My call for New Zealand to adopt a genuine progress indicator and my plan to
encourage distributed power generation from renewable sources fell on stony ground.
However, areas where other seeds I planted fell on more fertile soil include measures to
control low-ball share offers, the change to the right -hand rule, and a bill to make it an
offence to carry a high -power laser pointer in a public place without reasonable excuse.
My Summary Offences (Possession of High -power Laser Pointers) Amendment Bill
unanimously passed its Committee stage in the House on 25 June, and I am hopeful it
will pass its final reading later this evening.
On my lapel I wear the White Ribbon. This is a statement of my stand against
violence towards women and children. Domestic violence —men against women,
women against men —is a major challenge for New Zealand and a blot on our nation’s
escutcheon. I have been proud to be a caucus champion speaking all ove r New Zealand
on this Government’s determination to reduce the staggering number of our children
harmed each year.
Adolescent sexual and reproductive health and rights is another concern of mine. It is
an important area for consideration in all countries,  including New Zealand, and it is
possibly the most effective area for intervention by a donor country in a developing
country. In 2013, as a member of the New Zealand Parliamentarians’ Group on
Population and Development, I visited the Solomon Islands. Th e purpose of the visit
was to meet with key parliamentarians, policy makers, and key regional leaders in
sexual and reproductive health and rights to encourage scaled -up action to address these
issues in the Solomon Islands. Family planning and investment in this area is also the
most cost -effective investment a country can make towards its own sustainable
development and the well-being and empowering of its women and children. It is also a
fundamental human right. However, despite decades of international agreement on the
need to ensure universal access to family planning, progress in the Pacific has been slow
and inequitable.
Following my visit, upon returning to New Zealand, I wrote a discussion paper
entitled Adolescent Sexual Health and Reproductive Ri ghts in the Solomon Islands—the
unmet needs . I forwarded this to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade. I am
delighted to report that the feedback I have received suggests that in future, more of
New Zealand’s aid to the Solomon Islands will be used in  addressing these unmet
needs.
One comes into Parliament passionate, with a host of good intentions, but one must
also have a plan. The passion has never left me, and I am grateful that in looking back
on my time in Parliament I have been able to progress  my plan to further many of the
projects in which I have had a particular interest. At this stage I wish to acknowledge
the unanimous support my member’s bill has received from across the House and note
for the uninitiated that despite the theatre of question time, there is an enormous amount
of cooperation in the House, especially in the select committees. I particularly wish to
acknowledge the collegiality of all members of the Education and Science Committee,
19410 Valedictory Statements 23 Jul 2014
which I have had the pleasure to chair, and t heir willingness to work towards the
common good. It is just as well, as otherwise one could be worn down by the relentless
negativism that sometimes seems to pervade “Planet Parliament”.
Being an MP can be a lonely role. May I thank my family —Jenny, Carl a, and
Leisha; my brothers, Rob and Don; my sister, Julie; and my sister -in-law, Wendy —
whose steadfast personal support has always been there, though I am sure my brother
Rob has never voted for the party I represent, as many of the Opposition can probably
testify.
Talofa lava and fa‘afetai ma soifua to Telea and Fati Menefata, who have cleaned
Bowen House from the day I arrived and have always had a cheery smile and greeting
every morning. The parliamentary messengers —always ready to help and keep me
hydrated during the debate. I could almost use you now! My Manurewa secretary, Jenny
Collins—Jen came to me having worked for the Prime Minister. She is hugely
experienced, capable, and ever -helpful. I will miss you, Jen. Jamie Lee Burns, my
parliamentary secr etary for many years —safe travels overseas, Jamie. The Pride, the
Zephyrs, the O group, Dave Knowles, and my oldest mate, Lou Borok, have always
been there for me.
It is a great pleasure to see my old parliamentary colleague and friend George
Hawkins, lon g-serving Manurewa MP, and Jan up in the gallery. George, there is a
gathering tonight in the National Party caucus room —I am sure you will feel right at
home.
My friends from all over the House —go well, and I hope our paths cross in the
world. My mates i n the Parliamentary Rugby Team —a pack of good bastards. We won
the Parliamentary Rugby World Cup in 2011. Good luck in 2015.
Finally, I wish to record and place on record my deep appreciation for the long -term
and steadfast support of Manurewa activists Richard and Penny Laughty.

items.speaker: The old adage is undeniable
items.text: you have got to get into it before you get out of it. I
have been in it for two terms. It has been my whole life and all -consuming. I look now
to a life free of the strictures of a party whip, where I  can attempt to create my own
reality again. Thank you. Je ne regrette rien. Kia ora. Adieu. Farewell.

items.speaker: JOHN HAYES
items.text: This afternoon I come to say farewell and
to share a few final thoughts with you, my colleagues, and the Wairarapa community.
But first I want to thank the Wairarapa, Tararua, and Central Hawke’s Bay
communities, who three times elected me as their representative, each time by a greater
margin.
It has been a pr ivilege to have represented the people of the Wairarapa for 9 years —
it actually feels like 9 long years. It has been an experience that few of us get. No one
arrives here as an electorate MP without the support of many people, too many to name.
Some of them are here today. Thank you for coming.
I particularly want to acknowledge the late John Falloon and the late Juliet Hensley.
You departed too soon. I would never have made it here without your support. I want to
acknowledge John and Helen McFadzean, Sue Perry, Snow and Di Peterson from
Waipukurau, and Bernard Cleary, my kneecapper in Carterton. I acknowledge Keith
Hancox in Masterton, Richard Ellis in Pahīatua, Alister Plimmer, Stephen Kerr, and
many, many others, including my family Emily, Neve, Corrin a nd Luis Cunha up in
Kuwait and Matthew, Louise, Edward, and James Hayes, and especially Helen, who has
carried the brunt of long absences and my distractions. They have tolerated, not
approved, my being here.
Being an MP is not a job; it is an all-consuming life, and constituents deserve no less.
I am deeply indebted to Yvonne Payne in my Masterton office for 9 long years, and to
Janet Castell in Waipukurau, Rebecca Algie and Maureen Fenemor in Dannevirke, and
23 Jul 2014 Valedictory Statements 19411
the wonderful Emily Broadmore here in Parliament. There are many others like Paul,
Jane, and Mike at In Style Travel, Lou and Fiona at Capital Travel, and AJ at Lamb -
Peters Print in Greytown, who consistently made the impossible possible. Stan and the
late Nola Mangin have been superb neighbours, who without any fuss covered all those
things I was never around to fix, like the cows jumping the fence. Thank you. I would
not have survived here without your support. I need to apologise to the crew of the
Maranui—Captain Povey, Doug, Mike, and Andrew—for never being around when you
were short of crew.
Nine years have passed really quickly —almost a quarter of a working life. It has
been an interesting time. My friend and sounding board John Schnellenberg told me  in
2005 that I would develop a carapace. I had never heard of the word, but I can say now,
Schnell, that you were right. Politicians need a tough outer shell. Mine formed pretty
quickly when Michael Cullen whacked Finlayson and me around this Chamber one
afternoon.
I guess Parliament reflects our collective character and personality as a country. I am
no saint—no, I am not. Much of my first term here was spent reflecting on why I had
come. The atmosphere was toxic, not helped by a Speaker who was shrill a nd screamed
and by loopy committee chairs Pettis and Yates. Visits to parliaments in Denmark and
Sweden showed that parliamentary debate can be respectful, focused on issues, and
without narcissistic tone. Better behaviour in debates might encourage more m embers
of the community to come here and make a contribution. It might also arrest the decline
in the numbers of people who are voting.
I have brooded about our inability as a society to be more generous of spirit and
accepting when people get something w rong. The media, especially, fall over
themselves to beat up on anybody who buggers up—that is a Papua New Guinean word.
“So what?” you say. Well, I think the “what” is the question. Why would anybody
expose themselves to public life when the risk of a mis take is the public pillorying,
which inevitably follows? We collectively pay a price in not creating an environment
conducive to attracting more good leaders to Parliament. We could move our country
forward further and faster by focusing on what is importa nt; we bog down by arguing
with each other.
For more than 10 years the Wairarapa electorate has been trying to progress a couple
of irrigation schemes. It is a simple task to collect and store water that falls at the wrong
time of the year and then to use  it in the summer drought, but very little progress has
been made. Why? Is it leadership that is wanting? Yep, sometimes. Are Resource
Management Act requirements a constraint? Yep. Are Māori demands a constraint?
Sometimes they can be. Are nimby issues the problem? Yes. Well, let us be up front and
be clear that affected landowners will be fairly compensated for their land and the
disruption. Irrigation is the quickest way to grow our national income, and the whole
country wins.
It is difficult to fathom why simple, sensible, straightforward concepts have become
so difficult to implement. Were I New Zealand’s next Prime Minister, I would ensure
that the next Parliament got rid of a plethora of unnecessary legislation and excessive
regulation. Three years i s not long enough. This year’s election is going to cost
taxpayers $27 million, together with the time they have invested in MPs, who are going
to be distracted by parliamentary campaigning. Were I Prime Minister —and do not
laugh, Brendan; it is not too la te to nominate —I would promote a 4 or 5 -year term to
spread the cost over more years. Doing so would give Parliament a more reasonable
time to implement its programmes.
Colleagues from across the House —and Cam has just said it tonight —often say that
Parliament provides a wonderful experience. Having spent time here and in the Foreign
19412 Valedictory Statements 23 Jul 2014
ministry, my curiosity is satisfied. To those contemplating a political career, I will say
two things: if you have got kids, do not come near the place, because they are going  to
be short -changed; and if you want a really fascinating job, head to the Ministry of

items.speaker: Foreign Affairs and Trade. The big advantage
items.text: there is no election every 3 years.
Besides, foreign affairs ministers come and they go.
Constituent work is rewarding. F ew beyond the beltway understand how
Government works. That is where I have tried to add value. The Labour candidate for
the Wairarapa dropped a leaflet in my letterbox the other day proclaiming that he should
be my member of Parliament because he had been  compère at the Golden Shears
competition this year. I have no doubt that that requires some skill, but not the sort that
is going to make him a competent member of Parliament. I doubt the community will
elect a candidate who has so little experience and e xpertise. People who live and work
in cities assume provinces work like the cities they live in. They do not. Much of my
time has been spent bridging that gap. I have often felt like a scribe in an Indian bazaar
drafting letters for people. But there is a satisfaction from securing good outcomes and
seeing common sense prevail.
The campaign to keep Mākōura College from closing in 2006 was a tough battle for
an Opposition MP, but the outcome, keeping the school open, was a victory for the
Masterton communit y. That issue taught me the critical importance of school
leadership. It is great to see the school’s roll today in a very different place to the
projections of ministry officials, who used to walk up my drive on a Sunday morning to
beat me up —the same off icials who wanted to close the school rather than address 6
years of Education Review Office reports pointing out dysfunctional relationships at
senior levels in the school. I acknowledge and congratulate Mākōura’s outstanding
principal Tom Hullena. He has  more than doubled the school roll, topped the country’s
National Certificate of Educational Achievement results, and in the last 6 weeks
received the Prime Minister’s recognition for Excellence in Leading - Atakura Award,
here last month.
The residence status of many Pacific families is a concern. Too many Pasifika people
have irregular immigration status. They make no demands on social welfare —I see
them in my electorate —but they live in fear. Their children do not easily sit in school
and they do not ac cess health care. These families are often desperate. They are
vulnerable to being ripped off by unscrupulous lawyers and others who charge fees and
deliver no results for them. It is a large but hidden problem. I urge Pasifika people to get
appointments w ith your MPs after the election, because they can help you regularise
your status without charge.
When constituents have sought help, my driver has been a simple test: is it fair?
When the answer was no, then I have always gone into bat. In provincial New  Zealand
interpersonal issues are held much more intensely than in our big towns. People are
inclined to stop talking to each other. If they only would talk to each other, most
problems would dissipate. The impact of the Horizons One Plan proposed for the
Tararua a couple of years ago would have been that it removed $62 million each year
from the local economy in the Tararua area. Bringing people to Parliament for a meal
and a libation in my office afterwards was a formula that generally got people talking to
each other. They then took responsibility and established frameworks for sorting out
their problems. They got to common-sense outcomes.
I think that economic and social progress in provincial New Zealand will happen
only if we who live in provincial ar eas take responsibility for our own affairs. No one
owes us a living. Those who think —and I am talking Wairarapa at the moment —that
Wellington-based ratepayers are going to subsidise activity in the Wairarapa are at best
misguided. They do not live on my p lanet. No one owes us a living. Air New Zealand
23 Jul 2014 Valedictory Statements 19413
demonstrated that a few months ago when it ended the air link to Auckland. That is why
I worked so hard with others to secure the restoration of a financially sustainable air
service between Masterton and Auc kland. Eighteen people came to a meeting on
Monday at Masterton’s town hall. As we speak contributions are now being put into a
trust account held by accountants Amy Kerr and Associates. Subject to an undertaking
to improve the runway, I am confident that an air service based on an Air Chathams
Metroliner with Wairarapa livery will resume in September.
It is not possible to win on every issue. I spent a year trying to advance a plan to turn
Masterton’s old hospital into an integrated family health centre. At the time the
recession was in full swing, and the proposal offered 70 immediate jobs and about 50
full-time positions when completed. Two letters from Māori asked for the site to go into
the land bank. Despite an assurance from a colleague, Pita Sharple s’ clout was greater
than mine and the building went into the land bank. After Opus International
Consultants’ evaluation a local Māori leader told me 4 months later that they no longer
wanted the complex. I have always stood the ground for Māori on issues  like the seabed
and foreshore and Treaty settlements. I suggest, though, that Māori could well reflect
carefully on their actions if they want to carry the support of most Kiwis into the future.
A growing number of Wairarapa people are keen to see an end to the grievance
industry, the end of Māori seats, and the coming together of all Kiwis. I support the
Prime Minister’s call for consultation about a new flag when Treaty settlements are
completed. A new flag may help strengthen our nationhood.
Finally, a couple of things about foreign affairs. I was pleased in the last Parliament
to complete a Foreign Affairs, Defence and Trade Committee inquiry into New
Zealand’s relationship with the South Pacific. The Government did not have a majority
on the committee,  and the report had more than 40 recommendations unanimously
supported by all parties. This led to our being able to host the first ever Pacific
Parliament last year in this Chamber with more than 50 Pacific participants. It was great
to have five Fijians there at that gathering. Since 2005—being here—I have consistently
argued privately with colleagues that it was better to engage Fiji than talk to them by
megaphone, as Helen Clark and Phil Goff did. The Pacific Parliament could never have
progressed had I not been here.
There have been some interesting interactions over these 9 years. I think of a visit to
Israel with colleagues Paul —“Hutch”, down here —Phil Goff, Kennedy Graham and
Jacqui Dean. During that visit, I realised the extent to which the majorit y of Israeli
politicians did not have the slightest interest in resolving issues with Palestinians. That
was a disappointing lesson to me, because I left that visit thinking that the Palestinian
leadership was a bunch of people whom you could do business w ith. Before that visit I
had not appreciated the extent of segregation being practised in Israel towards Arabs. To
Israelis, I simply ask you: have you no humanity?
Finally, can I say thank you to all parliamentarians from all parties. It has been fun
working with most of you, and I have made some good friends, including in other
parties. Thanks also to all the staff in the parliamentary complex, especially the library
and our staff here providing water and other things. Can I just say thank you one and all,
and wish you all the luck you deserve for the next election. Cheers.

items.speaker: CHRIS AUCHINVOLE
items.text: Thank you very much indeed, Mr Deputy
Speaker, for the call to give my valedictory statemen t. It is a privilege that is given to
retirees: 15 minutes of uninterrupted discourse, where the opportunity is given to say it
the way it really is and the way I see it, and I intend to do that now. If we glance
overseas back to Westminster, where our par liamentary system began, before it was
improved by the New Zealand system, we see that the parliamentary media over there
have adopted the sobriquet of “pale, male, and stale” for those whom Mr Cameron has
19414 Valedictory Statements 23 Jul 2014
decided should no longer hold Cabinet warrants. Ho w cruel! How cruel is that to
sensitive people? Well, if you cannot take the heat, do not stand in the kitchen. This is
Politics 101, after all.
Mind you, all jokes aside, I have always thought that members of the media try to see
in others that which the y least like about themselves. Let us think about that for a
moment. Every day at a quarter to two as we come to the House, I have in my diary
“available to media”. I approach the melee of people, cameras, and microphones.

items.speaker: Sometimes they say
items.text: “Gidday, Chri s.” That is it. There have been, perhaps, three times
when I have had that wonderful surround sound of microphones and cameras —very
exciting. Unfortunately, it was always over a tragic association with Pike River, rather
than the sort of fun that our Ministers have.
But does the Westminsterial sobriquet apply over here? Are we, as retirees, pale,
male, and stale on this side of the world or on this side of the House? I do not think so.
Oh no, I do not think so. Well, not yet, at any rate, but as my old fri end Roy Hodgson in
Rūnanga used to say—a good old coalminer—“Hang on. Let’s have a think about that.”
So I have given it a bit of thought.
Pale? OK, I certainly do not have a ruddy or dark complexion, but roseate enough on
a frosty morning not to be described as pale.
Male? I make no apology for being a male. I hope I am seen as a considerate,
compassionate, and communicable male, and I make no apology for that. If I have
faults—and I am sure I do —well, I do not think I can blame my gender for my
behaviour, without it being a cop -out. There ain’t nothing wrong with being a bloke if
you behave yourself properly. I am pleased, none the less, that our new National
candidate for West Coast - Tasman is Maureen Pugh, thereby enhancing the opportunity
for gender balance in the party.
Stale? I do not think so. I have achieved more for the electorate in the last year in the
cumulative improvement in West Coast - Tasman health infrastructure than ever before,
and have we not had such a wonderful Minister of Health? I have contributed as much
on an annual basis to select committee work in the last year as in any other, and have
spoken more frequently in the Chamber. I have had a speech that went trending on
Twitter. Lianne Dalziel had to say it was “trending” and not “trendy”. It was viral on the
internet, in the opinion of TV3 —and this was after I had actually announced my
retirement. So stale? No.
So if that is the successful rebuttal of the Westminsterial criticism of gentlemen of
European ancestry of a certain age  and career achievement, and if I have successfully
rebutted that, why the hell am I retiring? That is a good question, but here is an answer,
because it is a question that does require answering. When I joined the National Party —
signed up by Keith Holyoak e, who said “Be careful when you sign that membership
form. You may end up in Parliament.”; that was in Kaikohe, circa 1968 —I actually
made a commitment to work to support the party; not to seek to support myself, but to
support the party. I am now 69 years old, and although so many people say I do not look
it, well, I am!

items.speaker: Hon Chris Tremain
items.text: Nah, you don’t look it.

items.speaker: CHRIS AUCHINVOLE
items.text: Well, thank you. I do not know of any other serving
National MPs who are 69 years old, but as we sign up to 3 -year brackets of tenure,
would you really want to still be trundling around Parliament at 72? You need quite an
ego if you thought you could not be replaced effectively by a younger person. I guess
the only extenuating circumstance w ould be if you were a party leader who had a
Scottish mother from the Isle of Skye, but even then you would be pushing it.
I guess this is the reality. Keeping a balance of diversity —age, gender, and
ethnicity—in a caucus is a long game, not a short one. Have we not all benefited from
23 Jul 2014 Valedictory Statements 19415
the inclusion of people of diversity and different ethnicity in this Parliament? I have got
one sitting right beside me here, Kanwal Bakshi, who makes a huge contribution, and
National has certainly changed under the John Key  leadership. Each of us has to think,
though, about the future of the party and the part we want to play in it. We would all
like to be here for ever, but with my own retirement and the retirements of colleagues
from National now, the real effect will be f irst in 2017 when National will have an
incredibly strong team —fresh, but all with 3 years’ minimum experience as MPs,
youthful yet mature, vigorous and energetic, and, may I say, multi -shaded, gender -
balanced, and fresh. That is the way it will be on this side of the House.
I have no wish to be partisan, but, hey, consideration should be given to how we will
look as a party in comparison with one another in 3 years’ time, or, indeed, in 6 years’
time, because you have to plan that far out for refreshment and strength should some of
the party’s older incumbents cling to the backs of their seats —and some of us do have a
tendency to do that. Speaking entirely for myself, I wish to be part of a refreshment
process, rather than a stagnation process within the p arty, which will occur if people do
not leave and allow replacements to come in. I think that the best way to do that is to
retire at my present stage. So, although I am not personally seeking re -election, I am, of
course, still steeped in the process of the election cycle.
The political messages, though, that are put out by all the parties have a different
emphasis if one is thinking as a voter rather than as one to be voted for. It gives you a
different slant on things. It is interesting to see the way parties want to differentiate
from one another. One of my regular phone -callers on the Coast brought this to my
attention when he asked: “What about those parties that want to bring back smacking?
Is it because they want us all to smack kids, or do they ha ve a secret dream of being
smacked themselves if only the law would allow it? You just don’t know nowadays, do
you?”. He does have a point.
The other point he made —and I am absolutely sure it will not cause any offence —
was to ask why some parties insist o n having binding referenda. He said: “It sounds to
me like the way people always try to tell us what we should do and should not do with
natural resources on the Coast, when they do not even live here themselves.” He went
on to say: “The really strange par t is that the parties that say we should have binding
referenda are always minority parties and, by their own mandate, they should not expect
to be in Parliament, because they did not achieve majority support.” He has a point. He
has a point, and I really look forward to continuing to benefit from the West Coast
wisdom and the philosophical observations of people once I am outside and home
again.
I do not intend to speak any further on the new and emergent parties that hope to
hold us in thrall to their wh ims and wants. In my view, MMP is a reality that I think
would be a pity to lose. As well as providing opportunities for new philosophies, one of
its vulnerabilities is that it can attract charlatans from time to time, but the electorate is,
I trust, developing a maturity in the way that it views and uses MMP.
So what have I been able to contribute and what have I gained from my 9 years in
this place? For me, the most significant part of the parliamentary process as a
backbencher is the select committee sy stem. This is our second House, our senate, our
House of Lords, as this is where the public have a direct interface with the legislative
process. This is where the public are asked what they think of the legislation being put
forward. In my experience, the  adversarial relationship between parties and individual
members is subsumed to less of a partisan system, where members each consider the
evidence put before them in submissions from people, often based on a personal or
observed experience. I have always been impressed by the sincerity and depth of
explanation that the public provide. Organisations too, be they corporate bodies,
19416 Valedictory Statements 23 Jul 2014
commercial organisations, or community groups, come in with carefully prepared and
sharply focused submissions to argue a point. Each and every submission is considered,
weighed, and then reported back to the committee by the appointed officials who are
assisting the committee.
I would like to think that my main opportunity to make a contribution here has been
through the committee process, and I am extremely grateful for the appointments that I
have had to those committees. I have developed a deep appreciation of colleagues from
all sides of the House in the way that we have the capacity to work together within the
committee system. It is always a bit of a surprise when you come out of the committee
system. I remember when we did the review of the —oh, I will not bother to deal with
the individual Acts —but after some of the complex ones, where we had worked
together very well as part ies, we would come out and suddenly you could hear people
speaking as if they wanted nothing to do with it and saying how dreadful it was. I can
remember saying to a Minister once “This was not a reflection of the way those
members spoke in the committee.”, and they said “Chris, they are not speaking to you in
the committee. They are speaking to their membership in the public, and it is not to their
advantage to look as if we all work together too easily.”
But representing people, be they individuals or en tire electorates, is a big privilege,
and the West Coast - Tasman electorate will always be special for me. It is a delight to
see that people have actually come up from the West Coast and Tasman to be with us
today, and I think we will give them a little clap for that. It is a hell of a long way to
come. It is particularly nice to see three —one, two, three—Young Nats. There are four
or more Young Nats in the back of the gallery. They have been with me since the third
form, I think, at Greymouth High. They are at university now, and they are doing very
well.
The West Coast - Tasman electorate will always be special for me. There were
aspects of political opportunity that held special appeal for me when I first arrived in
2005, but I chose, and was advised, to concentrate my attention on serving the
electorate, and I have stuck with that prime intention. All politicians, in my experience,
wish to achieve the best they can for the people they represent, with each party having
separate ways of achieving that, and I have always been comfortable with promoting the
policies of National. There have been good times in the electorate and times of awful
tragedy. Both the good times and the tragedies are part of the political journey as an
MP, and it has been very pleas ing to me to have seen the level of agreement between
parties in processing the Pike River royal commission recommendations towards
workplace health and safety reform.
It has been a great time to be in Parliament over the last 9 years. New Zealand plays
a significant part in world affairs as a small nation with a developed, and still
developing, economy. People are not afraid of New Zealand. We do not threaten people
because of our size or aggression or anything like that. New Zealand views are listened
to and sought. I think it is fair to say that we have been well served by Foreign Ministers
from all parties over the last few decades, and we are regarded as a very responsible
world citizen. I hope the influence we have built up can be used in some of the complex
and tragic dynastic problems that are occurring at the moment between Governments, to
the detriment and horrifying physical cost to all their citizens.
Finally, I looked up “valedictory” in my Chambers Dictionary. Normally, it is a final
speech of a graduand leaving a place of learning. For me, that is a fit. It is a fit, leaving
here. Thanks directly to my National colleagues and to the Prime Minister and his staff
for the leadership they have provided. There is no greater call than that your coun try
needs you, and, gosh, New Zealand does need you, John Key. Thank goodness we have
23 Jul 2014 Valedictory Statements 19417
you as Prime Minister. This is a dynamic place. It has managed without me before —
before I arrived—and it will manage without me after I have left.

items.speaker: Hon Members
items.text: No!

items.speaker: CHRIS AUCHINVOLE
items.text: Well, all right, all right. You are so kind. But it will,
honestly. Members and staff will concentrate on themselves, the job in hand, and their
individual and collective party aspirations, as before, and that is w hat should happen. I
will not be any more memorable than any other politician who has served here and
moved on.
But here is the one thing I wanted to leave with you: I do not expect the majority of
you to remember me in any shape or form, but I will remem ber each of you—each and
every one of you —for all the transactions we have engaged in. I will treasure all the
exchanges we have had, I promise you that, be it at the select committee, in the debating
chamber, in Copperfield’s, in Bellamy’s, or in the gym;  on social occasions, on formal
occasions, in private conversation, in private meetings, or in public engagements; be it
with the security staff, Parliamentary Service staff, the travel team, the media team, with
Brent’s messengers, the Clerk’s Office, IT help services —bless them —the
communications unit, the research unit, the library, the exemplary In Style Travel taxi
service headed up by Paul Rossiter, Air New Zealand Koru Club, the electorate teams,
the Young Nats, my office staff past and present, and,  bless them, those who have left
us: the late Dan Strong, my electorate chair in Motueka, and the late Margaret Dougan,
who worked for me and supported me in Motueka. To the voters of West Coast -
Tasman and the National Party, who provided me with 9 years  of representation for the
West Coast - Tasman electorate, and to my darling wife, Elspeth, and my family, I
thank you all, and I thank each and every member, no matter which party you choose to
belong to or which path you choose to walk along. Thanks for 9 unforgettable years.
Thank you.

items.speaker: COLIN KING
items.text: Thank you for the opportunity to make this,
my final statement, in the debating chamber of the 50 th Parliament of New Zealand.
May I begin by acknowledging some of those who have put up with the 4 -metre swells
across the Cook Strait today to be with us: my electorate chair, Brian Moore, and his
wife, Roberta; campaign chair, Alan Holdaway; branch chair and hoarding manager,
Barry Ho ldaway; and branch chair, Don Moore, and his wife, Sue. May I also
acknowledge Sir Doug and Lady Kidd. I also acknowledge my staff—my most valuable
staff—in Blenheim and Amberley: Cathie Ferguson, Willie Kaulback, Rose Parsons,
and Jan Chisnall, and my parliamentary staff over years, Margaret Traill and now Karen
Scarlett. Thank you for your support. It was just fantastic and well beyond what
anybody could possibly expect.
I must acknowledge, also with great pride and satisfaction, the support I have
received from my wife, Lynnette, and our children, Nickolas, Natasha, Laressa, and
Katrina. I must also take the opportunity to acknowledge the wonderful support that I
have received from the National Party while I have had the privilege of being an MP for
9 years, both from the political wing and from the party membership. Thank you for the
guidance and support over those 9 years. I wish the National Party every success in the
forthcoming election, and we wait with bated breath for the election result on 20
September. Go well!
Last week I did something that I had hoped to do for many a year, and that was to
visit the whale -counting operation that occurs every year at this time in the Tory
Channel and Cook Strait. Fortunately, on the day that we went out the obs ervers
perched up on Tory Channel sighted a large humpback whale cruising through the Cook
Strait on its way to the Tropics. We were able to just motor straight out there and watch
these guys in their 4 -metre runabout in a 3 -metre swell dart the whale to t ake a DNA
19418 Valedictory Statements 23 Jul 2014
sample. Just to give you some understanding about how difficult it was, I could hardly
hold my camera, my iPhone camera, to actually capture the moment to post it on
Facebook. From the point of view of what has gone before us in history, in the context it
was most uplifting. You could entitle the situation: “Whaling —from Decimation to
Restoration”. These old ex -whalers are now spending endless hours looking into the
mist of the Cook Strait to identify that pencil shape of a whale coming towards th em.
The good news is that about 100 whales came through the Cook Strait during the
month, and is that not fantastic? There are more ways for the whales to go, but through
the Cook Strait is a bit like the drafting race—you can count them. So from that point of
view it is a good measure.
I want to make the point that although we may have a strong view on how people
earned their living in years gone by, they did sustain themselves and we should neither
condemn nor ridicule. Sure, the land -based whaling opera tions did not decimate the
whales. The damage was done by the fleets of whaling vessels from other nations that
hunted the whale to near extermination, taking up to 4,000 whales a year, year on year.
However, I make the point because I personally have serious concerns, along with many
others, about our attitude to sustainable management around the coastline. Today there
are 10 times as many people out on the coastline collecting kai moana. The targeting of
fish, the catching of crays, the taking of paua and  other delicacies has greatly improved,
and yet we still argue that it is our birthright to help ourselves to such a resource.
As rational human beings we know that continuing such a harvest of our kai moana
will result in serious consequences for us toda y and for our future generations. It is
therefore with much pride that I draw on the example of the community of Kaikōura,
who over the last 8 years, based on the principles of gifts and giving, were able to reach
an agreement across the full range of stak eholders: iwi, commercial fishers, recreational
fishers, Forest and Bird, and the wider community. They were able to agree amongst
themselves as to the best way possible of managing their coastline between the Conway
River and the Clarence River. I was ama zed to witness the cooperation that existed on
that group of Te Korowai people. It is with pride that I now look forward to this process
of seeing the passing into law of the Kaikōura (Te Tai o Marokura) Marine
Management Bill, which will enshrine the mana gement plan into law and protect it for
the benefit of all Kaikōura and others who visit in the many years ahead.
What made this achievement possible was that those involved, the community,
clearly understood what was at stake. Local iwi —that is, Ngāti Kuri—led because they
held the kaitiaki over the area, the commercial fishermen pulled in the same direction
because they owned the quota and they knew what sustainable management was all
about, and the wider community stuck to the task because they knew a nd valued the
employment and they valued their environment. There is no doubt in my mind that this
situation is going to have to be replicated throughout New Zealand. Such iconic places
as the Marlborough Sounds, the Hauraki Gulf, the Wellington headlands,  Bay of Plenty,
and the Northland coastline —to name but a few —will need to address this situation as
pressure remains and grows. Again, it will require skilful leadership, a willingness to
agree and make those gifts and giving. We must face up to the chall enge, otherwise we
will end up in exactly the same position as those whalers who lost their careers, their
opportunities, and their profitability overnight because of a culture of greed and a race
to catch the last whale.
My second point that I would like  to make is the importance of hands -on learning
within our education system. We must appreciate these very important students who, in
the future, will continue to fix things, build things —be it trucks, be it motorcars, be it
buildings, be it bridges, be it roads, be it essential infrastructure, and all other manner of
things. To do this, the education system must equally value these people as we do
23 Jul 2014 Valedictory Statements 19419
doctors, nurses, lawyers, and accountants, and design an education curriculum
accordingly. I just put it out here in very plain terms. To put it simply, we want to create
many Einsteins, but to create an Einstein you need to also have 1,000 skilled technicians
to be able to make those things.
I wish to mention two people by name at this time. It is always dangero us doing that,
but two people have had a big effect on my policy development. Firstly, Stuart
Middleton, from the Manukau Institute of Technology, who when I first came into
Parliament was already talking about what was lacking within our education system.  He
has gone on to do some wonderful things around empowering youth, especially Pasifika
youth. I take the opportunity here to say how heartened I am to see the Pasifika people
taking grasp of education and being aspirational. I also want to make mention o f
Stewart Thompson, who worked with me in developing the trades academy policy,
which was introduced by the Government in 2009. Stewart Thompson convinced me
that the passion of an inspiring teacher is what makes the difference. Stewart’s
technology classe s were full to overflowing, and total engagement with education
existed in spades.
I ask those responsible for education in the future to maintain the momentum we
have for hands -on learning and skills -based education. Education must be relevant to
the lea rners for them to remain engaged and to develop the skills necessary to be
successful in life, and that is a pretty high threshold. We must keep them engaged. We
are beginning to do better, but there is a lot of work we need to do yet.
The third point I w ant to leave with the House is my concern around a growing
reluctance in this country —and this is my observation —to undertake physically
demanding work. We should be concerned when we see those who want to continue
living in one location and are not willin g or courageous enough to collect up their
families and move to where employment is better and more available, where the cost of
living is less and the price of providing a roof over one’s family’s head is also less. New
Zealand has one of the most generou s welfare systems in the world. However, for New
Zealand to remain a First World country, we must possess the attitude as stated by
George St John and restated by President J F Kennedy: “Ask not what your country can
do for you; ask what you can do for you r country.”—that it is good to create wealth and
seek ownership.
I admire greatly those Eastern European families who came here in the 1950s and
1960s. I was only a child at the time. They made New Zealand their home and they
started afresh after experien cing the Second World War, the Cold War, and the Iron
Curtain. It now concerns me that we do bring enthusiastic workers from the Pacific
Islands to do the harvesting and cultivation within the horticultural sector and that we
need to bring thousands of wor kers to fill the needs of the dairy industry. Is it not
blindingly obvious to all that in doing the work that some of us despise, these
newcomers end up creating wealth for themselves and their families to enjoy into the
future? It is all symptomatic of a nation that is losing its way when a newcomer can
come here and see opportunities that we cannot. Individually, we hold the key to our
own success: careful living and good, honest, hard work. Personal responsibility and a
desire to aspire should be the aim  of us all. Lose this and we become no better than a
domesticated animal.
Sir Henry Maine, speaking on social structure, put it well when he said: “Nobody is
at liberty to attack private property and to say at the same time that he values
civilisation. The  history of the two cannot be disentangled.” For the institution of
private property has been a wonderful institution for teaching man and woman
responsibility, for providing motives to integrity, for supporting general culture, for
raising mankind above t he level of mere drudgery, for affording leisure to think and
19420 Valedictory Statements 23 Jul 2014
freedom to act. To be able to retain the fruits of one’s labour, to be able to see one’s
work made manifest, to be able to bequeath one’s property to one’s posterity, to be able
to rise from the  natural condition of grinding poverty to the security of enduring
accomplishment, to have something that is really one’s own —there are advantages with
this difficult to deny.” In drafting policy and bringing forth legislation in this House,
may all members continue to recognise the value of those who toil in the sun or labour
under the tin roof, neither despising the value of that work or thinking that it is beyond
one’s dignity, because the wealth of this nation was created on the back of physically
demanding labour.
In conclusion, may I express my sincere thanks to all members of the House for the
courtesy that they have accorded me. Thank you too for the joy of working for the best
interests of all New Zealanders, particularly in the primary sector and in the science and
education sector, while in Parliament. I am sure, though, that those who are coming
behind us will be more than equal to the task. We do live in a blessed land.
To the parliamentary sporting trusts, what fun we had in raising money for the most
worthy of causes, and in the camaraderie of winning two Parliamentary Rugby World
Cups—one in Paris and the other in New Zealand. There was also the pleasure of
coordinating the parliamentary and diplomats’ annual cricket challenges, and winning a
few. That was quite good. I always remember Paul Swain leaving the House, having
won that year against the diplomats. That having been said, we have not won for many
years, for about a decade. I am asking the House to make sure that they support Ian
McKelvie as he carries on the mantle of looking after the shield and keeping that cricket
match going. It has been going for over 40 years, and it is actually quite an illustrious
shield with some great MPs’ names on it.
If I have one disappointment in leaving Parliament, Mr Speaker, it is possibly one we
share together. It is that wisdom has not prevailed when it has come to storing water in
North Canterbury. Sadly —and this again is my observation, because I know that some
of my Green colleagues would disagree —it is my view that a dog in a manger attitude
still prevails, making progress slow and difficult.
Finally, I wish to thank the taxpayers of New Zealand for providing the funding for
three new hospitals while I was MP in the electorate of Kaikōura. I am also delighted to
have witnessed, as MP, the Te Tau Ihu Treaty settlement situation that has provided
eight iwi with their settlements, which will restore their economic base into the future,
and also to being a witness to, and being part of, the 8 years’ labour of love —the
management of the Kaikōura coastline, the result of which is the bill I have here, under
a pile of papers. I look forward to it being put through the House completely by the time
the House rises. I thank the Minister of Conservation and I also thank the Leader of the
House for putting that in place. We are very satisfied with everything that is going
forward.
Just to conclude, for the most part, from my own point of view what is most
satisfying is the momentum that has been achieved arou nd education—the importance
that has been put on the hands-on learning situation. Education is relevant. It needs to be
relevant. If it is not relevant, you will have disengagement.
I want to thank everybody for the situation that I have enjoyed over the last 9 years. I
acknowledge my wife and children. I acknowledge those people who have travelled
across the Cook Strait. I acknowledge those people who are supporting departing
members. I also acknowledge all the members in the House. We have worked in the
very best interests of New Zealand. Kia kaha. Stand tall. Be proud. Thank you very
much.

items.speaker: Hon CHRIS TREMAIN
items.text: In life there are many different
definitions of succe ss, and in Parliament the same goes. There are many different
23 Jul 2014 Valedictory Statements 19421
definitions of what makes a successful politician. Nine years ago I entered Parliament,
and, I have to say, I was pretty naïve. Some would probably argue that that has not
changed too much. I ha d just won the Labour -held seat of Napier, the first time in 50
years, and I thought I had been pretty successful at that point in time. But like all
politicians across this House, I entered this place with the intention of helping to create
a better New Z ealand. We all have the same purpose, just different ideas of how we
might achieve that goal. But success in Parliament is not defined by just winning a seat
or becoming a Cabinet Minister. Success comes with many different faces.
I recall in my first year  a gym session with Rodney Hide —you might not want to
think too hard about that —at the Bolton Hotel. We had a discussion about what made a
successful politician. “You’ve got to take scalps.” was Rodney’s advice, as he sweated
away on the cycling machine. “ You can’t be successful in this place unless you take
scalps.” was his advice. Shortly after, I was presented with a completely different face
of success, from the Hon Jim Sutton, who in his valedictory reflected on the importance
of retaining family to en sure a successful political career: “Public life is often a selfish
business. It can be all-consuming.”, he said. “Those closest to public figures often pay a
high or unfair price. To those I have hurt, I say ‘sorry’.”, said Jim. “To those who
follow me here, I say ‘try to do better than I did’.” Throughout my own political career I
have reflected on these words of sage advice.
For most, however, political success is defined with a more public face. On a daily
basis we politicians are built up and we are cu t down. Whether it be the number of bills
you pass, the number of times you are mentioned in the press, or your performance in
select committees, success here is very transparent. This all culminates in an annual
ranking of Ministers and MPs. It is a humbl ing experience, and for some a crumbling
experience. It is definitely not for the faint -hearted, that is for sure. The fact of the
matter is that only a few of us make it to the very top of this game. There is only a small
number of John Keys and Bill Engl ishes, and Helen Clarks and Michael Cullens. To
those from across this House who make it to the very top in this game and who then
stay there, you have my absolute respect. It is no mean feat, and staying there is even
more difficult.
To John Key and to Bi ll English, I applaud you for your outstanding partnership and
your leadership. I have been a member and a leader of many teams in my life, so I can
genuinely say that being a part of this team has been an absolute privilege. To Cabinet
and to my wider cau cus, I congratulate you on leading our nation through one of the
most difficult periods in our history. There is a depth to our team, often overlooked by
commentators, that continues to provide new and exciting talent when others such as
myself decide that  their time in this place is at an end. That is exciting. Rejuvenation
while a team is on top is often the hardest, but actually it is the best thing to ensure
longevity. Can I thank all of my team for your support of both my wife, Angela, and my
family throughout my time in this place.
I have not been one of the political rock stars. I have not climbed to the very top of
the political ladder. In saying this, I am proud—I am very proud—to have been part of a
team that has made, and continues to make, a huge  contribution to this nation. I am
proud of the part that I have played in that team. To use one of my dad’s analogies, it is
all very well for the wingers to take the glory, but if the props and the hookers did not
win the ball—[Interruption] That is right. There are some good props around, Mr Sabin.
Listen to this. If the props and the hookers did not take the ball, there would be no
applause for the Twinkletoes. I guess I have been one of those in the middle of the ruck.
Some commentators say that you n eed to watch those behind you more than those
across the other side of the House. Well, that has not been my experience —far from it. I
have absolutely loved my time here and the friendships that I have made, including
19422 Valedictory Statements 23 Jul 2014
many across the other side of the Hous e and in the media. Thank you very much as
well.
Recently I attended the Aspiring Leaders Forum, where the Maxim Institute brings
together 120 of our young leaders. My own son Sam, who is in the gallery today, was
fortunate to be an attendee there. The Wa rehouse Chief Executive Officer, Mark
Powell, gave the keynote address and had another definition of success. He defined
success as when you are part of something bigger than yourself and when you help
others to flourish. It is a great definition of success and to this end Parliament has many,
many more examples of successful people who by other measures have not risen to the
top or who have by their actions allowed others to shine. I have many examples of these
people whom I want to acknowledge this evening.
Can I start by thanking the people who have supported me while I have been in this
place: my electorate office team —Tania Wright, Vicki Sanders, Sue Boyle, Sharon
Coates, Sue Page, and Mary Crarer. Tania and Vicki have been with me from day one.
Electorate agents, as we across this House all know, are the unsung heroes of an MP’s
business. Day in and day out they deal with all spectrums of our society. Being an
electorate MP is an incredible job. The diversity of the role is both challenging and
rewarding. I want to thank the people of Napier, Wairoa, and the Hawke’s Bay for
giving me the huge privilege to represent you over the last 9 years.
One of the more memorable experiences was being asked to be the guest of the Go
Natural Lifestyle Club to open i ts new gazebo. I consulted my wife, Angela, as I was
too scared to go on my own. She agreed to join me. I spent more time that Saturday
morning deciding what to wear than on any other occasion I have ever been to since.
Should I be in casual or formal dres s, or should I be in my birthday suit? Who knows?
Well, we arrived at 11.30 a.m., in time for a tour and lunch. To this day I will never
forget driving up the pine -enclosed complex, pulling over in the car -park, and watching
the reception party walk down t o greet us both. Ange leaned over and whispered in my
ear: “My God, CJ, they really are naked.”
In my neighbouring electorate, I want to acknowledge my good mate Craig Foss and
his electorate staff, particularly Susanna Clark. We have worked closely together to take
Hawke’s Bay forward. Reflecting back on my maiden speech, I set goals around Napier
health, Napier community policing, the Hawke’s Bay Airport, business growth, and
apple exports to Australia. Nine years on, I can confidently say that we h ave made good
progress. We have secured a 10-year commitment to the Wellesley Road Health Centre.
We have got community police in at Maraenui and in Tamatea. We extended the
Hawke’s Bay Regional Airport runway, and we have championed business growth,
trying to get an oil and gas industry and new irrigation up in the Hawke’s Bay. There is
still more work to do there, Fossy, actually. Although still only small volumes, our
efforts did help to ensure that apples can now be exported to Australia. I want to than k
both Phil Goff and Tim Groser for their efforts in achieving that for us. Thank you.
The partnership between Craig and me, under the brand “Backing the Bay”, was a
key factor in holding our seats for three consecutive terms. Craig, I have appreciated
your friendship and support. In that regard, can I thank my Napier electorate team, who
are out there supporting my replacement, Wayne Walford, as we speak. Some of you
are here tonight. There are so many who have contributed, and too many to mention you
all, but to my electorate chairs over the last 9 years, Tom Johnson, Marshall Savidge,
Duncan Watson, Lynne Trafford, and now Ian Mayne, thank you very much.
To the National Party board, particularly my regional chairs, Patricia Morrison and
Malcolm Plimmer, and national chairs, Judy Kirk and Peter Goodfellow, thank you for
your support behind the scenes, enabling your MPs to bask in the sunshine.
23 Jul 2014 Valedictory Statements 19423
To all the people of this House, from the cleaners to the security guards, who ensure
the smooth running of Parli ament, thank you. If there was ever a group of people who
quietly go about ensuring that others can flourish, it is you.
My time on the backbench was a huge learning opportunity. There is no better place
to learn the craft of politics than on the Oppositi on backbench. It is a great place to
make a few mistakes and to live to fight another day. One big mistake that I made
required an apology to my leader at the time, Don Brash. Early in my time as a
constituent MP, we received a visit to Napier by the Earth race biodiesel boat. One Peter
Bethune visited my electorate office asking me to visit his boat in the Port of Napier. I
was busy, but in the course of the conversation I worked out that he would be in
Wellington during the next parliamentary sitting, so I  agreed I would come and visit
with a few colleagues. I suggested to Nick Smith that this would be a great opportunity
to give Don some much-needed profile. Ah, not such a good idea! Nick agreed to invite
Don. The rest is history and has become the stuff o f walk -the-plank legends. Don,
please accept my sincere apologies for that particular idea.
To Mac Dalton, Alistair Shelton, Pat Humphries, and Stefan Slooten, who have
supported me in my parliamentary office, thank you. In particular, can I acknowledge
Pat Humphries, who has worked in this amazing institution for much of her life. From
junior backbench MPs to two Prime Ministers, Pat Humphries has supported MPs to
rise to the top of the ladder. Pat, thank you. [Interruption] Yeah, give her a clap.
To my whip’s office team, a huge thank you for your support over the 3 years I
served as a junior and senior whip. At the heart of that office is Sue Reid, who has
guided many new whips in the right path. Thank you, Sue. I have often described the
whip’s role as 50 percent sergeant major and 50 percent local pastor in the church. It is a
role that requires the trust of the caucus. We were a tight team, as we are today. There
are lots of stories that the whip becomes party to, many of which are not appropriate to
share. However, I have one story I would like to tell that involves another apology, and
this one is to Louise Upston. She is thinking: “What the heck have I done here?”.
During the start of my parliamentary year, I was asked by the Young Nats to send a
party representative to the Massey campus to participate in O -Week. I asked Louise to
be our representative, to which she agreed. At 12 p.m. I received a call from the Young

items.speaker: Nats
items.text: “Where is Louise?”. I called Louise. “I’m at the front gate.”, she said. “We’r e at
the front gates as well.”, said the Young Nats. It turns out that I had sent Louise to
Palmerston North instead of to Wellington. I am sorry about that, Louise.
Can I thank my ministerial team, headed by Keith Mason, Jenna Raeburn, and Mary -
Jane Rendell. Like Pat, Keith, who is up in the gallery today, has been a senior private
secretary in this Parliament for over 20 years, working to support the success of
Ministers across both sides of the House, for that matter, and now he is supporting
Minister Parata. Although I was a Minister for only 2 years, it is an incredible workload
that goes through a Minister’s office, with huge diversity. During my time it was great
to lead a review of the Fire Service, to initiate significant change in the gambling sec tor,
to introduce the right-hand turn law, to introduce online passports, to oversee the whole-
of-Government information and communications technology strategy, and to lead the
second tranche of local government reform, amongst all manner of other things.
I want to pay a huge tribute to the public sector, especially to the team at the
