Department of Internal Affairs. Under the leadership of Colin MacDonald, the
Department of Internal Affairs has transformed into a modern, forward -looking
department. Congratulations. There are many in the department who deserve a mention,
none more than Marilyn Little. She has worked tirelessly for both sides of this House,
providing outstanding advice, helping others to take the credit from her work.
19424 Valedictory Statements 23 Jul 2014
When one comes to Parli ament, we are all fortunate to give maiden speeches, and
one’s valedictory is the chance to reflect on that speech. In my maiden speech, I
commenced with a mihi: “Whāia te pae tawhiti kia tata. Whāia te pae tata. Whakamaua
kia ū, kia tī-na.”
[Draw the dis tant and not so distant horizon closer to you. When that is achieved,
grasp it firmly and permanently.]
The mihi speaks of reaching for the stars, pursuing one’s dreams. At the time it was
remarked how unusual it was for a Pākehā New Zealander to use so mu ch Te Reo in his
maiden speech. I actually think our intake surprised more than a few and set a tone for
the National Party, one that has truly connected us with middle New Zealand, not the far
left or the far right. We came from vastly different walks of life: nurses, builders,
diplomats, shearers—Colin King—teachers, shoe salesmen, teen parents, and even real
estate agents. We understood what made Kiwis tick. A few of our number have risen
through the ranks and many of us have been the solid core of the N ational caucus,
providing stability, consistency and connection to people at the coalface. We have been
the props and the hookers of the team. This connection has been continued through the
2008 and 2011 intake, which is absolutely fantastic.
When a mains tream party loses that connection with the aspirations of middle New
Zealand, the results speak for themselves. To my colleagues, I say to never ever forget
that. In regard to the goals I set in my maiden speech, I am proud to see how much
progress has been made in the area of Treaty settlements and to see the huge progress in
my own rohe. Although there are still settlements that need to be completed, we are in a
totally different place from where we started. The Hon Chris Finlayson will be knighted
at a f uture time for his service in this area. You can hold me to that! In my maiden
speech I expressed concern at the lack of progress in our nation, at the lack of
opportunities for my children and at the huge numbers of people leaving our shores.
In spite of the Christchurch earthquakes, the global financial crisis, and the meltdown
of our second -tier finance sector, New Zealand is now judged as one of the best
economies in the Western World. Just today Australia’s Treasurer, Joe Hockey, called
New Zealand’s economy the envy of the world. It is fantastic to see the turn -round in
the migration statistics. I am exceptionally proud to see that. Nothing else reflects
people genuinely seeing a brighter future in Aotearoa than those migration statistics.
In addition to the goals that I set in my maiden speech, I am proud of my affirmative
votes in the smacking legislation, the seabed and foreshore legislation, and the marriage
amendment bill. In each of these bills I learnt that leadership is not always about
following the status quo or majority opinion; leadership is about challenging the status
quo for something that you believe is genuinely better. Under John Key’s leadership we
have made huge progress. I am excited about the future of this country and the prospects
available to all children in our nation, including my own children. With the economy in
such great shape it is an excellent time to leave this House in search of new
opportunities. I have already bought into two new businesses and am exploring a third. I
am looking forward to re -engaging with my entrepreneurial passion. It is going to be
challenging but exciting.
In particular, I will have more time to spend with my family,  and it is my family
whom I would most like to thank as I come to the end of my valedictory. In my maiden
speech I said that I would endeavour to put families at the pinnacle of Government
policy, because, I said, without strong families we have nothing. I  have a strong family
and they are here tonight, and even some of the members of my wider family in the
provincial club —you know who you are. To my mother, Pam, thank you for your
support, and for giving me the opportunity and the independence to do all th at I wanted
from a very young age. To my father, I miss you hugely and wish that you could be here
23 Jul 2014 Valedictory Statements 19425
with your family tonight. Dad, I am wearing your cufflinks tonight. To my brothers,
Mark and Simon, we have often been measured against our father’s success,  on the
sporting field and in life. Each of us, however, has cut our own different paths. I am
confident that he would have been very proud of each of us and of our young families.
In saying that, I was never able to emulate my dad’s prowess on the sportin g field.
However, let the Hansard record for eternity that I did captain the Parliamentary Rugby
Team to victory in the 2011 Parliamentary Rugby World Cup.
To my wife Angela’s parents and family, particularly to Trevor and Jeanette —thanks
for Angela and f or your huge support of me and our family. To Ange, Sam, Will, and
Lily—I love you all dearly. Thank you for giving me this opportunity.
So, have I been successful in this parliamentary career? By some measures, certainly;
by others, not as well. Sorry, R odney, I did not take any scalps while I was here, but I
have been part of something bigger than myself, most definitely, and my efforts have
allowed others to flourish. Yes, I have achieved that. I started my maiden speech in Te
Reo, and will end it in ou r first language. In 2012 I took the Prime Minister to Wairoa,
honouring a commitment I had made to the wonderful, wonderful people of that part of
my electorate. On that day we had a number of pōwhiris, where we did not have a
speaker to introduce the Pri me Minister. That role, and the waiata, fell to me. Upon our
return to the caucus on the following Monday, I was required by the Prime Minister to
sing that waiata in the caucus room, possibly the first person ever to do so at the
National Party caucus. It  was rough. I will not make you suffer that again. But I will
close with a whakatauāki—a proverb—that talks of a new beginning, a touch of frost, a
new dawn. I think it is appropriate as I leave this place and pursue an exciting new
future.
Whakataka te hau ki te uru, whakataka te hau ki te tonga. Kia mākinakina ki uta, kia
mātaratara ki tai. E hī ake ana te atākura, he tio, he huka, he hauhunga. Tēnā koutou,
tēnā koutou, tēnā tātou katoa. Kia ora.
[Cease the winds from the west, cease the winds from the so uth. Let the breezes blow
over the land, let the breezes blow over the ocean. Let the red -tipped dawn come with a
sharpened air, a touch of frost and a promise of a glorious day. So greetings and
salutations to you collectively and to us all. Thank you. ]

items.speaker: Hon KATE WILKINSON
items.text: When I first entered this
House 9 years ago I was a list member of Parliament in a Labour -held safe seat. I leave
this place as the e lectorate member of Parliament for Waimakariri in a National -held
seat. This just goes to show that anything can happen and one should never ever take
one’s electorate for granted. Now I will leave this place, never ever to suffer defeat as
an electorate M P. I especially want to thank the 16,787 voters of Waimakariri —well,
actually, one of them was me—who entrusted me with their electorate vote and with the
responsibility of representing them in Parliament. What a tremendous honour and a
privilege. Constituency work has always been for me the most satisfying aspect of the
job. There is nothing better than seeing a constituent come into my office with a
problem and leave without it. Of course, not all problems are able to be solved. To the
20,489 Waimakariri voters who had the common sense and wisdom to give National
their party vote, well done, thank you, and long may that trend continue and long may
National be the party of choice for you. By the way, when I first stood, our party vote in
Waimakariri was in deficit by 6,790 votes. We won the party vote that election by 81
votes, a good reflection that indeed every vote does count. In total, that is a turn -round
of about 20,000 party votes during my tenure.
I have been an Opposition backbencher and a Government backbencher. I have been
a list member of Parliament and an electorate member of Parliament, and I do not need
to comment on which is better. I have been given the absolute privilege of being a
Cabinet Minister. That is like being selected for t he All Black team. Not everyone gets
19426 Valedictory Statements 23 Jul 2014
to be an All Black, and not every All Black gets to play 100 test matches. So I feel very
honoured and privileged to have been selected for the team and to have been able to
play my part. Thanks, in particular, to our P rime Minister, the Rt Hon John Key.
Without a doubt, he is one of the best Prime Ministers in New Zealand’s history. I will
certainly take some reflected glory in having been selected as part of his Cabinet team
for just over 4 years, and his caucus team. For those who have not yet read the
biography, I feature on pages 194 and 215.

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: It’s a good read.

items.speaker: Hon KATE WILKINSON
items.text: It is a good read. The stewardship and governance of
New Zealand, shown especially by both the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance,
Bill English, throughout what have undoubtedly been some of our most challenging
times have been outstanding, and I will always be proud of being part of that team.
Special thanks must go to my electorate team o ver the years, my National Party
volunteers, friends, and family, many of whom are here today and who have travelled so
far just to be here. It is a bit embarrassing, really. If they had not believed in me,
supported me, befriended me, advised me, fed me, and looked after me, I would not
have been here in the first place, I would not have been able to be here for 9 years, and
my tenure here would not have been so fantastic. Thank you also to them and to the
National Party for honouring me with this opportun ity. To my class of 2005, thank you.
To my caucus colleagues, it has been a fantastic journey together. Those remaining do
have a huge responsibility to keep looking after our country, making sure it does not get
into the wrong hands, protecting both our e conomy and our environment. I know that
you will do this well. To my fellow valedictors —if that is a word —all the best with
your post -parliamentary lives. To Natalie, Nat, Natto —she hates that —my executive
assistant and then my senior private secretary, yo u are the best person I have ever
worked with. You seemed to understand me, which was no mean feat. You held our
team together in room 4.3. I will not embarrass you by tabling in the House your long -
awaited reference from me, but here it is. Pick it up lat er over drinks. To all my team,
who are all here except for Svar, who I understand is, hopefully, watching this from
Russia, thank you for all your support and friendship over the years.
They say things happen in threes. Well, I was a member of Parliament in Canterbury.
Under my watch the worst natural disaster, the earthquakes, happened. I was Minister of
Conservation. Under my watch the worst environmental maritime disaster, the Rena,
happened. And I was Minister of Labour. Under my watch the worst workp lace safety
disaster, Pike River, happened. Can I say that at least as Associate Minister of
Immigration I did not let Mike Tyson into the country.
Like every Canterbury member of Parliament, the earthquake events will always
stand out for me. What a rema rkable time to be a member of Parliament for an
electorate and in a home town that was devastated by the earthquakes. I feel honoured to
have helped our district in my capacity as MP through what has surely been its darkest
time, from shovelling silt durin g those early days to informing residents of each and
every new service and funding the National -led Government provided towards our
recovery, as well as the hours and hours of work helping our residents navigate through
the repair and rebuild of their homes. We have all learnt so much together, developing a
new vocabulary along the way and learning about resilience and community —concepts
we lived and which held us together so well. To the Hon Gerry Brownlee, Canterbury
and Christchurch owe you a huge debt of gratitude. Your legacy will be remarkable.
I have always believed that New Zealand is the best country in the world, and that
was certainly borne out during my nearly 4 years as Minister of Conservation. What a
fantastic portfolio to have had the privi lege of holding. I remember to this day my very
first kiwi release. To hold one of those iconic, beautiful birds was a treasure I shall
always remember. On this first occasion I was given some very sage advice as I was
23 Jul 2014 Valedictory Statements 19427
holding the kiwi firmly, fondly, and possessively. I must admit that the advice was not
that welcome. Basically, I was advised in no uncertain terms. They said: “Minister, the
idea of a kiwi release is you actually let go of the kiwi and release it.” Thank you,
Gavin. One of the absolute high lights, apart from naming one of our kākāpō Jack —
who, by the way, is now 3 years old, fit, well, and starting to boom—

items.speaker: Hon Members
items.text: Oh!

items.speaker: Hon KATE WILKINSON
items.text: Exactly. One of the highlights has to be taking Prince
William to Kāpiti Island. What a delightful young man. I would not mind hanging him
up in my wardrobe. I have a photo hanging in pride of place on my wall of the prince
flanked by the Prime Minister and me. I must admit there was a fleeting moment when I
considered cropping the photo, but I did not. The trick, as we all know, with photos is to
try to stand in the middle so there is no possibility of being cropped out. Sorry, Nathan.
I also remember, when I was Minister of Conservation, having to do a media stand -up
with my colleague Gerry Brownlee, who was then Minister of Energy and Resources.
There were some critics who said I was not even there, so I just want to put it on the
record once and for all that I can assure them I was there; it is just that the camera lens
maybe was not wide enough for the both of us.
In my time as Minister of Labour there were good times and bad times. The ink on
my warrant barely had time to dry when I was told that my 90 -day trial bill would be
one of the first in our term to go on the Order Paper. It has now been in place for just on
6 years. The protections we built into the legislation worked, and in that time there has
been no amendment needed apart from, of course, extending it from small businesses to
all businesses. Indeed, that on e piece of policy and legislation was credited with having
provided 13,000 new jobs in its first year. We had finally caught up with what had
happened in most jurisdictions throughout the world. It would be sad if ideology
reversed all this. It has helped so many and hurt so few.
Most memorable, sadly, was the Pike River mining tragedy. I cannot resile from the
absolute fact that 29 men died under my watch. Although I was not personally
responsible, I was the responsible Minister, and it happened under my watch. We all
wish we could turn back the clock and prevent such a disaster and keep those men safe.
We cannot, but I am proud of the setting up of the Royal commission inquiry and now
the implementing of its recommendations, putting the spotlight on workplace safety. We
often have a national culture of “she’ll be right”, but it too often is not right. We lose a
worker about once a week and a farmer once a month, and a farmer is hurt about every
30 minutes. So often, those deaths and injuries could have bee n avoided. We need to
change that culture and simply look after our workmates. Governments can do only so
much and can be only so effective. Workplaces and workmates can do more.
The food safety portfolio is a fascinating one, although when I was first gi ven the
portfolio, a good friend of mine did comment that if the Prime Minister had looked
inside my fridge, he would not have given me food safety. Anyway, it started for me
with the folic acid debate —not the most memorable one for me. Throughout all the
discussions as to how many slices of bread one would need to consume to get the daily
intake of folic acid, remarkably it went unnoticed that, actually, I cannot even eat bread.
However, the portfolio ended for me with a success, having negotiated with our
Australian counterparts on a joint health claims standard. I even had the Australian
Minister who chairs the forum make a special trip over here to see me, not particularly
happy about trying to convince New Zealand to go with the Australians and not opt out
of a joint standard. We won through in the end; otherwise it would have stifled
innovation and cost our businesses millions, if not billions, of dollars. There are two
lessons from that. Firstly, we have definitely not lost our sovereignty to Australia , and,
secondly, if it is good news, it does not always get the good publicity it deserves. In
19428 Valedictory Statements 23 Jul 2014
fact, more column space was spent on my being mistakenly referred to as “Kate
Middleton” than on this food treaty success.
Our work in select committees, as has  been said, often goes unnoticed by the public.
They do not often see the collaborative approach to make good law, whatever our
respective ideologies and beliefs. My first success in a select committee was changing
the word “the” to the word “a”, and one o f my last successes was changing “can” to
“may”. Words can, indeed, make a difference. Yet we still have some really, really
stupid laws, or maybe it is just that we have enabled some of our laws to be interpreted
stupidly. Why, for example, can I no longe r use my business card in the regulated
period? Apparently, that is deemed electioneering. It is a business card, for goodness’
sake, and I am not even standing for re-election.
Local successes are always the sweeter. I am particularly proud to have been
instrumental in obtaining our health hub in Rangiora, and thanks must go to the Hon
Tony Ryall for his support on this and for making it happen. This is a milestone eagerly
and long awaited by residents to supplement our world -class St John Ambulance
paramedic team serving residents after hours, an award-winning response model. It is so
much more worthwhile and responsible to look pragmatically and objectively for
solutions rather than negatively focusing on the problems. I always preferred to work
hard beh ind the scenes and help solve problems in priority to trying to attract any
headline.
We all have a best-before date and a use-by date, although I believe that some do not
recognise either. But I was reminded of that at a university club day I was attendi ng, to
help out and support our wonderful, energetic, and enthusiastic Young Nats. A student
coming up to our stand made the comment to me: “You look familiar. Do I know you?”.
Since I am not one ever to use the phrase “Don’t you know who I am?”, one of ou r
helpful Young Nats started to say “Oh, she is a local MP. She is a Minister.”, etc., when
the inquirer interrupted and said: “I know. You remind me of my grandmother.” That
was a reality check. Still, the alternative to getting older is worse, but it doe s serve to
remind us that this is not a job for life. It goes very quickly and we must make the most
of each and every day. Most of us come to this place to make a difference, to make New
Zealand a better place. Some do it better than others, some have dif ferent views on how
to make that difference, some do it differently than others, and probably some do not
make any difference at all. I hope in my small way that I have made some small
difference to some people.
It is a remarkable thing, though. As soon a s I made the decision not to stand again,
my bucket list magically got bigger and bigger. So now it is time to start emptying that
bucket. A big job, I know, but I am up for it. Until 20 September I have a job to do, but
then I am away to tick off the first agenda item on my bucket list. It will be the first time
in 9 years that I have not had to ask the permission of our whips. Obviously, there will
be some things I will miss about this place, but there are also things I definitely will not
miss. No longer will I have to ask for leave to go to the Christchurch Show Day or to go
on holiday. I will always cherish my time working with and for our residents of
Waimakariri as their MP. I have loved the job. I have valued the opportunity. I have
been humbled by t he privilege. But now it is time to step away and tread a different
path, or, as my GPS frequently tells me, “route recalculation”.
As some have been known to say, I have been around for over 30 million minutes so
far—not all in this place, although nearl y 5 million minutes have been spent here. It is
time for me to use those remaining minutes differently. There are now more restaurants
and bars in Christchurch than before the earthquakes —more than 120 new ones. I have
not tried them all, so I can start working my way through them. Bucket list, here I come.
In closing, can I say that in 2005 I was so excited to be here, and now, 9 years later, I
am so excited to leave.
23 Jul 2014 Valedictory Statements 19429
Waiata
Sitting suspended from 5.56 p.m. to 7.30 p.m.
SUMMARY OFFENCES (POSSESSION OF HIGH-POWER LASER
POINTERS) AMENDMENT BILL
Third Reading

items.speaker: Dr CAM CALDER
items.text: I move, That the Summary Offences (Possession of
High-power Laser Pointers) Amendment Bill be now read a third time . It is a huge
pleasure to be speaking in the House a mere 1 hour and 50 minutes after my valedictory
speech. It was something I did not expect I could do and—
Denis O’Rourke: Coming back.

items.speaker: Dr CAM CALDER
items.text: It does not betoken a comeback. No, no, it does not betoken a
comeback. It merely betokens my delight and appreciation at being able to introduce for
its third reading a bill th at has been a long time in gestation. I have to acknowledge at
this stage the support this bill has received across the House. It has been unanimously
supported—

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: It was a good dinner break Cam, was it?

items.speaker: Dr CAM CALDER
items.text: —by my colleagues across the House. Mr Twyford was one of
those to support it. I did not see him at the post -gathering celebrations but he would
have been welcome had he not been so busy, as would my colleague here from New
Zealand First, who is sitting in his leader’s position at the moment.
It is a pleasure to be at this stage, the third reading of the Summary Offences
(Possession of High -power Laser Pointers) Amendment Bill. Those who watch
Parliament TV will have been aware that there was a lot o f debate about this bill at the
Committee stage. I believe Mr O’Rourke was part of that debate. Mr Prosser certainly
was part of that debate and spoke fulsomely in favour of said bill. He is only human. It
was the right thing to do because this bill is sma ll and perfectly formed, and it will
actually significantly increase the safety of all of us who travel by air in New Zealand.
We have got an excellent airline, Air New Zealand. I was privileged to go along to its
annual parliamentary gathering last night.  Once again it surpassed itself in the
excellence of its presentation, and, in fact, it is doing very well on the world stage.
Something like this in New Zealand will improve safety. Legislation does not stop
idiots behaving idiotically. We know that. How ever, the fact that somebody will not be
able to go out and stuff a high -power laser pointer, which many speakers in previous
speeches in the House did point out are actually weapons, in their pocket and expect to
get away with it will mean it will have a preventative aspect.
I first became aware of the dangers of laser pointers in a sporting occasion, strange as
though it may be to report, in 1997 in Montpellier. What was the occasion, I hear you
ask? It was the world pétanque championships. What was happ ening? Some recidivists
in the audience were trying to put off some of the favoured players by shining laser
pointers in their eyes. Even those of us who are not partial to the beautiful game
normally—there are not many people in New Zealand who are totall y immune to the
delights of football. But many of us were watching the World Cup and we saw the
Russian goalie—it was shown all round the world —who was attempting to be in full
modus operandi for deflecting a corner kick. He was, in fact, struck in the fac e, in his
eyes, by a laser pointer. Shortly after there was another attempt on the goal and he failed
to repel that.
That is just a sporting occasion —but, of course, it is never just a sporting occasion.
But it is not talking about the loss of life. More important is the potential loss of life that
could come from laser pointers being used against the pilots of aircraft. Many people in
19430 Summary Offences (High-power Laser Pointers) Amdt Bill 23 Jul 2014
the House, many colleagues across the House, have pointed out the dangers of this. I
believe that this bill will have a pr eventative effect and reduce the chances of this
happening.
Last year there were 119 reported laser attacks on aircraft and helicopters. The point
was made by the New Zealand Airline Pilots’ Association that those are just the ones
that were reported in New Zealand, because foreign aircraft would report their strikes to
their authorities back home. So this bill is timely. This bill is necessary. It will be a
valued legislative tool to improve public safety in our country. I appreciate the
widespread support it has received to date in the House, and I commend this bill to the
House.

items.speaker: PHIL TWYFORD
items.text: I think it is well known that Labour
members are supporting the Summary Offences (P ossession of High -power Laser
Pointers) Amendment Bill. I wanted to use just a few brief moments to pay tribute to
Cam Calder, who gave his valedictory speech this evening. Cam is one of the good guys
of Parliament. The Deputy Speaker is also one of the go od guys of Parliament, but he is
not leaving, as far as I know.

items.speaker: Darien Fenton
items.text: Yes, he is. He is.

items.speaker: PHIL TWYFORD
items.text: Is he?

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: Sadly, he is.

items.speaker: PHIL TWYFORD
items.text: Crikey! That is terrible news, Mr Deputy Speaker. That is
terrible news. All of the good people on the National benches happen to be leaving. I do
not know why that is. But I just want to say that Cam Calder has been a very collegial
parliamentary colleague since he entered this House. He was alw ays good to work with
on the select committees and a good contributor.
This bill will be the legacy of Cam Calder’s parliamentary career. We are supporting
it because we think it is a modest but useful contribution that will prevent some risk to
the travelling public, and particularly the hazard posed by people using laser pointers to
interfere with aircraft that are coming in to land. So Labour is supporting this bill. We
look forward to its progress.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: On behalf of Cam, probably, I
would like to thank Phil Twyford for those nice words. I am sure that they are most
welcome. Yes, I would just like to congratulate Dr Cam Calder as well on the fine
contribution he has made to this Parliament, on this Summary Offences (Possession of
High-power Laser Pointers) Amendment Bill, and also on his great speech this
afternoon. I think there were two words that we had to look up in the dictionary, but
apart from that—

items.speaker: Dr Paul Hutchison
items.text: What about the French?

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: The French was fine. But apart from that, Cam mentioned this
bill in his speech. I think his dedication and desire to make a difference in this
Parliament goes far beyond this bill. It is something that is nice to be able to do today on
Cam’s last official day, you could say, in the House. His contribution is such that it is
much bigger and stronger than this bill, and it is something that we thank you very
much for, and we thank you for your friendship and your support in this Parliament and
for the work that you have done for the National Party.
This bill is a practical piece of legislation that will make a difference. I think during
the select committee process we have all been impressed with the way that all members
of Parliament from the different political parties have worked together constructively to
get the best result we could for this bill. It is something that many New Zealanders
probably do not th ink about that often but it actually can make a huge difference if it
actually does occur in the public arena. There is the issue of a plane being under the
guidance of one of these hand -held lasers, which could cause an accident to occur.
23 Jul 2014 Summary Offences (High-power Laser Pointers) Amdt Bill 19431
Should such an a ccident have occurred, then I think the public would have demanded
that Parliament do something about it. To take this action before that actually occurs is
something that does not often happen in politics or in legislation, but when it can and
does occur it is something that we should all welcome with open arms. I look forward to
the other smaller political parties in this House —the Greens and New Zealand First —
adopting a similar rational approach to the one that Labour has taken to this bill. That is
something that we look forward to.
There were some changes during the progress of this bill through the Transport and
Industrial Relations Committee, really to make sure that we had the best possible
legislation going forward that would cover all the bases an d deliver the right results for
our communities. This is a good piece of legislation. It is something that I think Dr Cam
Calder should be proud of, and we thank him for his wider contribution. We look
forward to the bill passing through this House this evening. Thank you.

items.speaker: DARIEN FENTON
items.text: It is a big day for Cam Calder. I want to join with
others in congratulating him on his valedictory today and also on his third reading
speech on this bill, t he Summary Offences (Possession of High -power Laser Pointers)
Amendment Bill, which was very enlightening. In fact, I have to say that Cam Calder
has lit up this Parliament over his time while he has been here. But he has decided to
turn out the lights on his parliamentary career, so we say that with some regret and we
say farewell to him. [Interruption] I could do more. Do you want more? Would you like
some? OK.
It is a big deal to get a member’s bill through the Parliament and it does not happen
for many members. Certainly I have tried many times. I have had four bills drawn from
the ballot. But I did not have a cooperative party opposite me that was prepared to be as
accommodating as the Labour Party has been with Cam Calder’s bill, in terms of the
spirit with which we conducted the examination of this bill in the Transport and
Industrial Relations Committee and the camaraderie with which we have worked over
the time spent on this bill and on many other bills, in fact. That is a disappointment for
me, but, however, this is Cam Calder’s legacy, and it is not a bad one to leave, actually.
When you think about it, aircraft are very much on our minds at the moment because
of the horrific downing of Malaysia Airlines flight MH17. It just gives you a reminder
of the reality of what happens when a plane comes down, by whatever means. Lasers
and the pointing of high -power lasers being used to deliberately interfere with a flight
path, to shine a light into the pilot’s eyes, and the consequences on public safety an d on
human life, are enormous.
The only note of disappointment I would want to contribute to this debate is that I
missed all the excitement during the Committee stage. I understand that exercised
Government members for just about the whole night, 2 weeks ago. I thought: “Well, this
is great. They are practising their debating skills on such an important bill. They are all
getting up and saying what they think and congratulating Cam Calder, and so on.” But,
of course, the really disappointing thing —it was really disappointing—was that it was
about defeating a Labour member’s bill. That is the truth —that is the truth. It is such an
abuse of parliamentary process. I think that member Cam Calder, who is such an
upstanding MP, probably felt pretty uncomfortable  about that. However, we will get
through the Committee stage of the parental leave bill tonight, and it will be ready to
pass after the election, when Labour wins the election.
Having given my congratulations to Cam Calder, I do say it is a worthy bill, which is
why Labour is supporting it. I really hope we have the same camaraderie tomorrow
when I deliver my valedictory, and you will join me in a verse of solidarity. Thank you.

items.speaker: JAN LOGIE
items.text: I rise to take a short call on the third reading of the Summary
Offences (Possession of High -power Laser Pointers) Amendment Bill, and would like
19432 Summary Offences (High-power Laser Pointers) Amdt Bill 23 Jul 2014
to offer my congratulations to the member on going out in such style. Not many MPs
would get to have a bill passed on the  evening of their valedictory. I think that is quite
an achievement. I do think you are one of those MPs who have worked really
collegially in this House and will be missed.
We are supporting this bill, of course, because it just makes sense and is a good  idea.
I would like to say, though, that some of the joy of this moment, Dr Calder, has been
tainted for me, I have got to say, by the behaviour on the last members’ day of that side
of the House. I notice that things are moving quite quickly this evening on this third
reading. There is actually not much substance. Although it is a very, very important bill,
there is not a huge amount of detail to it. The fact that that side of the House took 23
speeches on the last members’ day to discuss this bill, which has very little detail to it,
does make me very sad, because it was about a political point. That your party chose to
use your bill to do that has tainted it somewhat, I think.

items.speaker: Scott Simpson
items.text: What a sanctimonious, arrogant comment from that Green member.

items.speaker: JAN LOGIE
items.text: I am being called sanctimonious and arrogant for sharing my
disappointment at the fact that this has prevented New Zealand families getting 26
weeks’ paid parental leave before the election. I think that is a bit o f a shame. It was
also a shame hearing some of the members on that side of the House after the debate
last time saying “Well, that was fun.” as they prevented families getting 26 weeks’ paid
parental leave. It was one of the more disappointing moments for me in this House. But
I will leave it there, on a final note of congratulations again to the member on making a
difference and on going out with such flair.
SIMON O’CONNOR (National —Tāmaki): I am really pleased to take a call on
the third reading of the Summary Offences (Possession of High -power Laser Pointers)
Amendment Bill, and to shine a little light on Dr Cam Calder. In fact, I have been
shocked during the course of this bill. I have le arnt two things: first and foremost,
tonight I have learnt you can deliver a valedictory speech and then return to the House
and give a speech. I have almost been as shocked as I was in the Committee stage when
I found out that Mike Sabin was a police officer.

items.speaker: Mike Sabin
items.text: Really?
SIMON O’CONNOR: Yeah, I am still recovering from that.

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: What’s his family background?
SIMON O’CONNOR: Yeah, exactly. Quelle horreur! I do remember, actually, in
speaking in defence of what the last speaker was accusing this side of, that we actually
saw it as relatively important to draw out the important consequences of this bill. I
remember that Committee stage well. In fact, my father was here at that time. I su spect
he is listening in again. He certainly sent his best regards to you, Cam, as you delivered
your valedictory.
This is an important bill. I think the member opposite, Darien Fenton, addressed it
well when she referred quickly but quite appropriately t o what has happened with flight
MH17—not so much the particular nature of how that airliner was downed but the fact
that the bringing down of an aircraft by whatever means is a major incident.
Dr Calder, right at the start, indicated just the sheer number  of times that this
problem with lasers is reported by New Zealand pilots, but, importantly, noted that a lot
of the reports go to other airlines, as is appropriate. This is a problem. It has taken Dr
Cam Calder to see that issue, to engage with the commun ity and those experts in the
field, and to take the time and effort to draft this bill, bring it to the House, guide it
through the House, and bring it now here to the third reading, where —well, looking at
the clock at the moment —it will, I assume, pass un animously tonight. I think it is an
excellent legacy for Cam. Again, an earlier member alluded that not many members of
this House have the opportunity to even have a member’s bill, to get one drawn out, and
23 Jul 2014 Summary Offences (High-power Laser Pointers) Amdt Bill 19433
then if it is drawn out to have it concluded in the House. So, Cam, I think that is yet
another achievement that you have brought here.
I say “yet another” because this bill, a good bill, sits alongside an enormous amount
of other work that Cam has done. I want to quickly highlight two of those elements. The
first, of course, is as a hard -working MP in the heart of Manurewa. As someone who
briefly worked alongside you, Cam, I saw day after day that hard work. It has now
translated into something like this bill here around the summary offences. I think y ou
will be missed, Cam, from this caucus, from this House, and by the people of
Manurewa. I will miss you, mate —that has to be said. The other side, though, is this
Summary Offences (Possession of High -power Laser Pointers) Amendment Bill. It is
not the on ly contribution you have made. Obviously as the chair of the Education and
Science Committee you are bringing to a closure the cross -party inquiry into parental
engagement in schools. I think that is fantastic, as well. But this bill is important, and I
am really pleased that everyone, basically, is supporting it.
The misuse of lasers is a problem. I was talking to police officers a few months’ back
when I had the privilege of going out with them on patrol. They were indicating that
even those on an eagle helicopter were getting blinded. We had in a public meeting i n
Tāmaki a few weeks after that some people from the Airline Pilots’ Association noting
the trouble that it was causing them. We in the Transport and Industrial Relations
Committee have taken quite a bit of time to go through this bill, and I think that wa s
reflected in the Committee stage.
I just want to touch on, as we hit this third reading, some of the elements that the
Committee of the whole House considered. The first is around the name of the bill. I
think actually it was the Hon Kate Wilkinson earli er who, in her valedictory, indicated
that words are important and good wording leads to good ideas. We have changed the
name of this bill, retitling it by using the words “high -power laser pointers”. Initially,
the bill title mentioned hand -held lasers, a nd we thought that it was actually just a bit
too specific. Lasers do not necessarily have to be hand held.
This was a bill whose title we thought we could broaden out. The changed title,
which talks about high -power lasers, accurately reflects the types of lasers that it can
control. We had a lot of debate in the Committee stage around what those types of lasers
were, and a few constituents actually were emailing me at the time —obviously, there is
everything from military use to those interested in astronomy.
One of the things I know Cam rightly pushed for and pushed back against was
around the whole question of the commencement date. Once this bill gets the Royal
assent, should it come into immediate effect? Others said we should push it out for
weeks, o r months. I think, Dr Calder, we came to a good agreement that we would
allow this legislation to come into effect 28 days after it receives the Royal assent. I
would suggest that there is an element of sort of natural justice in the way you have to
give people an opportunity to understand the law and integrate it.
The seizure of lasers was something that was particularly brought to my attention in
a public meeting by a representative of the New Zealand Airline Pilots’ Association
who, it had turned out, w as actually a constituent of mine, so it was doubly good, and
who was wondering about the seizure of these lasers. She was querying why there were
not particular elements or provisions in the bill about this. We considered this, and the
reason it is not sp ecifically there is that we are able to draw on the search and seizure
legislation, which this Government has proudly already pushed through, so we were
able to use that. I think that is an illustration not only of this Government but of the
House understa nding the import of existing legislation and how we use that moving
forward.
19434 Summary Offences (High-power Laser Pointers) Amdt Bill 23 Jul 2014
The last area, as you would expect, was around the whole definition of what a hand -
held laser or a high -power laser device is. We took a long time considering this. We
wanted clarity not only for the public but obviously for the police and the courts. They
are ultimately the ones that need to manage this. We basically went down the line. I
have to read it here specifically. It is the Customs Import Prohibition (High-power Laser
Pointers) Order 2013. So this is an existing law on the statute books, a regulatory
power, given—and I have forgotten the exact name of the official, but they define what
a laser is.
One of the big elements of that is that a pointer needs to have an output of greater
than 1 milliwatt, but I think Dr Calder, in his speeches throughout all stages, has noted
that even the smaller powered lasers can have an impact, but we have felt that it is the
right way to go by defining this as a power output greater than 1 milliwatt. And what is
important here—and those who have heard me talk on various elements of legislation
would note this—is consistency. So this Act in the name of Dr Cam Calder will use the
same structure as that customs import prohibition. [ Bell rung] Although that was a bell
that rang, this is ultimately a bill about lights, and I want to end as I began, which is—

items.speaker: Scott Simpson
items.text: Bells and whistles!
SIMON O’CONNOR : No, no bells and whistles, unfortunately. That might be a
member’s bill for the honourable member for Coromandel. I think, actually, banning
whistles in the likes of Mission Bay late at night would go down very well with my
constituents. But I turn back to Cam Calder, who has sponsored this bill, created this
bill, and drawn it through the House. Cam, I think it is absolutely fantastic that even
post-valedictory you get the opportunity to speak in this House, and may I join with
other colleagues who have spoken in thanking you for your service to Crown and
country and for being just a bloody good mate.

items.speaker: RICHARD PROSSER
items.text: It is always a pleasure to follow the erudite and
enlightening Mr Simon O’Connor. I am very pleased to rise to take a final c all on the
third reading of the good Dr Calder’s most excellent member’s bill, the Summary
Offences (Possession of High -power Laser Pointers) Amendment Bill. New Zealand
First supports this bill. We are proud to support it and pleased to have the opportuni ty to
support it. This is a fine bill, and we in New Zealand First believe that it will make a
quite splendid law.
This is a short, simple bill but it will have quite far -reaching effects. By removing
powerful hand -held laser pointers from the hands of pe ople who have no legitimate
purpose for possessing them, Dr Calder’s bill —his swansong, his legacy for this august
institution—will make New Zealand a safer place. Of this there is no question. As we
debate, even as we plan their demise here in this House of the people, there are ne’er -
do-wells out there who look to the skies with lasers in hand and malice aforethought. Dr
Calder’s bill will make flying in New Zealand a safer undertaking. Removing powerful
lasers from persons of nefarious intent will materi ally lessen the risk and incidence of
such devices being used to interfere with airliners on approach to our airports, with
other aircraft, and with police and rescue helicopters. Indeed, it will make driving on
our roads safer, as well.
We are fortunate here in New Zealand that we have not, as yet, suffered greatly in
the way that some nations have as a result of the same kinds of idiots who think it funny
to blind pilots by using their dangerous toys to dazzle, and to distract drivers on the
motorway. This has happened in other parts of the world, and it would have been only a
matter of time before this country came to suffer similarly. Fortuitously, Dr Calder’s bill
has come before this House and through its processes just in the nick of time.
Via this new mechanism, we the people can negate the potential for harm posed by
such persons and their illicit use of these devices. We can remove the said devices from
23 Jul 2014 Summary Offences (High-power Laser Pointers) Amdt Bill 19435
the possession of the aforementioned scoundrels and bang said scoundrels up at Her
Majesty’s pl easure for a short, sharp 3 months. May it be an unpleasant and
uncomfortable 3 months for anyone so convicted.
Tonight we have been treated to Dr Calder’s valedictory speech as he prepares to
depart these halls for whatever adventure life has in store for  him next, and a fine
speech it was too, I might say —as fine a speech as this bill is a fine bill. Standing
ramrod straight and fixing us with a gaze every bit as steely and direct as any laser
beam, Dr Calder has bid us farewell and left us with this, his  legacy. Well done, I say,
Dr Calder. Well done and thank you—fair winds and flat seas.
We have come to the end of this process of lawmaking. At the conclusion of this
debate we shall vote this bill on to the statutes and into law. It will be a fine law. It is a
necessary law, and, as I have said, a law that has found us just in the nick of time. I do
not intend to delay the passage of it unnecessarily. Over the course of this bill’s passing
through the House, we have learnt about the need for such a piece  of legislation, we
have examined the science of lasers, we have heard harrowing tales from overseas and
from the skies above us, and we have learnt about legitimate uses for lasers, as well.
I bought another one myself only last week. Strolling as I was with no particular
intent, as one does, through one of the admittedly less well -trod corridors of one of the
lower floors of my extensive armoury, I discovered a certain sporting long gun that I
had somehow omitted to fit with a laser sight. That omission,  I can tell the House, has
now been rectified. But that is a legitimate purpose, and what we are dealing with here
is improper use. This bill addresses that improper use. It is a fine bill from a fine
member who will be genuinely missed. We support it, and  I commend it to the House.
Thank you.

items.speaker: MIKE SABIN
items.text: I am very pleased to be able to take my last
call on this bill, the Summary Offences (Possession of High -power Laser Point ers)
Amendment Bill, and I will join with all others in this happy moment, this happy -fest,
to congratulate Dr Cam Calder on his fine valedictory speech today, but more so on his
outstanding contribution to New Zealand, to the community of Manurewa, and to  us, as
a caucus team. You will be sadly missed, my friend. I am saying that only because if I
need a diagnosis of something on the cheap I will obviously be coming to see you.

items.speaker: Hon Michael Woodhouse
items.text: He was an expert on prostate cancer.

items.speaker: MIKE SABIN
items.text: Was he? Well, I will withdraw that request.
In all seriousness, can I just acknowledge Dr Calder for getting a member’s bill
across the line. When it comes down to it, when parliamentarians come and go, there are
very few who will get the honour of being a Minister. I guess that in that position,
certainly, the legacy that Ministers leave is the ability to really be in charge of the
legislative agenda, and many laws are made or taken away, and so forth.
The other vehicle for p arliamentarians in the main is the member’s bill, and many
members’ bills are in the ballot. Some have merit and probably many do not, but the
fact of the matter is that to get a member’s bill drawn from the ballot is pure luck. To
actually succeed in getting a member’s bill passed into law is about skill, determination,
and having an absolute understanding of what this place is about and what the
community needs in terms of legislation.
Members’ bills face exactly the same scrutiny as any Government bill,  so the point I
want to make on that is that although Dr Calder’s effort on this laser bill is something
that most people will not stay awake at night wondering about, it is a very important
piece of legislation. He should be commended for the fact that he  has been a
parliamentarian who has successfully brought a member’s bill through this House and
has been successful in getting it passed. So I just offer my congratulations on that score.
19436 Summary Offences (High-power Laser Pointers) Amdt Bill 23 Jul 2014
Surprisingly enough, we had some quite robust debate on the bill an d a lot of
discussion on a number of the facets of the bill. One of the main ones was whether it
should be about high -power laser pointers or just about hand -held lasers. [Interruption]
Yes, so there was a lot of discussion on that and on where that should  land. I certainly
raised the analogy of when we have the unlawful possession of a knife, for example —
so, the possession of a knife in a public place without a reasonable excuse —where the
offence is not determined by the length of the knife, but it is simp ly that the knife is in
the possession of a person, without reasonable excuse.
I sort of felt that Dr Calder’s point in terms of the same rule applying to a laser
pointer was actually very valid. But as we progressed and looked in more detail at the
implications for all those university professors out there and all those teachers and
people who frequent the land of the hand -held laser, it was clearly determined that with
this being a preventative piece of legislation, it should fall squarely in the area of  high-
power laser pointers, which would ultimately cause the most damage. If Dr Calder can
just remind me, is it 60 miles that the laser could reach?

items.speaker: Dr Cam Calder
items.text: Yes.

items.speaker: MIKE SABIN
items.text: It is an astonishing distance. So Dr Calder gracefully accepted the
advice of the officials, and I actually think it has landed in a very sensible space on that.
The point is that it was last year, I think, when there were more laser strikes on aircraft
than ever before. The Civil Aviation Authority—if I am correct; I am not exactly sure—

items.speaker: Dr Cam Calder
items.text: That’s correct.

items.speaker: MIKE SABIN
items.text: Yes, the Civil Aviation Authority reported that there were more laser
strikes than ever before in the last year, and there has certainly been in excess of 100
strikes a year in recent years, which is phenomenal. When you see how these things
reflect in a cockpit, it literally blinds the pilots. It is horrendously dangerous, which is
why I think that over a number of years now we have actually se en hand -held lasers
used in warring countries to literally bring down aircraft. We have seen them used
against rescue helicopters and a police helicopter.
It defies belief why some idiots out there would think that that is a fun or an
interesting thing to  do, or would even consider doing something as stupid as that.
Possibly it is because they do not know of the impact of them —that they can be so
effective at literally blinding the pilots or bewildering them—but I think that many have
come to that conclusi on, because there has been a lot of publicity on this for a number
of years. So one can only assume that they are actually doing it, knowing full well that
they could bring about a pretty significant outcome. We have seen them doing it at
vehicles from ove rpasses, and so forth. Dr Calder pointed out that we have even seen
them used at the Football World Cup, and they have certainly been used at rugby
matches, and so forth.
There are some serious idiots out there, and this law is about those serious idiots and
about saying that, actually, this is not on and that there will be a consequence to doing
it. This bill will make it an offence to be in possession of a high -power laser pointer
without reasonable excuse, and so it should be. So it is a preventative th ing, rather than
a punitive move, and that is why there is a 28 -day period, I guess. It is to get some
education out there, and to get the police in the right space in terms of them using this
bill as a deterrent. Prevention will always be better than cure  and, my goodness me, if
there was ever a commercial aircraft taken down, heaven forbid.
So in that sense, this bill is in many ways about preventing the loss of life. Although
we have trifled and we have had a bit of fun, Dr Calder, I think it is fair to  say that the
reason this House is supporting this bill is that it is just good, practical, common sense.
It is not the New Zealand First variety of common sense, of course, because that is just
sort of sloganized, populism stuff. This is the real common s ense that New Zealanders
23 Jul 2014 Summary Offences (High-power Laser Pointers) Amdt Bill 19437
actually know and understand, not the one that you just paint on a sticker and that
means that that is what we must have.
In any event, the bill is practical, it is common sense, and it is preventative, and I
think in that sense i t certainly has deserved the support of the House. It has had the
support of the House. I think that Dr Calder should be commended for the fact that he
has been willing to concede some points in this bill, to ensure that it was a bill that was
fit for purp ose right across the House, and with the officials, and so forth. I think the
Labour Party certainly raised some concerns and said that it should apply to high -power
laser pointers. I think that Iain Lees -Galloway famously said in the House that he
actually uses a laser pointer at home to play with his pussy. I was not quite sure where
he was going with that one. I mean, I usually use a ball of wool or something like that,
but fine, play with your pussy with a laser pointer —fair enough. We all have our
different ways of entertaining the cat. Although we did trifle with that, the reality is that
a low-power laser, or one under 1 milliwatt, is it—

items.speaker: Dr Cam Calder
items.text: Under 1 milliwatt.

items.speaker: MIKE SABIN
items.text: It is under 1 milliwatt. You know, if i t is good enough for Iain Lees-
Galloway to play with his pussy, it is probably not likely to cause the sort of damage
that a high-power laser pointer would, and I think that is why we have—

items.speaker: Moana Mackey
items.text: Grow up.

items.speaker: MIKE SABIN
items.text: I am fully grown, I think. I was supposed to be a lot taller, of course,
but something went wrong along the way.
So can I just join the House in commending Dr Calder for this piece of legislation. It
will ultimately be something that does save lives. In all seriousness, I think that the
member should be commended for that, and I wish him very well in his life beyond
politics. He will be remembered well here, and will be a friend to us all for a long time.
Thank you.

items.speaker: ANDREW LITTLE
items.text: It is a pleasure to rise and speak on the Summary
Offences (Possession of High-power Laser Pointers) Amendment Bill. I think that as we
enter the final sitting days of this 50 th Parliament, it is appropriate and timely to embark
on what I think we are all really here for —that is, to act as parliamentarians.
Occasionally, it is permissible to shed the political colours and banners under which we
arrive here in order to celebrate and honour the traditions of this fine Hous e and the role
that it plays at the heart of our democracy. You see that in valedictory speeches, or you
usually do. There were some valedictory speeches in which that generosity of spirit was
not expressed today. That, unfortunately, reflects the true sta te and the modern state of
today’s National Party —lacking in generosity, charmless, graceless, a miserly and
miserable party—which explains, no doubt, why Cam Calder is leaving.
Cam Calder is somebody whom I have come to know in my 3 years here and is a
man amongst men, but he is one of those men who I think genuinely epitomises the
spirit of leadership, compassion, and humanity, which is not widely found in every
political party in this House. Cam Calder has a number of other redeeming features to
him. It helps that he hails from Taranaki —the mighty province, the great province, and
the province generating great wealth not only in its minerals and its financial resources
but in its people. Cam Calder is one of them and he wears, I see tonight, the colours of
Taranaki—a region of which he is so proud even though he does not live there
currently. Of course, he is also known for another great achievement and that is his
pétanque playing. We do not often talk about that about Cam but he is an accomplished
and, indeed, an international-grade pétanque player. I defy any member of this House to
challenge Cam Calder to a game of the mighty boules and see whether they can hit the
kitty or do whatever it is they do with their very heavy, hefty little items.
19438 Summary Offences (High-power Laser Pointers) Amdt Bill 23 Jul 2014
But I want to talk about the legislation —because that is what we are here for, after
all—and to join with my colleagues who have, I think, been very generous not only in
their acknowledgment and honouring of Cam Calder, the author of the bill, but also in
paying due heed and seriousness to the objectives of the bill, which is, as Mike Sabin
has said, a public safety measure. It is about the safe conveyance of passengers and
crew on aircraft. I know that Richard Prosser said the bill is about ensuring that t here is
not improper use of these high -power lasers. Actually, it is not that. It is about the
possession of high -power lasers without reasonable excuse and that is not a subtle
difference; it is a very important distinction. There are very few legitimate uses for these
sorts of devices. Obviously, lecturing, training, and imparting information are some of
them, but there is no need for people to be walking on down the streets or hiding behind
the bushes and dazzling passing traffic whether it is cars, trucks, whatever, and certainly
not air traffic.
This is a well-directed piece of legislation and it rightly has the support of the House
and it has the support of the Labour Party. I think it will send a very clear signal and a
very clear message to those wh o think that this is some zany sort of fun now that there
is an explicit sanction against it and some real penalties against those who would
behave in that sort of way. I congratulate Cam Calder on having the bill selected and
shepherding it through all th e stages. I think there was a pretty good and detailed and
serious consideration of it at the Transport and Industrial Relations Committee. This
will be a good piece of legislation, as that reflects the author of it and the contribution
that he has made to this House in the time that he has been here.

items.speaker: ALFRED NGARO
items.text: It is always good to speak after the member Andrew
Little because he also provides a little platform to speak on. We know that t he party
slogan of the Labour Party is “Vote positive”, but he could not stay on message. He
began negative, and talked about the National Party and all its negatives tones. Some of
us wondered how Labour got its branding and logo. We sort of think the par ty members
got together and they realised that the polls were not doing well, so they had a little
committee. They met together and they questioned what was going wrong. What was
going wrong was that they kept on talking negatively about everything that wa s going
on. So what they said was this: “Let’s go out there and let’s tell people to vote positive.”
The difficult thing for Mr Little is that every time he tries to act positive it is very
difficult and he goes negative. But he did go back on message. I w ould have to give you
that, Mr Little. You went back on message and became very positive as well at the same
time.
I want to join in that positive stance because really tonight is the night we want to
congratulate our member, our colleague, “Mr Tripod” he re, the honourable member
Cam Calder —because he is an honourable member. One thing I have absolutely
enjoyed about our colleague in our time here is that on the many times he has stood up
in the House he has been very passionate, he has been honest, and he  has been true to
his convictions and what he believes is important for the communities that he serves.
Here he is. Yes, he is the man from “the Naki”. He may live on the Shore but when the
opportunity to serve Manurewa came, he went in there, boots and all.

items.speaker: Even today I actually said to Cam
items.text: “That’s right —Manurewa hard.” He said:
“Alfred, we’re no longer going to go there. It’s Manurewa proud.” And he began to tell
me about the reasons. He said that for the community that he serves out in Manurewa,
so many times things have been hard. He said he wants to change that. For the time that
he has been there serving that community —over 6 years —he has been talking about
how this community can be proud of the place that they live in, of the things that they
have there, of the schools and the services they deliver. So I really want to commend
you, Cam, because you have been absolutely a champion of the community of
23 Jul 2014 Summary Offences (High-power Laser Pointers) Amdt Bill 19439
Manurewa. When people look into that community they may judge it by all sorts of
different things, but  as you have worked in there you have wanted to say that
Manurewa, its community and its people, should be proud of the place that they live in,
should be proud of the community that they serve, and should actually grow that
community from the inside out t o be transformative. I want to commend you for the
Government that you have been working in and the role that you have played as well.
It is an honour for anyone to be able to have their own member’s bill drawn, and we
have talked about it being the roll of the dice. There you go —you have come out of the
ballot and you have had your member’s bill drawn. But as my colleague here Mike
Sabin said, it is one thing to get drawn; it is another thing to take the bill to completion.
One thing that I know from my c olleague here is that as Cam Calder has worked on the
Summary Offences (Possession of High-power Laser Pointers) Amendment Bill—

items.speaker: Mike Sabin
items.text: He’s lobbied like you wouldn’t believe.

items.speaker: ALFRED NGARO
items.text: He has lobbied in a way that has made a difference and here is
the proof in the pudding. He has been the chairman of the Education and Science
Committee where he has had to work in a collegial way, knowing that the fact is that the
balance of power can sway either way. That is testament t o your chairmanship. That is
testament to the fact that you have lobbied and you have worked. You wanted to get a
collegial and consensual response to supporting the things that you have led as well.
You have done that and you have done a great job with your bill as well.
There is another thing I want to say about this bill—and it is my first time to speak so
it is actually an honour to be able to speak to this bill. But can I say that people have
commented that it is only a small bill. But it is a small t hing that makes the difference.
You may tick it as an output saying yes, the purpose of this bill is to be preventative in
its impact. But you see it is the outcomes that I often look at, which do make the
difference.
So here are some of the outcomes that  I think make a difference. The bill tells
juvenile offenders who are out there and it tells young people —and we have all been
young in our days—that when they go out there that, yes, you can be a little bit cavalier,
you can maybe go out in a bit of folly  and play. I am trying to use these words that I
know that Mr Cam Calder would use. But the fact is that there comes a time when you
need to be responsible, and I think that is the key word. This is preventative because
people are going to be responsible e ven for the things that they take into their hands.

items.speaker: You have talked about this
items.text: that a hand -held laser can be used in a way that it can
become a weapon. So here is an outcome that it is doing. It is sending a message to
people who are out there to be aware and be responsible for their actions as well.
The second outcome that I think is important is that it puts in the hands of our
enforcement agency a tool that enables them to use this in a way that actually ensures
that they can enforce this provision. It  allows them to be able to take action, if needed,
and to enforce the legislation and the laws that come out of this bill as well.
When we think about this we think about the Malaysia Airlines tragedies and so forth
and what happened there. I began to thi nk about this hand-held laser legislation and the
impact that it could have and I thought about NZ474. That is the 6.40 flight that leaves
Wellington through to Auckland. I know that often Cam and a number of us Auckland
MPs catch that flight. I think on a verage there would be about 12 to 15 MPs on there.
Could you imagine if that flight NZ474 was coming down to land in Auckland and it
was blinded by a laser, all of a sudden it lost its path, and the tragedy of all tragedies
happened and 15 MPs of Parliamen t were tragically taken away? That would be a
tragedy of all tragedies. We could have been in that situation.

items.speaker: Dr Cam Calder
items.text: Some people may disagree with that.
19440 Summary Offences (High-power Laser Pointers) Amdt Bill 23 Jul 2014

items.speaker: ALFRED NGARO
items.text: That is right. We laugh at it and we jest, but the  truth of it is
that in the wrong hands, in an irresponsible way, we know that hand -held lasers can
cause damage. We know that, for instance, as has been quoted, the number of incidents
of laser strikes has increased and it can only increase unless this bi ll, which is an
important bill, enforces a key message of responsibility for people who are out there as
well.
What we also know is important is that this has caused damage. Here is some of the
evidence that we know is out there. In June 2011 a young boy who played with a laser
purchased in Thailand reflected the beam in his eye through a mirror and he suffered
damage to his eye. We know they cause harm. In June 1998 at a Waikato rugby union
game approximately 30 cases of arc eye were reported after a rugb y match. So we know
that it does happen, we know the impact that it has, and we know the damage it can
cause.
I just want to finally finish up on this. I just want to acknowledge my colleague. He
will go out there. I just say that it is a proud moment to be able to ensure that at this
third reading he has got unanimous support. Not many bills get unanimous support, so
that you can say that right across the House people support its intent, they support its
action—not only its output but its outcomes —to trul y make a difference to our
communities. I salute you, Dr Cam Calder, and thank you for your work and for your
service to New Zealand, to this Parliament, and to the National caucus.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: This is a split call—Sue Moroney.

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: On the issue of every party in the House supporting
this Summary Offences (Possession of High -power Laser Pointers) Amendment Bill,
can I say that, yes, it is supporte d by every party, and therefore how bizarre it was that
the bill was filibustered for so long, given every party supports it.
But before I come back to that issue, can I just congratulate Dr Cam Calder on his
valedictory speech today, on his parliamentary career, and on the very, very good timing
of getting a third reading of a member’s bill through on the same day as his valedictory.
That is some remarkable feat of timing, and I congratulate him on that.
However, on the issue of timing, I am very disappo inted that this bill has been used
to stop families from getting 26 weeks’ paid parental leave. I think it is a very great
shame that that has been the primary use of this bill, because it deserves so much better
treatment than that by the National Party. But that is indeed what has happened. It is an
important measure that is being dealt with here. It is one that is worthy of Parliament’s
time, but it was not worthy of that much parliamentary time, quite frankly. I do take it a
little personally. I had my parents here on their 59 th wedding anniversary, and they had
to sit and listen to the most bizarre, boring speeches from the National Party about
lasers.
Denis O’Rourke: That’s normal.

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: I know it is normal. But I had to explain to my parents why this
was happening. The fact that it was happening was an affront to New Zealand families,
and that is the great shame of it. I know that the National Party members opposite have
just made reference to a couple of times whe n the Labour Party has filibustered. Can I
say that the Labour Party has never filibustered to get in the way of supporting families.
That has never happened, and shame on the National Party for using this bill in order to
do that.
However, my congratulat ions go to Dr Cam Calder. I think it is a great shame the
way that this bill has been used, but I congratulate him none the less on bringing it
forward to this Parliament, having it debated, and getting it through its third reading.

items.speaker: STEFFAN BROWNING
items.text: I am pleased to be able to speak briefly to this
bill, the Summary Offences (Possession of High -power Laser Pointers) Amendment
23 Jul 2014 Summary Offences (High-power Laser Pointers) Amdt Bill 19441
Bill, as well. I note that when it was first presented to the Tr ansport and Industrial
Relations Committee following its first reading it needed some tuning as such. Tuning
maybe is the right word when we are talking about lasers. It is good that the bill has
ended up where it is, and I congratulate Dr Cam Calder on th at. The current bill is
probably what was aimed for in the first place, and it was probably a little bit broad
initially.

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: Excuse the pun.

items.speaker: STEFFAN BROWNING
items.text: Yes, many puns. That is one of the congratulations. Th e
other congratulation is, again, for Dr Calder’s valedictory speech and some of the points
in there. Some I might have found a little bit too much towards the National Party style
and philosophy, and I did not agree with it all, but I felt it was a very g ood speech all
the same.
I would like to congratulate Cam as well—and I just use this laser bill in terms of the
protections it is intending —on his wearing of the white ribbon. As a White Ribbon
ambassador I have looked even further today, Cam. I fully in tend, and it will be on the
Hansard, to get you nominated to be an ambassador for the future. We have talked
about it at times, and it is a shame that I have not had the response from White Ribbon
to ensure that this has happened. But we need a couple of r eferees, and the job will be
done.
I would like to leave with those congratulations. Again, in terms of filibustering, I
find it is a shame as we could have had another bill through, such as the foreign -
chartered vessels bill. If we had managed to get som e other bills through too, that bill
would have stopped a lot of harm to another bundle of people. It is great that this bill is
here, but the foreign -chartered vessels bill should get through. It would be great if
National would see the way to get it through next week. Thank you.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: This is a split call—two National calls.

items.speaker: SCOTT SIMPSON
items.text: It is a pleasure to rise in support of
this very good bill in the name of my friend and colleague Dr Cam Calder, the
Summary Offences (Possession of High -power Laser Pointers) Amendment Bill. I have
not participated in this debate previously, nor did I sit on the Transport and Indust rial
Relations Committee, but I have had an opportunity to hear some of the debate —some
of the very good debate —that has occurred in the lead -up to this third reading. I have
got to say that I am disappointed to hear from the members opposite who somehow
want to discount the role and right of this member, Dr Cam Calder, to bring his bill to
the House, to have it debated fully and properly and have it adequately considered by
this House, because they think that their bill somehow has some kind of precedence,  or
some kind of greater moral importance or substance than Dr Calder’s bill. That is an
arrogance of enormous proportion, but it is an arrogance of proportion that we see so
often, particularly from members of the Green Party and the Labour Party.
It is a very big day for Dr Calder. I have had the very great privilege of knowing Dr
Calder for a good number of years. In fact, in a previous life I was chair of the northern
region of the National Party, and I well remember a conversation had, maybe about 10
years ago, when Dr Calder asked to meet with me and he had an important matter to
discuss.

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: In Auckland?

items.speaker: SCOTT SIMPSON
items.text: We were in Auckland at that stage. Dr Calder said that he had
an important matter that he wanted t o discuss me, and so I met with him over coffee, I
think, and he revealed to me that he wanted to pursue a parliamentary career. He wanted
to offer himself to the National Party as a candidate. He said that he wanted to take his
voluntary role further, to the next step, to become a candidate and then ultimately a
member of this Parliament, and he did that. He has worked hard and diligently all that
19442 Summary Offences (High-power Laser Pointers) Amdt Bill 23 Jul 2014
period of time. He sought selection a couple of times, then ended up as a list MP, and
has done six very good, solid years, not only on behalf of his party but on behalf of this
Parliament and the people of New Zealand. I want to congratulate him and I want to
share my words of support, along with other members who this evening have also
wanted to express their su pport, and congratulations on his very fine valedictory speech
delivered this afternoon.
This bill is one that is very important. I do not share the view of Opposition members
that it is somehow of minor importance. This is a bill that is all about closing off an area
of potential harm and risk to New Zealanders, particularly when they are travelling. I
think that it is a very important matter. I like the way that the select committee has
relabelled the bill, to indicate the better definitional approach to  the naming. To call it
the Summary Offences (Possession of High -power Laser Pointers) Amendment Bill
does, I think, more accurately reflect the type of laser it seeks to control. Those
possessing these lasers will be treated in the same way as someone who  maybe is
carrying a knife in a public place without lawful cause or purpose, and I think this is
very appropriate. As a previous speaker —my colleague Mike Sabin from Northland —
said, there are some irresponsible ratbags who are part of our society. They ar e
irresponsible. They are irresponsible in their actions and they are irresponsible in the
way that they use these devices, with real harm and potential harm being done to people
on public transport, particularly aircraft.
This is, I think, a very good bi ll. It is a bill that has been well considered both at the
select committee and in this Chamber. Currently, there are no laws to govern the
possession of hand-held lasers in a public place. One would think that even with modern
technology moving quickly, i t would be the responsibility of this House to keep up to
date with these things. That sometimes is not the case, and so sometimes it is beholden
upon members to use the member’s bill process in this manner to achieve the result that
Dr Calder has been able to do.
It is very appropriate that tonight, on the same evening that Dr Calder has given his
very fine valedictory after six very successful years of contribution to this House, to the
National Party, and to the Parliament of New Zealand, we should be p assing this bill in
his name. It is my absolute pleasure and delight to stand here, as one of the final
speakers in this debate, in support of his wonderful personal achievement. I congratulate
him, and endorse this bill with enormous energy to the House f or its finest
commendation. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: I want to thank my
colleague and friend Scott Simpson for the opportunity to sh are this call and I also give
acknowledgment and congratulations to Dr Cam Calder not only on getting this
Summary Offences (Possession of High -power Laser Pointers) Amendment Bill
through to the finish line but also on his contribution to the National Par ty caucus and
also to the class of 2008, of which he is such a valued member who will be missed. One
of the things we will miss, I think, is his erudite articulation, his ratiocination, and the
extra-large words he is able to inject into his speeches.
He is a member of the parliamentary sports club, the Parliamentary Rugby Team. We
will miss him rising like a salmon from the middle of the line -out, leaping for and
catching those balls for the half back to spread wide and, as our colleague Chris
Tremain said, for those twinkle-toed wingers to get all the glory. What we will not miss
are those embarrassing things that poke out the bottom of his shorts and that he calls
legs, which skinny sparrows would be embarrassed to call legs. Nevertheless, somehow
they do eject him into the air, and he can catch the ball with such aplomb.
At the risk of injecting a little bit of negativity in here, I want to add my voice to the
rejection of the criticisms that somehow in the Committee stage of this bill there was
23 Jul 2014 Summary Offences (High-power Laser Pointers) Amdt Bill 19443
