filibustering of the worst sort. I will say two things about that. Firstly, it is the
chairman’s prerogative to decide the length, quality, and quantity of the debate in the
Committee stage, no one else’s. Secondly, if there was a textbook written about
filibustering, it was written by the Labour Party in 2011 at the end of the 49th Parliament
in the Committee stage of the Royal Society of New Zealand Amendment Bill. Those in
that Parliament will remember the Royal Society of New Zealand Amendment Bill. It
was not  filibustered for a day; it was not filibustered for a week. We spent about 9
months talking about a bill that did not matter so that that party could avoid a member’s
bill in the name of Heather Roy being passed in that Parliament. It was unsuccessful—

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: It wasn’t against families.

items.speaker: Hon MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: Oh! See, there is the moral high ground. It was
not as noble as Sue Moroney’s bill. There we go. It is the arrogance of the noblesse, and
I do not accept it. I do not expect we would agree with that at all.
I want to just touch on Darien Fenton’s comments, because she spoke with a note of
sadness, I think, of the fact that she had had four bills drawn out of the members’ ballot
but was not able to get one passed. I just want to remind her that she will go down in the
history of the 49th Parliament as the first member for 88 years in this Parliament to have
a member’s bill defeated at the Committee stage. She was the unfortunate victim, I
suppose, of the fact that the Government had changed between the second reading and
the Committee stage of the bill she had. But she will be noted for that. I certainly
acknowledge her for her efforts, and we will hear her valedictory tomorrow, I think.
It is  time, as we come to the end of the 50 th Parliament, to acknowledge the
contributions of all members. I particularly want to talk about Dr Calder’s commitment
to Manurewa because I know as much as anybody how hard it is to be a list MP in a red
seat and to act in all respects like a constituency MP. It is a thankless task. “List MP” is
a pejorative term amongst some. But I have seen his effort, his energy, and the
commitment he has made to the people of Manurewa and the people of New Zealand. I
think he can hold his head high and describe himself as one of this Parliament’s best list
MPs in serving the community that this party, this caucus, asked him to serve. I think
that of all the things he will be remembered for, it will be this bill, it will be his collegial
support of this great Government, and it will also be his commitment to the people of
Manurewa. For that, Dr Calder, you can hold your head high. I commend you and I
commend the bill.
Bill read a third time.

PAID LEAVE) AMENDMENT BILL
In Committee
Debate resumed from 25 June.
Clause 2  Commencement (continued)

items.speaker: ALFRED NGARO
items.text: Kia orana, Mr Chair.

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Meitaki.

items.speaker: ALFRED NGARO
items.text: Meitaki maata, Mr Chair. I rise to take a call on this Parental
Leave and Employment Protection (Six Months’ Paid Leave) Amendment Bill. I want
to begin by saying that we know that families are important, and children are important
to us. I know that in the last Committee debate on this bill there were a number of
accusations coming from across the Chamber. I wanted to stand to speak because one of
the accusations was that we as politicians on this side of the Chamber, in this
Government, do not care for families and do not care for children, and that is absolutely
19444 Parental Leave etc. (Six Months’ Paid Leave) Amdt Bill 23 Jul 2014
not tr ue at all. I also want to make the point that the comments that seemed to keep
coming from the other side were that because we oppose this bill, we do not care for
children, we do not care for families, and that is not true at all.
It is not true at all, because when we look at the record of this Government, and at
the things that are absolutely important to this Government —at a time when we had the
global financial crisis and at a time when things were difficult —it has been said time
and time again that t his Government actually stood firm and stood strong on the things
that were absolutely important, and that is our children and our families and the things
that matter most to most Kiwis. So I just want to put on record that we absolutely do not
agree with the comments that have been made from the Opposition at all.
So how do we show that? This Government has actually said quite clearly in regard
to paid parental leave that it was not against the aspect of the time period. In fact, it has
shown in Budget 2014 that it has been extended by another 4 weeks. Why? Because the
fact is that, as in all Governments and in governance, you have to balance your
responsibilities along with the rights that are actually important, and that is what this
Government has absolutely done. These are the things that actually show.
For those who are New Zealanders out there, those who are Kiwis out there, those
who are mums and dads and families out there, who want to know what this
Government has done and is doing in that regard,  Budget 2014 was really clear. We
wanted to continue that role of working for families in New Zealand. So what is
important is around health —free general practitioner visits and free prescriptions for
children under the age of 13. We have increased that ab ility so that the mums and dads
who are out there know that when their child is sick, they can take their child to the
doctor and can get a prescription. In fact, it was Mr Faafoi who was talking about being
down in Porirua where he saw prescriptions sitti ng on a chemist’s shelf, waiting for
parents to pick them up. Mr Faafoi actually talked about that. He talked about
prescriptions in Porirua—you will remember that in his speech —and about how parents
were waiting to pick them up, but they could not afford them.
It is quite clear that the extension by this Government to have not only free general
practitioner visits but also the ability to pick up those prescriptions, Mr Faafoi, is
important. We do care to ensure that families do get the medication they nee d, as well.
He is getting ready now. I can see a speech coming from him, but there is more to come.
The other thing that is important is that 4 weeks’ extra paid parental leave has been
extended to a number of caregivers who were not traditionally eligibl e, and that
becomes important. We have increased the parental tax credit by $70 a week to $220 a
week and extended it by 2 weeks to 10 weeks. That, we know, is truly making a
difference to those families out there.
What is also important out there is the issue around education. We know that
ensuring our children can get into early childhood education makes a difference to their
ability to go from the non -compulsory sector into the compulsory sector. We think that
is important. In order to be able to do tha t, again the party of actions has ensured, Mrs
Martin—the fact is that we have increased early childhood education services, to get
more kids participating and to keep fees down, so that parents can access those services,
like Nukutukulea, for instance, in  Māngere, where we took the Prime Minister, and
where he met with that Niuean preschool and where they celebrated and enjoyed the
fact that we have extended those hours as well.

items.speaker: Le'aufa'amulia Asenati Lole-Taylor
items.text: Same name, last one.

items.speaker: ALFRED NGARO
items.text: That is right, Mrs Asenati Lole - Taylor. They made sure that
they enjoyed the opportunity to extend their care. This is what they actually said. They
said: “Thank you, Prime Minister, because under your Governm ent we have thrived as
23 Jul 2014 Parental Leave etc. (Six Months’ Paid Leave) Amdt Bill 19445
well.” So we know that participation in early childhood education has grown as well
under this Government.
The other thing that is important is to say that we care for our children. I have been
involved in a sector where we know that our children are vulnerable. The issues of
abuse and neglect have been of great concern to this Government as well, so we have
extended support for vulnerable children. It includes eight new children’s teams to work
with at-risk children and families, and to support children in care as well. That becomes
absolutely important as well. With extended and expanded paid parental leave, a nd
increasing the parental tax credit, this will give parents more choices about what is best
for them at an important time for their families as well.
The other thing we have done as well that is important is around, again, extending
the ability for heal th, early childhood education, and secondary education, and I know
that becomes important. I know that Ms Martin is talking about the fact of charter
schools and so forth, and we know that that becomes a point of difference, because it
gives communities—[Interruption] Here we go again.
I challenge Ms Martin to go to those communities, look them in the eye, and say to
them that their vision for their children, young and old, and parents who are looking
after their children —I challenge that member to go to them and say to them that,
actually, their vision of a better tomorrow and a better outcome for their children is not
valid. I challenge her to do that. She will not do that. Instead, she will sit here, with
parliamentary privilege, and begin to quote all the things that she thinks go wrong, but
she will not enter those communities. Why? Because they are the very communities that
have actually asked for it, they need it, and they want it, as well. That becomes
absolutely important to what we are doing.
I just want to begin to slowly sort of sum up what I want to say on this, because I
think it is absolutely important. It is making a difference. I do want to say that those
schools—and I want to acknowledge the Rise UP school as well —are really important.
They have said there in Māngere that these are the things that they need for their
children, whether young or old, children who have got parents, and parents with their
children whom they are bringing along. They are saying that that is absolutely important
to them as well.
We know that the fact is that as a Government we are doing all the things that are
necessary and that are needed to care for children, from health to education. At the same
time too, we want to say that caring for children is not just abou t extending parental
leave. It is about a whole range of things that make a difference to our families in our
communities as well. I stand on behalf of the Government to say that we oppose this
bill, but what we do support is children. We do support parent s in their role to care for
their children as well, hence the stance that we are taking at the moment. I stand here as
a father of four children and a grandfather of two, knowing the fact is that the things we
are doing do make a difference. I am confident  in knowing that fact. What I do support
is the fact that—

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: I move, That the question be now put.

items.speaker: KANWALJIT SINGH BAKSHI
items.text: Sat sri akaal, Mr Chair. Thank you for
your consideration of my call. It is my pleasure to discuss clause 2 of this bill, the
Parental Leave and Employment Protection (Six Months’ Paid Leave) Amendment Bill.
National is very concerned about the future of this country. That is why we have been
working on very well -managed spending, where we can afford what we have achieved
in these 6 years. What we can afford in the Budget is because of that well -balanced
spending. However, at the same time I would like to say that children and families are at
the forefront of every Budget. At the same time we want to ensure that as a country we
attain a balance between the bringing up of our children and the financial implications
19446 Parental Leave etc. (Six Months’ Paid Leave) Amdt Bill 23 Jul 2014
for the nation due to the increase in the amount of paid parental leave. Also, we have to
consider the intergenerational effects on the debt that this bill seeks to create for our
children, whose well-being we are all seeking.
To share with you some facts, al l of us know that the recent Budget announcement
by our finance Minister invests almost $500 million in developing our children. Further,
the investment made by the National-led Government in various sectors of the economy
will no doubt result in more jobs  and higher wages. The flow -on effect of this is that it
will result in better lifestyles for our families. There is further facility for the
Government’s participation in health and well -being of our children. The Government
announced free GP visits and f ree prescriptions for children under the age of 13 years.
We extended paid parental leave by 4 weeks, which we consider is affordable at this
stage.
We do not think that this country can afford the reckless spending that this bill
proposes. There is an in crease in the parental tax credit by $70 to $220 a week, and
leave is extended by 2 weeks to 10 weeks. These are some of the measures that we have
taken now. New Zealanders understand that all this comes at a cost and that the
Government is doing everythin g practically possible to look after each of our citizens,
young or old. We debated all these issues in the Government Administration Committee
and also considered them in the submissions. However, we were unable to reach an
agreement. During the select co mmittee there was huge discussion about these issues
and whether the Government can afford these measures or not. Increasing paid parental
leave to 26 weeks is unaffordable right now.
Families will benefit from the growing economy and from jobs with highe r wages. It
will also be appropriate that they are among the first to benefit from the Government’s
spending as the economy picks up.

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Order! Narrow it a little.

items.speaker: KANWALJIT SINGH BA KSHI
items.text: Changes to paid parental leave and the parental
tax credit, alongside other measures in Budget 2014, will provide increased, targeted
support within the current economic conditions for working parents and newborn
babies. In t he first year of the child’s life, particularly in the first 6 months, it is
important for the newborn baby’s development to get full -time personal care. It is also
important for the parents and the caregivers to get support to manage budgetary and
other m easures. Encouraging the attachment of mothers and caregivers to the labour
market has broad economic and social benefits and can support a stable family
environment for their children to grow up in. I think this is appropriate for the
Government, which ha s already made some real progress on this area, and I think we
will continue as time proceeds.

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: I move, That the question be now put.
A party vote was called for on the question that the question be now put.

items.speaker: TIM MACINDOE
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr
Chairperson. The member Jacinda Ardern has twice now taken a closure motion, once
when it was rejected by you. It is my understanding that under the Standing Orders it is
not possible to do that more than once for any particular clause, and I am wondering

member can take more than one closure motion. It was a change by the Standing Orders
Committee. I could be wrong, and I am happy to seek advice on it, but it is my

items.speaker: MIKE SABIN
items.text: I leapt lightning -like to my feet there, Mr
Chairperson. I want, firstly, to take a minute to acknowledge the member Sue Moroney,
like I did with Dr Cam Calder. Yes, getting a member’s bill drawn is luck, but actually
bringing it to the House is challengi ng; I absolutely can see that. Although, obviously,
National has a policy difference, I just want to acknowledge the member for the fact that
she is very passionate about the Parental Leave and Employment Protection (Six
Months’ Paid Leave) Amendment Bill.  She has lobbied strongly on it, and I
acknowledge the efforts that have gone in there.
From the perspective of National, clearly we depart in policy on a couple of levels. I
would have to say that on a personal level I also believe that paid parental leave is not
actually the answer to vulnerable children, and it is not actually the answer for
communities in the sense that the most important role that a parent will have is to
support, to love, to nurture, and to bring up their child, and that is not ne cessarily
something that is about the Government. In fact, if one asks me, I actually think that the
less involvement the Government can have in the bringing up of a child the better.

items.speaker: Denis O'Rourke
items.text: Disgraceful.

items.speaker: MIKE SABIN
items.text: W ell, it is not disgraceful. Why does the member think it is
disgraceful? Why does the member think it is disgraceful?

items.speaker: Denis O'Rourke
items.text: The Government should be interested in children.

items.speaker: MIKE SABIN
items.text: No, no; I did not say that the Government should not be interested in
children, but the primary—

items.speaker: Denis O'Rourke
items.text: That’s a contradiction of what the previous speaker said.

items.speaker: MIKE SABIN
items.text: Well, the member is right off track. The member is right off track
because the Government is far less important in a child’s life than the parents. The
parents’ responsibility is one that will always be primary and will always usurp the
responsibility of anyone or anything else. I believe that very firmly. So although I do
see a place for paid parental leave—

items.speaker: Denis O'Rourke
items.text: It’s nonsense.

items.speaker: MIKE SABIN
items.text: It is not nonsense. It is not nonsense at all, Denis O’Rourke —it is
not nonsense at all, Denis O’Rourke. It is about ensuring, certainly from this par ty’s
perspective, that the primary responsibility of parenting is the responsibility of the
parent. Responsibility is about sacrifice. There are plenty of times in a parent’s life
when they will have to put themselves second and the needs of their child we ll ahead of
them. The sad reality is that in this country—

items.speaker: Tracey Martin
items.text: That’s what you’re saying, isn’t it, Mr Sabin —only people with
money can have children.

items.speaker: MIKE SABIN
items.text: That squawking does get to me. The sad reality is that in this country
the default position of far too many parents is that the Government should take the
primary responsibility role —it is the Government that should take that primary
responsibility role. That,  in my world, is wrong. If you ask me why so many families
are falling apart, it is because they have forgotten what it is to be a responsible parent. It
is not the role of the Government to take over the responsibility of parenting.
19448 Parental Leave etc. (Six Months’ Paid Leave) Amdt Bill 23 Jul 2014
When it comes to paid parental leave, most will actually put their child first and they
will make the sacrifices not for 14 weeks, not for 16 weeks, not for 26 weeks, but for 5
years or beyond. There is no magic figure that is the amount of time people should
spend with their children. The reality is that if a parent can spend the first 5 years, the
formative years, of a child’s life with them full time, that will be the best for that child.
It is not about 26 weeks. It is not about 18 or 16 weeks. Sure, there will be some—

items.speaker: Denis O'Rourke
items.text: An anti-parent speech.

items.speaker: MIKE SABIN
items.text: Well, that is absolute rubbish, Denis O’Rourke. That is absolute
rubbish. It is the parent’s responsibility to be a parent first and foremost, and that is not
about the Governmen t stepping in and usurping that role. Regardless of what support
exists out there, the primary responsibility should always be, and will always rest, with
the parent. Although I acknowledge that the member cares passionately about this
particular bill, the  Government opposes it because we believe we have got the balance
right.

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: Look, it has become obvious already that the National
Party members are going to continue to play their polit ical games with the Parental
Leave and Employment Protection (Six Months’ Paid Leave) Amendment Bill. This is
the last members’ day of the parliamentary session, of this term of Parliament.

items.speaker: Hon Christopher Finlayson
items.text: What a deadbeat. What a mediocrity.

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: And, yes, Christopher Finlayson, the National Party members are
at it again, playing political games in order to get in the way of families having the
support of 26 weeks’ paid parental leave. Well, it is  a disgrace. It is a disgrace, and it is
on display for the nation to see, so feel proud of yourselves, National Party members. I
do not think that the rest of the nation enjoys this at all. I do not think they are enjoying
seeing you actually be disrespectful to families in this way. I think it is a great shame.
Here we are, debating clause 2 of the bill, and we are supposed to be talking about
the commencement date. Just in case any of the members are interested —because they
have not spoken once about th e commencement date yet —this bill brings 22 weeks’
paid parental leave in on 1 July. It brings that in on 1 July next year, compared with that
Government’s offering of just 16 weeks. This bill would bring it in at 22 weeks and
then, finally, 26 weeks on 1 July 2017. Those are the commencement dates. That is
what we ought to be talking about. But I just say to all of those parties in here that
actually do respect families, that do really want to support families in this way, let us
just get on, do the voting, and do the right thing by families and by children.

items.speaker: KRIS FAAFOI
items.text: I move, That the question be now put.
A party vote was called for on the question, That the question be now put.
Ayes 56
New Zealand Labour 34; Green Party 14; New Zealand First 7; Mana 1.
Noes 63
New Zealand National 59; Māori Party 3; United Future 1.
Motion not agreed to.

items.speaker: JONATHAN YOUNG
items.text: I am pleased to stand and
speak on the Parental Leave and Employment Protection (Six Months’ Paid Leave)
Amendment Bill. I want to just say that I endorse Mike Sabin’s comments —and I am
sure many members of this Committee also endo rse them—regarding the responsibility
of parenthood.
Although one member across the other side talked about the responsibility of the
Government, the Government cannot be the parent of every child. Every child comes on
23 Jul 2014 Parental Leave etc. (Six Months’ Paid Leave) Amdt Bill 19449
to this earth because of two parents. What we need to do is continue to encourage adults
and teenagers in this country who end up being parents to take on the responsibility of
that parenthood with great seriousness. Although the Government might be there to
assist and prop up, sometimes we go too far. When we go too far, we dilute the
responsibility that people need to take for their individual lives and for their children. It
does not mean that this Government does not care. It does not mean—[Interruption]

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Order! [ Interruption] Order! Just
two things. First of all, I would like to advise members that barracking is not acceptable
in the people’s House. This is a place for debate. Members will conduct themselves
with t he respect for the traditions of the House as enshrined in the Standing Orders.
That is the first thing I want to say. The second thing I want to say is that this is a debate
on clause 2; we are not on clause 3.

items.speaker: JONATHAN YOUNG
items.text: The commenc ement clause —well, I believe that this bill
should not commence, because it goes too far. We believe that there needs to be some
support for parents. We do believe that, but we need to have support for parents that
goes far enough, but not too far, and tha t does not dilute the responsibility that parents
have.

items.speaker: Tracey Martin
items.text: No, no, no—not too far!

items.speaker: JONATHAN YOUNG
items.text: I do not know about you, but I was raised—

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: JONATHAN YOUNG
items.text: I do not know about that member across there, but I was
raised in South Taranaki, one child out of seven, by farming parents who worked
incredibly hard and who managed. And I believe that when people are face d with those
challenges of how to manage —yes, with the appropriate support but not so much
support that they abdicate their responsibility —then they develop resources, they
develop strength of character, and they develop ways in which they can care, not just for
their own family but for their community as well.
So many of the families in our community, when I was a young boy, helped each
other, and I think it is a sad day when that stops and all the help comes from the
Government—that faceless group of peo ple in Wellington who have this incredible
sense of obligation placed upon them by people who think that they do not have the
resources. I think it is important to find those resources amongst families, extended
family, amongst community, and amongst grand parents. I mean, how many
grandparents actually fulfil a great role of assisting their families and their
grandchildren? Many, many, many do, and I think that that is a great thing. It brings the
great sense of connection and purpose and fulfilment that they all have.
We believe that supporting parents is a very important thing. Supporting children is a
very important thing. The Vulnerable Children Act is one of the most significant pieces
of legislation to go through this Parliament, and that is all about  supporting children.
The Government Administration Committee that reported on Sue Moroney’s Parental
Leave and Employment Protection (Six Months’ Paid Leave) Amendment Bill could
not come to agreement. That is because there are differences of opinion. This is what—

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: No, it’s because we didn’t have the numbers.

items.speaker: JONATHAN YOUNG
items.text: No, there are differences of opinion, Ms Ardern. There are
differences of opinion, and that is what this place is all about. It is abo ut differences of
opinion. We can come into this debating chamber and we can debate our viewpoints,
and I think that is what New Zealand likes to see. There will be myriads of people out
there who will support Sue Moroney and myriads who will not. We are t he
representatives of viewpoints, not only our own but the viewpoints of others in our
communities. I know that, yes, there are people who are very concerned when they see
deprivation and when they see hardship, but the solutions to that are not always the
19450 Parental Leave etc. (Six Months’ Paid Leave) Amdt Bill 23 Jul 2014
same. So that is why sometimes we come to this place and we find that there are
differences of opinion.

items.speaker: TRACEY MARTIN
items.text: Kia ora, Mr Chairperson. I would like to speak
about the commenceme nt date, which is in clause 2. I believe that the commencement
date is appropriate —totally appropriate —for this sort of a bill, and actually should
probably be brought forward. But just while I talk about that, on the comments of the
previous speaker, Jonathan Young, I just want to remark on his hard -working parents in
the Taranaki, I believe it was. I agree with the honourable member Mr Young that his
parents were probably an exceptionally hard -working farming family, who were
supported by their Government  with family support for the first 15 years of his life.
They could capitalise on it for their first family home, and that got them ahead. If this
bill commenced on the commencement date in clause 2, it would merely be a step
towards restoring the support that families used to get before the neo -liberal movement
of the National Party. Kia ora.

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: I am going to do a very novel act in this
Committee tonight and speak to the clause, as I implore my colleagues across the other
side of the Chamber to give that a go. Clause 3 is the amendment to the principal Act of
the Parental Leave and Employment Pro tection Act 1987. I think it is a good
opportunity for us to reflect on the fact that multiple amendments have been made to the
principal legislation that set out originally paid parental leave. We often learn a lot from
history. We learn sometimes that po sitions change. That is particularly the case for
National. I applaud the fact that it has moved away from its ideological problem with
paid parental leave, because it did have that problem in the first instance.
Labour introduced this scheme in 2002, when  there was obviously a surplus at that
time because we ran nine Budget surpluses, FYI. At that time, Anne Tolley in 2002
stated the following: “This legislation … shows how the Labour -Alliance Government
is stuck in the radical feminist era of the 1960s an d 1970s … and is completely out of
23 Jul 2014 Parental Leave etc. (Six Months’ Paid Leave) Amdt Bill 19451
touch with women of the 21 st century and their diverse involvement in today’s labour
force. … This is bad legislation. It is a travesty.” Anne Tolley, a Minister of this
Government, called paid parental leave a travesty. And now members on that side of the
Chamber try to implore, hand on heart, that, yes, they believe in it but just a little bit. So
enough that we can have it to just where they are comfortable with it, but anything that
we suggest is a travesty.
Well, let me put on record tonight for those members of the Committee: one day you
will reflect on your position here and now, and you will be as ashamed as you are now
of Anne Tolley’s comments in 2002. It took only a little bit over a decade for a little bit
of reflection and to look back and say “Well, we were wrong.”, and surely you admit
that was wrong, because you have even taken a position that has gone further than what
was introduced in 2002. So it would be bizarre if you continued to agree with Anne
Tolley’s position. Just to be fair though, she was not the only one. Nick Smith in 2002
said: “I say that if a member went out of their way to draft a dumb bill, this would have
to be it.” He said that he had looked around the world at various paid parental leav e
models and this one was as bad as they get. Apparently Nick Smith has now moved to it
being so bad that National is going to keep it and extend it just a little bit, until it is
comfortable with it. Obviously he has supported the changes that the Governm ent made
in the Budget.
And it continued. It was not just 2002 because, of course, we extended paid parental
leave in 2004, because that is what Labour does. When we are able, we extend a scheme
that we fundamentally believe in. So what was said in 2004? We had Paul Hutchison
saying that Labour was “cementing in that State dependency rather than incentivising
individual responsibility.” For babies? Is that what he was implying? Judith Collins in
2004: “It is another example of this Government using taxpaye rs’ money to try to win
some votes.” Again, from babies? I am not entirely sure what she was trying to say.
I think the point that I am trying to make is that it is very easy to look back in
hindsight, but we are providing you the benefit of hindsight toni ght. I say to members
on that side of the Chamber that you have already acknowledged you were wrong 10
years ago. We are providing you with the benefit of the doubt to not make that mistake
again. You will one day reflect. We will read out again your quote s from tonight and
you will hang your heads when you realise how wrong you were. I urge this House to
pass the Parental Leave and Employment Protection (Six Months’ Paid Leave)
Amendment Bill tonight, to no longer let it sit on the Order Paper, and to do t he right
thing.

items.speaker: MIKE SABIN
items.text: I think the member Jacinda Ardern is quite
correct—things do change, absolutely. That is the nature of the beast. Positions certainly
do change. Polls change, leaders of political parties change, the global financial
conditions change, and the landscape in Canterbury changes, and that is pretty much
how it goes. Things do change, positions do change, and that is exactly the position that
New Zealand has found itself in in recent years.
What this Government has done, much to the criticism of people like Jacinda Ardern
and the Labour Party, and their friends over there, the Greens and New Zealand First, is
support those who are most vulnerable —support those who need it. On the one hand
those members have continued to vote against everything this Government has done to
grow the economy, while on the other hand they have criticised us for letting people, in
their view, fall through the cracks. I say tha t members cannot have it both ways. So the
member Jacinda Ardern is quite correct. Things do change.
For what it is worth, putting a figure of a matter of weeks —the difference between
National’s position of extending moderately paid parental leave and Labo ur’s position
in this bill, or the difference between having 14 weeks, 16 weeks, and 18 weeks and
19452 Parental Leave etc. (Six Months’ Paid Leave) Amdt Bill 23 Jul 2014
having 26 weeks —is not what we should be talking about, because the reality is that
children need their parents in their formative years. That is the case, re gardless of how
many weeks of paid parental leave exist. Sometimes that means that parents must be
prepared to make a sacrifice. The member Sue Moroney as a parent has, I am sure, done
that. Every parent in this Chamber knows that sometimes sacrifices must  be made.
Sometimes that means surviving on one income, not for 16 weeks, 18 weeks, or 26
weeks, but often for 5 years or for longer, because that is what children demand of good
parents. That is what good parenting is about. It is ensuring that those form ative years
are spent with the child.
So we can debate whether 16 weeks is where it should be or whether 26 weeks is
where it should be. I think there is actually a bigger debate to be had here about the fact
that New Zealand parents cannot expect that th ey can just go about their professional
working lives and not invest their time in their children, and then expect that they will
get the same results than if they had been willing to make the sacrifice and spend that
time at home with their children. Ulti mately, that is an important time for development
in a child’s life, and, yes, it is true that in spending that time with the children, many
parents will do it hard for a while. But in this modern era, when we look at, say, this
Government’s approach to su pporting families, even a $500 million package is
substantial. When we look at what we would consider to be the more financially
challenged or vulnerable families, for a family with two children that is earning
somewhere in the order of $50,000, it is esse ntially tax-neutral. It will receive from the
Government as much support as it will pay in tax.
In fact, actually, what the member Jonathan Young has said is quite right —actually,
more so. That seems to me to be quite unprecedented. Certainly when I was b ringing up
young children, I do not remember that to be the case. It is certainly the case that MMP
creates an environment where we see Labour Governments come up with lolly-scramble
ideas, and once families become reliant or dependent on a degree of suppo rt, it is very
hard to actually withdraw that support. That is not to say that to some extent there was
not some support needed in the first place, but what it is fair to say is that once people
are given an opportunity to have something that they do not n ecessarily need, they will
certainly want to hang on to that.
I am not so sure that MMP has been a particularly good electoral system for our
families, because in many ways what it has done is create a default position of: “What is
in it for me? What will the Government give me so that I can be a better parent?”. Well,
nothing. The Government cannot give anything to someone to be a better parent,
because being a better parent is not about defaulting to the Government. Being a better
parent is about making decisions that are in the best interests of that child.

items.speaker: KANWALJIT SINGH BAKSHI
items.text: Sat sri akaal, Mr Chair. Thank you
very much for the opportunity. We are debating clause 3 of the Parental Leave and
Employment Protection (Six Months’ Paid Leave) Amendment Bill.
I would like to start with the member opposite, Jacinda Ardern, who said that paid
parental leave was increased from time to time. I would like to remind her that i n 2007
the Families Commission gave a report to the Hon Ruth Dyson, then Minister of
Labour, in which it recommended that the paid parental leave provision be increased to
13 months by 2015, including a month for fathers. Labour chose to do nothing at that
time, and the recommendations were just kept aside. The Government at that time was
running in surplus, which is a very important point that the Opposition keeps reminding
us about —that it delivered nine Budgets in surplus. But did it consider these
recommendations? No, because Opposition members were not serious about them. They
want to take all the credit for what they have done, but what they have not done is think
23 Jul 2014 Parental Leave etc. (Six Months’ Paid Leave) Amdt Bill 19453
about the recommendations that were given by the Families Commission. They never
thought about those.
It is very important. We need to be responsible for our kids. I come from a culture
where we are totally responsible for our children. For example, I would like to share
with this Committee that I have got two sons, who are at the ages of 21 and 23—

items.speaker: Hon Christopher Finlayson
items.text: Far too young to have children that old.

items.speaker: KANWALJIT SINGH BAKSHI
items.text: No, no, they should not. They should wait for
some time. They are still living with me, and I am lookin g after them. It is not only me;
it is me and my wife. Both of us—

items.speaker: Hon Christopher Finlayson
items.text: Tell them to grow up.

items.speaker: KANWALJIT SINGH BAKSHI
items.text: I will talk to you about that later on. It is very
important th at parents be responsible for their children. I am not saying that the
Government should not look after kids. Vulnerable kids should be taken care of by the
Government, but the bulk of the responsibility should be on the parents. Parents have to
take that responsibility. They have to grow up and make sure they provide the best
facilities for their kids. There are cases where families are vulnerable and the kids are
vulnerable. The Government should come and pitch in with whatever they want to do. It
should help the families that cannot afford that.
It is a bit rich for Labour to take a stand on this now that it is in Opposition when it
had 9 years in Government to implement changes before the global economic crisis hit
the world. This Government has gone th rough tremendous financial constraints, and I
think that the leadership of the National Government has done very well. Now that it
will be affordable, the finance Minister is giving a 2 -week increase in paid parental
leave in the coming year, and a 2 -week increase later on. As the financial situation
improves for this economy, I think you will see further increases in these paid parental
leave subsidies to families. With these words I conclude my contribution.

items.speaker: KRIS FAAFOI
items.text: I move, That the question be now put.

items.speaker: MAGGIE BARRY
items.text: I rise to speak on the Parental Leave
and Employment Protection (Six Months’ Paid Leave) Amendment Bill in the name of
Sue Moroney. As we look at the principal Act, which is the purpose, of course, of
clause 3, we wonder really why we are here debating this one. The Budget that we
handed down in May has already dealt with a ll of this, so you are wasting the time of
the House. We have already moved into this space and taken ownership of it. Really
what we are looking at is the unaffordability of what has been proposed by the member
who is sponsoring this bill. In the very fir st reading—I remember it well—Ms Moroney
did indicate that she would like it expanded out from 26 weeks to over a year. You will
not stop at 26 weeks, and we cannot afford that as a country at this time. It is not
possible. She is nodding and smiling. So i t goes on. We go into a dark hole of
indebtedness over a very expensive, vote -buying element that you are trying to indulge
in. That is not in the best interests of the economy and of this nation. We have already
covered it.
I think there has been some kind of research through the archives and looking back in
Hansard on what other people have said and how, apparently, they have changed their
minds. The time is now better economically for us to be able to afford what we
proposed. The legislation that has be en changed in the Budget does allow for paid
parental leave. We have extended it out in a prudent and moderate fashion, which is all
we can afford at this stage. We cannot continue to borrow large sums of money to fund
unaffordable, election-grabbing things such as what this piece of legislation represents.
It really is not on. It has already been defeated. The Government Administration
Committee could not agree on it. There has been a lot of to -ing and fro -ing around
19454 Parental Leave etc. (Six Months’ Paid Leave) Amdt Bill 23 Jul 2014
things that might or might not be inclu ded in this bill. But really one wonders why it is
still before the House.
When we look at the principal Act of something like this bill, it is supposed to amend
the Parental Leave and Employment Protection Act 1987, but that has already been
done. We have already covered that off. Really, you need to move on. This may be the
last members’ day of the 50 th Parliament. There will be a lot that I can speak about
when we come to the fourth part of this. When we look at what this Government has
provided by exte nding the current 14 weeks out to 16 weeks —and that will be as of 1
April 2015—and then to 18 weeks as of 1 April 2016, then we are getting into territory
that is affordable, it is gradual, it is helping parents, it is helping children, and it is
helping families, which is what this John Key, National-led Government is all about.
We put families at the centre of our policies, which is why we spent $10.5 billion on
health. It is why we continue to invest in education and reach targets for early childhood
education. We are moving successfully to a stage where the economy can provide
families with the ability to get off the benefit. Something like 1,000 New Zealanders a
week are going off the benefit. They will be able to put their families, their children,
their households into a better state, into a better place, and remove them from poverty.

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: More jobs.

items.speaker: MAGGIE BARRY
items.text: More jobs, of course, as my colleague has pointed out. That is
also what we are providing with the economy.  It is incredibly important that we stay on
track. Bill English is a classic Minister of Finance with short arms and long pockets. He
has delivered two Budgets that have not thrown money wildly around. We are not about
that. This is not what this Government does. But what we do is we target the money that
is needed to the people that require it. The under -6s’ free general practitioner visits was
an important development. It worked so well that we have spent a further $90 million
and covered it off—

items.speaker: Tracey Martin
items.text: New Zealand First policy.

items.speaker: MAGGIE BARRY
items.text: Is there something wrong with the plumbing in the House?
There seems to be an inordinate squeaking noise. Perhaps there are chihuahuas loose in
the Chamber? It certainly sounds a  bit like it. There is a funny squeaking noise, which,
of course, is unintelligible. Even if we could hear it, it would not make any sense.
As far as we are concerned when we look at the Budget and the changes that we have
made, we are providing funding t o enable more pre -schoolers to attend quality early
childhood education. That is giving the best possible start in life. It is something that is
helping New Zealand’s most vulnerable. It is helping New Zealand children across the
board, and helping New Zea land families. We are rolling out eight more Children’s
Teams around the country to help protect our most vulnerable children from abuse. The
money that has been allocated in the Budget to sort out these historical sexual abuse
claims—those sorts of things —is really going to make a difference and send a clear
message to people who continue to perpetrate violence against women and children and
families. We are not about to let that happen. Judith Collins has done very good work in
this area. All of the entities, the ministries of Government, are working closely together.
That is another characteristic of this Government. We are able to work together with the
departments.

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: The member who has just resumed her seat, Maggie
Barry, asked a few questions, so I thought I would answer them. She asked the question:
“Why are we debating this?”. Well, it is for two reasons. I know they are not reasons
that she likes, but one is that this bill, the P arental Leave and Employment Protection
(Six Months' Paid Leave) Amendment Bill, has a parliamentary majority. This bill
defeats the Government. That is why we are here debating it. The majority of
parliamentarians in this precinct believe and know this is  the right thing to do. They
23 Jul 2014 Parental Leave etc. (Six Months’ Paid Leave) Amdt Bill 19455
know that it is, indeed, affordable. It is affordable, because this is an investment in our
children. There is no better investment that any Government can make than investing in
our children.

items.speaker: Maggie Barry
items.text: We’re already doing it.

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: That is reason one, Ms Barry, that we are here debating this.
Reason No. 2 is the National Government, for about a year now, has been trying to stop
the passage of the bill. It has been trying to stop it by doi ng exactly what people can see
its members doing tonight: filibustering and speaking on the bill for no other reason
than they want to stop it from passing. So those, Ms Barry, are the reasons why we are
here debating the bill. It is about democracy. The majority of parliamentarians—

items.speaker: Maggie Barry
items.text: You’ve been overtaken by events. It is no longer needed.

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: Can I remind Ms Barry that support partners of the Government
support this bill. It is clearly not unaffordable. T he previous Minister of Revenue for
this Government supports this bill. It is clearly not unaffordable. That is just a weak and
lame excuse for the National members, who cannot bring themselves to support children
and support families in this way. They are  completely wrong. They should be ashamed
of what they are doing this evening.

items.speaker: JONATHAN YOUNG
items.text: I think what we want to
probably make clear is that things are a  matter of balance, and when the sponsor of the
bill says that this Government does not support children or does not support families,
that is incorrect. We know, and she knows, that this Government introduced with the
Budget, and passed through all stages  into law on 16 May, legislation that increases the
number of weeks of paid parental leave from the current 14 weeks to 16 weeks as of 1
April 2015, and to 18 weeks as of 1 April 2016.
I think that the member she was referring to made a comment around aff ordability.
When I talk about balance and affordability, what we have to understand is that this
Government spends its money out of, essentially, a single bucket. So money we spend
in one area cannot be spent in another, and so we have issues. Last week, f or example,
the Hon Tony Ryall sent out a press release regarding people who need kidney
transplants. There are 600 on the waiting list in New Zealand, and we do a hundred a
year. So he has increased funding—

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: What’s this got to do with paid parental leave?

items.speaker: JONATHAN YOUNG
items.text: Yes, it does have something to do with paid parental leave,
because it has to do with the balance of funding that we seek to spread over the needs of
New Zealanders. We need to understand tha t when we say that some areas take too
much, it is not because there is a lack of concern; it is because there is also concern for
other areas where money needs to be spent. I think that is the rationale that we need to
understand when it comes to spending  the Government’s resources or the taxpayers’
funds.
So when the sponsor of the bill says that this Government does not care, I refute that.
What we are essentially saying is that her bill, though well intentioned, goes too far and
costs too much, because  it takes away money that needs to be spent in other areas of
desperate need for New Zealanders. So it is a matter of finding the balance. I think what
Mike Sabin has talked about and what I spoke about not long ago is that the balance
also around parental  responsibility needs to be considered, because as much as we
would like to make everything easy, we have got to understand that there is balance
needed.
I remember when parental leave legislation first went through —going back to the
principal Act in 1987 . I do not know about you, but I remember hearing Richard
Prebble speaking on the radio. I am not sure whether it was around this point in time,
but he said something about parenting that stuck with me all of these years.
19456 Parental Leave etc. (Six Months’ Paid Leave) Amdt Bill 23 Jul 2014
[Interruption] And he is one of th em, by the way. You know that. He said: “When it
comes to having children and you can’t afford it” —because that can be a relative thing,
for a start —“love your kids and enjoy them, even though there is going to be financial
pressure.” What he was saying, I  think, was that there is joy that comes with every
child. I think that we forget some of those great values.
I talked before about when I was brought up as a kid in South Taranaki on the farm
and out in the rural areas before I became a townie at the age  of 10. There were a lot of
things that we could not afford but we had a great life. You know, you think that you
can have a great life only if you have got all the support that comes from the
Government, and we do not believe in that. We believe that it i s appropriate to give
support where it is needed and where it is affordable, but sometimes when you go too
far you create other things that happen. Some of those things that happen are a lack of
community support and a lack of wider family support.
We have gone through our society with 14 weeks’ leave, and we have done that to
assist families who need to have a transition period when they can make decisions about
how they are going to manage financially —perhaps go back to work or, if not, then
make adjustments so their budget can cope. We have done all that. But now to extend it
out from 14 to 26 weeks—

items.speaker: DARIEN FENTON
items.text: I move, That the question be now put.
A party vote was called for on the question, That the question be now put.
Ayes 57
New Zealand Labour 34; Green Party 14; New Zealand First 7; Mana 1;

items.speaker: Independent
items.text: Horan.
Noes 63
New Zealand National 59; Māori Party 3; United Future 1.
Motion not agreed to.

items.speaker: TIM MACINDOE
items.text: I just want to point out to
anybody who may be listening that it is not the Government’s intention to drag out this
particular clause, clause 3, but, Mr Chair, you did just accept a closure motion when
only four members had spoken on this side of the Chamber, and there were other
members seeking the call.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: Nothing genuine about this speech!

items.speaker: TIM MACINDOE
items.text: I can assure Mr Little that this is going to be very genuine, and I
am happy to tell him why, if he would like to stop sounding like a foghorn and listen. A
number of Opposition claims have been made. He is clearly not interested in listening.
He is just going to filibuster from that side by preventing me from speaking.
First of all, I would like to acknowledge Sue Moroney’s husband, Shane, who is in
the gallery. I am sure it is a pleasure for her to have her husband here tonight. I do also
want to acknowledge that Sue has been incredibly lucky with members’ bills, because I
think she has had several drawn out in her time as a member. In my time here, I have
never had a single one drawn out. People who are listening may wonder. It is a little bit
like parliamentary lotto. If you get lucky, they get drawn out of the ballot.
I think there is an important point that does need to be made, and that is that the
members’ bills of the Opposition cannot be used to derail a Government’s Budget. It is
very important to remind every body who is listening that notwithstanding the very
narrow support for the Parental Leave and Employment Protection (Six Months’ Paid
Leave) Amendment Bill in the current Parliament of members, with the composition of
parties that are here, this bill has n ever been voted on by the New Zealand public. It has
23 Jul 2014 Parental Leave etc. (Six Months’ Paid Leave) Amdt Bill 19457
never been taken to the public for a mandate, and therefore it is a little bit rich for the
members opposite to claim the moral high ground on behalf of the 60 members of this
Parliament tonight who are voting for it, when 4.4 million New Zealanders have not yet
had a chance to vote on it. As I say, members’ bills of the Opposition cannot derail a
Government’s Budget, because a Government has to have the ability to budget for the
long term, to plan its fi scal strategy, and to work out how revenue and Government
spending can be organised in a responsible way to ensure that New Zealand taxpayers—
who, after all, will have to pay for anything that a Parliament commits expenditure to —
can afford it and that it has been factored in. This clearly had not been.
Even more important, it is worth nothing that in this year’s Budget there was $500
million of new spending for New Zealand families.

items.speaker: Kanwaljit Singh Bakshi
items.text: How much?

items.speaker: TIM MACINDOE
items.text: There was $500 million, and that did include an extension to
paid parental leave, and I was proud to support that. So I reject utterly any suggestion
that members on this side are not in favour of paid parental leave. We are, and we
demonstrated that with our Budget. We also broadened the scope with the extension of
the parental tax credit, which meant that more people qualify. Again, that is very
important, particularly for those at the bottom end of the scale, who most need support.
Thirdly—and it is allied to this —we have extended the opportunity for families in New
Zealand to access free doctors visits for children. Again, that is an important measure
that I am very proud of. So this is a family -friendly Government and that was a family -
friendly Budget, but this particular measure that we are debating tonight has not had the
endorsement of the New Zealand people.
I also just want to make a point about the accusation of filibustering because, boy,
that is rich. In my 6 years here I have list ened to the Opposition filibuster on the
Auckland governance bill to the point where there were 30,000 amendments tabled,
most of which wanted to change the date of commencement —30,000—and we had to
sit here all day on a Saturday listening to that nonsense . I heard the member whose
name this bill is in filibustering on the Royal Society bill, which was totally
uncontroversial. She had nothing of any value to say, nor did any of her colleagues. I
also heard them do the same thing on the Parana Park bill. If they would like me to talk
about the Parana Park bill, which was a wonderful little local measure for Hamilton, I
am happy to do so, but it would not be relevant. That is the sort of thing that they did —
talk irrelevantly. I point out that every member of t he Government who has spoken
tonight has dealt with the substantive nature of this bill. They have dealt with the issues
that arise from it, they have dealt with their responsibility to the taxpayer, and that is the
way it should be. That is not filibuster ing. That is responsible parliamentary debate, and
I am proud of my colleagues this evening.

items.speaker: TRACEY MARTIN
items.text: Kia ora, Mr Chair. Can I just compliment Mr
Macindoe on his contribution. Mr Ma cindoe is right, and Mr Macindoe is wrong. Mr
Macindoe is right that the Government has the ability to veto this bill because the
budget of it has not been worked out inside the Budget that those members placed in
front of the country. We know that. I thin k that what is most interesting, and probably
what the New Zealand public needs to understand, is that some of the frustration of the
Opposition is that we know that, Mr Macindoe. Your Government has that ability. Use
it. Do not continue this argument. Use  the veto—use the veto. Do not be so afraid with
regard to the election that is coming and the backlash that your party may receive from
the New Zealand people.
Where Mr Macindoe is wrong is that he said that there is no mandate from the New
Zealand people for this bill, and yet Mr Macindoe knows that like every other member’s
bill, it goes before a select committee and that the New Zealand public have just as
19458 Parental Leave etc. (Six Months’ Paid Leave) Amdt Bill 23 Jul 2014
much opportunity—and many, many took this opportunity on this bill; many more than
on other membe rs’ bills that have been out there —to put their voice into the
consultation process. Mr Macindoe knows that, so he knows that the New Zealand
public has had an opportunity to discuss this bill. Submission after submission after
submission was in favour of this bill.
Mr Macindoe and his party often use the fact that they have a mandate because they
are elected representatives of the country. They argue against having a binding citizens
initiated referendum on that basis, so they bring their voice, just as U nited Future brings
its voice. One might not like the deal they have now done with United Future because it
brought a vote to this House on the back of a deal with their Government, which it
chooses to use independently when the Government might not have w anted it to. It
might not suit Government members that the Māori Party, which they also did a deal
with to try to keep their Government going, chose to use its votes independently to
support this bill. But that does stand as a mandate under the arguments t hat National has
used before.
Mr Macindoe is an eloquent speaker —there is no doubt about it —and Mr Macindoe
is a good, honest, decent man, who loves his family and supports his electorate and who
actually believes in parents and children.

items.speaker: Mike Sabin
items.text: So do I.

items.speaker: TRACEY MARTIN
items.text: And Mr Sabin is not so bad, either. But let us get real. What
has been happening here is that the Opposition understands the position it is in. It
understands that the Government has the power of veto. Get on with it. If you are going
to veto the bill, veto it, and let the people of New Zealand see that and make their
decision when they go to the polls on the fact that you vetoed a bill that almost 100
percent of the submitters actually supported.

items.speaker: MAGGIE BARRY
items.text: When we look at the Parental Leave
and Employment Protection (Six Months’ Paid Leave) Amendment Bill and at the
purpose of this bill, we are really reminded that  this is not really fit for purpose. I have
mentioned that at other times, in my previous call, and I would like to draw attention to
what this Government has been doing instead in this space, which is a tremendous
thing. The work that we are doing in this space of allowing workers who have been with
their employer for more than 6 months but for less than a year to be entitled to some
form of unpaid leave is something that we are proud of.
I think it is important that we consult and that we are seen to be looking carefully at
what this country really needs: primary carers who provide permanent foster care akin
to adoption, such as Home for Life parents. People who have permanent guardianship—
that is, biological fathers and grandparents caring for grandchildren—need to be eligible
as well, as long as they meet the work test criteria, of course. A number of proposals
that we are putting together to modernise parental leave, which allow changes to allow
greater access and increased flexibility, are also available. We are taking submissions on
this through until about 25 August, and then we aim to have those in place by 1 April.
There are—

items.speaker: Tracey Martin
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Chairperson. Excuse me, but I am just
not sure what relevance the current speaker’s comments are having to the clause that we
are debating.

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: It is a point well made. I urge the
member to refer to clause 3, because that is what we are actually deb ating at the present
stage.

items.speaker: MAGGIE BARRY
items.text: Sure. Having said enough on clause 3, I will wait until clause 4
and devote my comments in more detail to that. Thank you very much.
23 Jul 2014 Parental Leave etc. (Six Months’ Paid Leave) Amdt Bill 19459
A party vote was called for on the question, That clause 3 be agreed to.
Ayes 60
New Zealand Labour 34; Green Party 14; New Zealand First 7; Māori Party 3;
Mana 1; United Future 1.
Noes 59
New Zealand National 59.
Clause 3 agreed to.
Clause 4  Purpose

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: I want to make a contribution on clause 4 because it is
the purpose clause of the Parental Leave and Employment Protection (Six Months’ Paid
Leave) Amendment Bill that we are about to debate, and I hope that members will stick
to that. Also, I wa nt to take a call because I think that those watching may be a little
tired of the moralising and the judgmental -type calls that are coming from the National
Party members about what good parenting is and what good parenting is not. I think I
would rather bring the debate back to making sure that there are choices for all families.
Opportunity and choice—

items.speaker: Mike Sabin
items.text: Rights and responsibilities—where does the measure lie?

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: —are what this bill is about, Mr Sabin. It is actually about
choices for families. It is not about requiring families to take paid parental leave. It is
not requiring families to have one of the parents in paid employment.
But the reality is that for most families these days, unless they are very, ve ry
wealthy, there is a need for both parents to be in paid employment. There is a range of
other things that we need to maybe address in our society. We need higher wages, for
example. That would be a good outcome, would it not, if we actually got the Nati onal
Party members to agree that higher wages were something that would be good to
resolve this issue? But no, they are actually spending their time making judgmental-type
contributions about parenting and what makes good parenting and what does not.
This bill is about choices. It is about choices for families. It is about the ability for
this country as a collective society to actually say that we want to invest in the future of
our society, that investing in children is a priority, and certainly within t he Labour Party
that is what we believe —that investing in children is a priority. We want the best, well -
rounded citizens of this country because we know that will actually give the brighter
future that the National Party members used to talk about. They have stopped it now but
they once talked about a brighter future. This bill is a practical measure to bring about
that brighter future that the National Party once believed in.
It is very sad to hear the National members’ speeches because I think that people will
hear them protesting far too loudly —far too loudly —that they do really actually quite
like children. Of course they like children! But if they really wanted to prioritise
families and children then they would be supporting this bill; they would not  be
speaking to try to stop it from having its votes. I agree with Tracey Martin that if the
Government really was going to be honest and authentic in its debate about this bill, it
would stop this silly nonsense of the filibuster and would let the bill pa ss, and then use
its financial veto. If Government members really believe they have a justified case for
saying it was unaffordable, then I ask them to use the financial veto. That is what it is
there for. I firmly believe that the Government has done this  and gone through all these
twists and turns to not use the financial veto because it knows that there is not the
financial justification for using it. The Government members know that in their heart of
hearts, and that is why they will not go down that track.
19460 Parental Leave etc. (Six Months’ Paid Leave) Amdt Bill 23 Jul 2014
I want to remind some of the speakers who have spoken on the previous clauses that
the bill does have public support. I say to Mr Macindoe that we know that because 96.4
percent of the submitters on this bill—and there were 3,800 of them—

items.speaker: Tim Macindoe
items.text: That is not a mandate.

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: “It’s not a mandate.” says Mr Macindoe. He is just running down
the whole system of democracy in this country. The select committee process brought
forward about 3,809 submitters, I think,  and 96.4 percent of them agreed with this bill,
as did a poll. The poll was not done by a political party. It was done, I think, by one of
the TV channels. It was of 1,000 people and it showed that even when the question was
put to them that it was going to cost $500 million, which it is not, by the way —even
then, with that amount of money being put into that loaded question, 63 percent of New
Zealanders said they wanted it. So this bill —and I know the National Party does not
want to hear this—does have wide public support in New Zealand. It has parliamentary
support. The only thing standing between families and 26 weeks’ paid parental leave is
the National Party.

items.speaker: Dr JIAN YANG
items.text: Ni hao, xiexi e. I rise to take a call on the Parental
Leave and Employment Protection (Six Months’ Paid Leave) Amendment Bill. As a
father of two I understand the importance of any support for families. Happy, stable
families are particularly important to the functioni ng of our society and to the quality of
life. Supporting families is a fundamental service that any Government should provide.
However, on the other hand, it is equally important that we manage our finances
responsibly and make sure that the Government does not overspend. In this context, this
bill is not balanced and it goes too far.
The National Government is committed to providing better services to New Zealand
families, including giving children the best possible start in life. That is exactly why our
Budget 2014 invests almost $500 million more in the well -being of New Zealand’s
children and families. Budget 2014 provides a comprehensive package of practical
measures, focused on young families and those vulnerable children who most need our
care and protection—for example, free general practitioner visits and free prescriptions
for children under 13; 4 weeks’ extra paid parental leave and extended to caregivers
other than parents; and an increase in the parental tax credit by $70 a week, to $220 a
week, and extended by 2 weeks to 10 weeks. The total fiscal cost of both the extension
of paid parental leave and the changes to the parental tax credit is more than $183
million over 4 years.
Additionally, we will be spending a further $30 million to increase p aid parental
leave eligibility, following a consultation process. Just this week this Government has
announced that parental leave payments will increase from 1 July 2014 to reflect the 3.3
percent increase in the average weekly wage over the past year. Th e maximum payment
for eligible employees and self -employed persons will increase from $488.17 a week to
$504.10 gross a week. The minimum parental leave payments for self -employed people
will also increase from $137.50 a week to $142.50 gross a week. The G overnment has
always said that it was prepared to extend paid parental leave, but in a way that is
affordable. When we could afford more, we would do more. That is exactly what we did
in Budget 2014. But Labour’s 26 weeks’ paid parental leave goes too far and it costs too
much.
National is focused on reasonably managing the Government’s finances. It is
important we get back to surplus  and get that under control. Countries with longer paid
parental leave entitlements than New Zealand’s include Portugal, Italy, Greece, and
Spain. We know what happened to those countries during the global financial crisis.
There is a real danger of runnin g up huge deficits, through unaffordable Government
spending. This bill is also poorly targeted. Bear in mind that only around 40 percent of
23 Jul 2014 Parental Leave etc. (Six Months’ Paid Leave) Amdt Bill 19461
families with newborns get paid parental leave. Labour’s policy is not targeted on need.
Twenty-six weeks’ paid par ental leave does not help a lot of the most vulnerable
children in New Zealand, who would benefit from much more targeted support and
services.
Progress reported.
Report adopted.

Economy—Credit Rating and Forecasts 
3. JOHN HAYES (National —Wairarapa) to the Minister of Finance : What 
recent reports has he received supporting the Government’s economic programme? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH (Minister of Finance) : Earlier this month the credit rating 
agency Fitch Ratings confirmed that it had revised New Zealand’s AA credit rating 
outlook from stable to positive. This indicates the credit rating’s likely direc tion over 
the next year or two. Fitch Ratings said that the Government’s fiscal consolidation and 
track to surplus in 2014 -15 are increasing the resilience of New Zealand’s sovereign 
credit profile, and it noted that the Government has a credible plan to l ift fiscal 
surpluses in the years ahead and to reduce net core Crown debt to 20 percent of GDP by 
2020. Fitch Ratings also said that New Zealand’s economic policy framework, business 
environment, and standards of governance ranked among the world’s stronge st from a 
credit perspective and warranted high-grade sovereign ratings. 
John Hayes : In confirming the positive outlook for New Zealand’s credit rating, 
what did Fitch Ratings say about New Zealand’s current and future economic growth 
prospects? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH : It noted that New Zealand’s macroeconomic record and 
prospects are supporting its credit rating. It said that real GDP grew by 2.7 percent in 
19382 Questions for Oral Answer 23 Jul 2014 
 
2013 and is expected to increase to 3.8 percent in 2014. This will be supported by, 
among other factors, reconstruction in Canterbury; dairy prices, which have moderated 
but are still at elevated levels; and a house -building catch-up. Fitch Ratings noted that 
although New Zealand’s average GDP growth over the past 5 years, a t 1.6 percent, is 
lower than the median among AA rated countries, it was less volatile and was higher 
than the 1.2 percent median growth rate among AAA rated countries. 
John Hayes : What other factors did Fitch Ratings note in respect of its po sitive 
ratings outlook for New Zealand? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH : One of the factors Fitch Ratings noted was New Zealand’s 
historical vulnerability around high net external debt and persistent current account 
deficits. I am pleased to report that  both of these indicators have improved significantly 
in recent years. For example, the unadjusted current account balance in the March 
quarter was a surplus of $1.4 billion —the largest dollar surplus ever recorded —and the 
annual 2.8 percent deficit is wel l under half the deficits of around 7 percent of GDP in 
the 3 years to 2008. So our net international liability position has improved. It was 65 
percent of GDP in March this year, well down from a recent peak of 85 percent of GDP 
in early 2009. 
John Hayes: And for my last question, what other reports has he received about the 
state of the New Zealand economy? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH : I have seen one report claiming that Government debt is 
larger as a percentage of GDP than New Zealan d had during World War II. This is 
completely false. Gross Government debt is currently around 35 percent of GDP. At the 
end of World War II it was around 150 percent of GDP. David Cunliffe has again 
completely misled New Zealanders.

TE URUROA FLAVELL (Co -Leader—Māori Party) : Speaking of individuals, 
not that  I do want to, I note that Colin Craig wants to be an MP, and Colin Craig 
introduced his latest attempt at a headline by calling it a wild and crazy idea. He is not 
wrong there. But more than that, the Conservative Party’s policies to get rid of the 
Māori seats, shut down the Waitangi Tribunal, and implement one law for all are 
ignorant, are dangerous, and are not welcome in the political system of our country. It is 
election time and once again political parties that are in trouble choose to pull the race 
card out of the hat to scratch the redneck part of our society. I can tell you that Māori 
are sick of it, as is this nation.  
Politicians have a responsibility to educate and inform, not act in such a way as to 
provoke racial division and tension. New Zeal and needs leaders who understand that 
indigenous rights are human rights, that cultural diversity and representation are good 
for democracy, and that the constitutional basis of our nationhood lies in Te Tiriti o 
Waitangi. I for one am proud to say that th is has been the consistent call of the Māori 
Party since we first entered this Parliament.  
We want all aspiring members of Parliament to understand that dedicated Māori 
electorate seats distinguish our democratic process here in Aotearoa. Actually, we mus t 
not forget that the first race -based law was introduced in 1858 and was called the 
English Laws Act. It was one single statute that imposed the culture, customs, and 
conventions of Britain on all New Zealanders. The Māori electorate seats are a 
conversation between Māori and the Crown —not for the majority of New Zealand 
making a decision for a minority.  
As the Chief Judge of our court Taihākūrei Durie said: “Like the Treaty of Waitangi, 
the Māori parliamentary seats stand as an enduring symbol of their c onstitutional 
status—and historic statements of principle, like symbols, are essential tools in re -
building our national identity.” Ever since the English Laws Act we have been in catch -
up mode, trying to build a more representative Parliament that encompa sses all New 
Zealanders, not just those with a British passport. The Māori seats have been an 
important mechanism to try to protect and develop Māori interests.  
Colin Craig needs to know that his party has no right —no right—to step in and try to 
take the rights away from tangata whenua. Only tangata whenua have the right to 
determine what is in our best interests. As parties to the Treaty, Māori should at least be 
guaranteed representation in the organs of kāwanatanga. In the past Labour tried 
measures lik e the Foreshore and Seabed Act, and it opposed the United Nations 
Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples —and look how that went down. We 
have been down that track before and we do not want a repeat run. The reality is that the 
19398 General Debate 23 Jul 2014 
 
New Zealand Governme nt, after advocacy from the Māori Party, signed up to the 
Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples in 2010 and it is here to stay.  
In fact, the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples states 
that indigenous peoples have the right to participate fully, if they so choose, at all levels 
of decision making in matters that affect their rights, lives, and destinies through 
representatives chosen by themselves in accordance with their own procedures. So we 
are where we should be, and  we should not have to put up with the divisive rants of

We have had over 170 years of attempts at assimilation, from various politicians and

today. The old assimila tion policy is hidden behind a few new terms and slogans, such 
as “one law for all”, or “we are all one people, we are all Kiwis”, and even “some of my

this day and age there is no place for political leaders who know nothing about our 
history and know nothing about us. There is no excuse for being ignorant and we, the 
people, will never ever tolerant policies that aim to take away from us, without our

Dr CAM CALDER (National) : Six years ago when I came into Parliament, some 
queried why. Why has he come in? Does Parliament need yet another doctor? When I 
announced my intention to step down, again some queried: “Why him? Surely some 
mistake? Parliament is losing too many of its doctors.” There was no talk, as far as I 
know, of McCully having any incriminating photographs.  
I have had many different roles in my life. Building roads, and a scrub -cutter in “the 
Naki”, Territorial Force soldier, dental surgeon, businessman and entrepreneur, medical 
doctor in accident and emergency, and a clinical research director for a private 
company—to name just a few. I have enjoyed them all. I have enjoyed them all, but at 
this point I would like to place on record that serving and working as a member of 
Parliament in New Zealand has been the best job that I have ever had. A huge amount of 
work, work of extraordinary variety, and I have relished every day! 
Though long viewing the prospect of life in the political milieu with the utmost 
distaste, I sought the chance to stand as a National candidat e in 2008 because I was 
extremely concerned about the future that my children would inherit if New Zealand 
continued down the track it was then on. Back in 2002, upon returning from living 
overseas with my family, I was shocked and disturbed at what I foun d in New Zealand. 
I was shocked and disturbed at the consequences for my children, and, indeed, all New 
Zealanders, if the myriad of challenges facing New Zealand was not addressed more 
comprehensively and more intelligently.  
As I saw it, I had three choices. I could return to live overseas, but I am a proud New 
Zealander, so that option did not appeal. I could stay and do nothing other than groan 
and grumble, but that did not appeal, because I believe that if one does not like 
something, one should do one ’s best to change it. The third option was to stay in New 
Zealand, to work to make it better, and to push my ideas for change on to the agenda. 
The choice was obvious —I joined the National Party. It was a huge pleasure to be 
selected to stand for National in the 2008 election in the vibrant and diverse community 
of Manurewa.

I have brooded about our inability as a society to be more generous of spirit and
