themselves to beat up on anybody who buggers up—that is a Papua New Guinean word. 
“So what?” you say. Well, I think the “what” is the question. Why would anybody

For more than 10 years the Wairarapa electorate has been trying to progress a couple

It is difficult to fathom why simple, sensible, straightforward concepts have become

ministry, my curiosity is satisfied. To those contemplating a political career, I will say

I think that economic and social progress in provincial New Zealand will happen

owes us a living. Those who think —and I am talking Wairarapa at the moment —that

Last week I did something that I had hoped to do for many a year, and that was to 
visit the whale -counting operation that occurs every year at this time in the Tory 
Channel and Cook Strait. Fortunately, on the day that we went out the obs ervers 
perched up on Tory Channel sighted a large humpback whale cruising through the Cook 
Strait on its way to the Tropics. We were able to just motor straight out there and watch 
these guys in their 4 -metre runabout in a 3 -metre swell dart the whale to t ake a DNA 
19418 Valedictory Statements 23 Jul 2014 
 
sample. Just to give you some understanding about how difficult it was, I could hardly 
hold my camera, my iPhone camera, to actually capture the moment to post it on 
Facebook. From the point of view of what has gone before us in history, in the context it 
was most uplifting. You could entitle the situation: “Whaling —from Decimation to 
Restoration”. These old ex -whalers are now spending endless hours looking into the 
mist of the Cook Strait to identify that pencil shape of a whale coming towards th em.

I want to make the point that although we may have a strong view on how people 
earned their living in years gone by, they did sustain themselves and we should neither 
condemn nor ridicule. Sure, the land -based whaling opera tions did not decimate the 
whales. The damage was done by the fleets of whaling vessels from other nations that 
hunted the whale to near extermination, taking up to 4,000 whales a year, year on year. 
However, I make the point because I personally have serious concerns, along with many 
others, about our attitude to sustainable management around the coastline. Today there 
are 10 times as many people out on the coastline collecting kai moana. The targeting of 
fish, the catching of crays, the taking of paua and  other delicacies has greatly improved, 
and yet we still argue that it is our birthright to help ourselves to such a resource.  
As rational human beings we know that continuing such a harvest of our kai moana 
will result in serious consequences for us toda y and for our future generations. It is 
therefore with much pride that I draw on the example of the community of Kaikōura, 
who over the last 8 years, based on the principles of gifts and giving, were able to reach 
an agreement across the full range of stak eholders: iwi, commercial fishers, recreational 
fishers, Forest and Bird, and the wider community. They were able to agree amongst 
themselves as to the best way possible of managing their coastline between the Conway 
River and the Clarence River. I was ama zed to witness the cooperation that existed on 
that group of Te Korowai people. It is with pride that I now look forward to this process 
of seeing the passing into law of the Kaikōura (Te Tai o Marokura) Marine 
Management Bill, which will enshrine the mana gement plan into law and protect it for 
the benefit of all Kaikōura and others who visit in the many years ahead.  
What made this achievement possible was that those involved, the community, 
clearly understood what was at stake. Local iwi —that is, Ngāti Kuri—led because they 
held the kaitiaki over the area, the commercial fishermen pulled in the same direction 
because they owned the quota and they knew what sustainable management was all 
about, and the wider community stuck to the task because they knew a nd valued the 
employment and they valued their environment. There is no doubt in my mind that this 
situation is going to have to be replicated throughout New Zealand. Such iconic places 
as the Marlborough Sounds, the Hauraki Gulf, the Wellington headlands,  Bay of Plenty, 
and the Northland coastline —to name but a few —will need to address this situation as 
pressure remains and grows. Again, it will require skilful leadership, a willingness to 
agree and make those gifts and giving. We must face up to the chall enge, otherwise we 
will end up in exactly the same position as those whalers who lost their careers, their 
opportunities, and their profitability overnight because of a culture of greed and a race 
to catch the last whale.  
My second point that I would like  to make is the importance of hands -on learning 
within our education system. We must appreciate these very important students who, in 
the future, will continue to fix things, build things —be it trucks, be it motorcars, be it 
buildings, be it bridges, be it roads, be it essential infrastructure, and all other manner of 
things. To do this, the education system must equally value these people as we do 
23 Jul 2014 Valedictory Statements 19419 
 
doctors, nurses, lawyers, and accountants, and design an education curriculum 
accordingly. I just put it out here in very plain terms. To put it simply, we want to create 
many Einsteins, but to create an Einstein you need to also have 1,000 skilled technicians 
to be able to make those things.  
I wish to mention two people by name at this time. It is always dangero us doing that, 
but two people have had a big effect on my policy development. Firstly, Stuart 
Middleton, from the Manukau Institute of Technology, who when I first came into 
Parliament was already talking about what was lacking within our education system.  He 
has gone on to do some wonderful things around empowering youth, especially Pasifika 
youth. I take the opportunity here to say how heartened I am to see the Pasifika people 
taking grasp of education and being aspirational. I also want to make mention o f 
Stewart Thompson, who worked with me in developing the trades academy policy, 
which was introduced by the Government in 2009. Stewart Thompson convinced me 
that the passion of an inspiring teacher is what makes the difference. Stewart’s 
technology classe s were full to overflowing, and total engagement with education 
existed in spades.  
I ask those responsible for education in the future to maintain the momentum we 
have for hands -on learning and skills -based education. Education must be relevant to 
the lea rners for them to remain engaged and to develop the skills necessary to be 
successful in life, and that is a pretty high threshold. We must keep them engaged. We 
are beginning to do better, but there is a lot of work we need to do yet.  
The third point I w ant to leave with the House is my concern around a growing 
reluctance in this country —and this is my observation —to undertake physically 
demanding work. We should be concerned when we see those who want to continue 
living in one location and are not willin g or courageous enough to collect up their 
families and move to where employment is better and more available, where the cost of 
living is less and the price of providing a roof over one’s family’s head is also less. New 
Zealand has one of the most generou s welfare systems in the world. However, for New 
Zealand to remain a First World country, we must possess the attitude as stated by 
George St John and restated by President J F Kennedy: “Ask not what your country can 
do for you; ask what you can do for you r country.”—that it is good to create wealth and 
seek ownership.  
I admire greatly those Eastern European families who came here in the 1950s and 
1960s. I was only a child at the time. They made New Zealand their home and they 
started afresh after experien cing the Second World War, the Cold War, and the Iron 
Curtain. It now concerns me that we do bring enthusiastic workers from the Pacific 
Islands to do the harvesting and cultivation within the horticultural sector and that we 
need to bring thousands of wor kers to fill the needs of the dairy industry. Is it not 
blindingly obvious to all that in doing the work that some of us despise, these 
newcomers end up creating wealth for themselves and their families to enjoy into the 
future? It is all symptomatic of a nation that is losing its way when a newcomer can 
come here and see opportunities that we cannot. Individually, we hold the key to our 
own success: careful living and good, honest, hard work. Personal responsibility and a 
desire to aspire should be the aim  of us all. Lose this and we become no better than a 
domesticated animal. 
Sir Henry Maine, speaking on social structure, put it well when he said: “Nobody is 
at liberty to attack private property and to say at the same time that he values 
civilisation. The  history of the two cannot be disentangled.” For the institution of 
private property has been a wonderful institution for teaching man and woman 
responsibility, for providing motives to integrity, for supporting general culture, for 
raising mankind above t he level of mere drudgery, for affording leisure to think and 
19420 Valedictory Statements 23 Jul 2014 
 
freedom to act. To be able to retain the fruits of one’s labour, to be able to see one’s 
work made manifest, to be able to bequeath one’s property to one’s posterity, to be able 
to rise from the  natural condition of grinding poverty to the security of enduring 
accomplishment, to have something that is really one’s own —there are advantages with 
this difficult to deny.” In drafting policy and bringing forth legislation in this House, 
may all members continue to recognise the value of those who toil in the sun or labour 
under the tin roof, neither despising the value of that work or thinking that it is beyond 
one’s dignity, because the wealth of this nation was created on the back of physically 
demanding labour.  
In conclusion, may I express my sincere thanks to all members of the House for the 
courtesy that they have accorded me. Thank you too for the joy of working for the best 
interests of all New Zealanders, particularly in the primary sector and in the science and 
education sector, while in Parliament. I am sure, though, that those who are coming 
behind us will be more than equal to the task. We do live in a blessed land.  
To the parliamentary sporting trusts, what fun we had in raising money for the most 
worthy of causes, and in the camaraderie of winning two Parliamentary Rugby World 
Cups—one in Paris and the other in New Zealand. There was also the pleasure of 
coordinating the parliamentary and diplomats’ annual cricket challenges, and winning a  
few. That was quite good. I always remember Paul Swain leaving the House, having 
won that year against the diplomats. That having been said, we have not won for many 
years, for about a decade. I am asking the House to make sure that they support Ian 
McKelvie as he carries on the mantle of looking after the shield and keeping that cricket 
match going. It has been going for over 40 years, and it is actually quite an illustrious 
shield with some great MPs’ names on it.  
If I have one disappointment in leaving Parliament, Mr Speaker, it is possibly one we 
share together. It is that wisdom has not prevailed when it has come to storing water in 
North Canterbury. Sadly —and this again is my observation, because I know that some 
of my Green colleagues would disagree —it is my view that a dog in a manger attitude 
still prevails, making progress slow and difficult.  
Finally, I wish to thank the taxpayers of New Zealand for providing the funding for 
three new hospitals while I was MP in the electorate of Kaikōura. I am also delighted to 
have witnessed, as MP, the Te Tau Ihu Treaty settlement situation that has provided 
eight iwi with their settlements, which will restore their economic base into the future, 
and also to being a witness to, and being part of, the 8 years’ labour of love —the 
management of the Kaikōura coastline, the result of which is the bill I have here, under 
a pile of papers. I look forward to it being put through the House completely by the time 
the House rises. I thank the Minister of Conservation and I also thank the Leader of the 
House for putting that in place. We are very satisfied with everything that is going 
forward.  
Just to conclude, for the most part, from my own point of view what is most 
satisfying is the momentum that has been achieved arou nd education—the importance 
that has been put on the hands-on learning situation. Education is relevant. It needs to be 
relevant. If it is not relevant, you will have disengagement.  
I want to thank everybody for the situation that I have enjoyed over the last 9 years. I 
acknowledge my wife and children. I acknowledge those people who have travelled 
across the Cook Strait. I acknowledge those people who are supporting departing 
members. I also acknowledge all the members in the House. We have worked in the 
very best interests of New Zealand. Kia kaha. Stand tall. Be proud. Thank you very 
much. 
Hon CHRIS TREMAIN (National —Napier): In life there are many different 
definitions of succe ss, and in Parliament the same goes. There are many different

definitions of what makes a successful politician. Nine years ago I entered Parliament,

changed too much. I ha d just won the Labour -held seat of Napier, the first time in 50 
years, and I thought I had been pretty successful at that point in time. But like all 
politicians across this House, I entered this place with the intention of helping to create 
a better New Z ealand. We all have the same purpose, just different ideas of how we 
might achieve that goal. But success in Parliament is not defined by just winning a seat 
or becoming a Cabinet Minister. Success comes with many different faces. 
I recall in my first year  a gym session with Rodney Hide —you might not want to

successful politician. “You’ve got to take scalps.” was Rodney’s advice, as he sweated

have reflected on these words of sage advice.

experience. It is definitely not for the faint -hearted, that is for sure. The fact of the

Dr JIAN YANG (National) : Ni hao, xiexi e. I rise to take a call on the Parental 
Leave and Employment Protection (Six Months’ Paid Leave) Amendment Bill. As a 
father of two I understand the importance of any support for families. Happy, stable 
families are particularly important to the functioni ng of our society and to the quality of 
life. Supporting families is a fundamental service that any Government should provide. 
However, on the other hand, it is equally important that we manage our finances 
responsibly and make sure that the Government does not overspend. In this context, this 
bill is not balanced and it goes too far. 
The National Government is committed to providing better services to New Zealand 
families, including giving children the best possible start in life. That is exactly why our 
Budget 2014 invests almost $500 million more in the well -being of New Zealand’s 
children and families. Budget 2014 provides a comprehensive package of practical 
measures, focused on young families and those vulnerable children who most need our 
care and protection—for example, free general practitioner visits and free prescriptions 
for children under 13; 4 weeks’ extra paid parental leave and extended to caregivers 
other than parents; and an increase in the parental tax credit by $70 a week, to $220 a 
week, and extended by 2 weeks to 10 weeks. The total fiscal cost of both the extension 
of paid parental leave and the changes to the parental tax credit is more than $183 
million over 4 years. 
Additionally, we will be spending a further $30 million to increase p aid parental 
leave eligibility, following a consultation process. Just this week this Government has 
announced that parental leave payments will increase from 1 July 2014 to reflect the 3.3 
percent increase in the average weekly wage over the past year. Th e maximum payment 
for eligible employees and self -employed persons will increase from $488.17 a week to 
$504.10 gross a week. The minimum parental leave payments for self -employed people 
will also increase from $137.50 a week to $142.50 gross a week. The G overnment has 
always said that it was prepared to extend paid parental leave, but in a way that is 
affordable. When we could afford more, we would do more. That is exactly what we did 
in Budget 2014. But Labour’s 26 weeks’ paid parental leave goes too far and it costs too 
much.  
National is focused on reasonably managing the Government’s finances. It is 
important we get back to surplus  and get that under control. Countries with longer paid 
parental leave entitlements than New Zealand’s include Portugal, Italy, Greece, and 
Spain. We know what happened to those countries during the global financial crisis. 
There is a real danger of runnin g up huge deficits, through unaffordable Government 
spending. This bill is also poorly targeted. Bear in mind that only around 40 percent of
